Excel

Follows Data Visualisation All 6 scripts ready

Excel comes after Python on purpose, and that changes what the module is about. They already know every concept in it — mean, median, outliers, grouping, correlation, charts. Nothing here is new statistics. What is new is a grid, a formula bar, and a tool that recalculates itself the moment a cell changes. Six sessions, because the mechanical surface is real: the lookup family and pivot tables are a full session each, and those two are what a fresher analyst interview actually asks about. Every session runs on employees.csv — the same file they have had since statistics day 1, which is why day 1 opens with the fifty-two lakh salary sitting on row 5 where anybody can see it.

What this module deliberately does not teach, so you can say so when asked. No macros and no VBA — it is a programming language, they already have a better one, and no fresher job asks for it. No Power Query, because Power BI does the same job in the next module and does it better. No array formulas. No OFFSET or INDIRECT.

What that time buys instead is a full session on the lookup family and a full session on pivot tables, which are the two things an interviewer will actually reach for. Day 1 also spends eighteen minutes on the dollar sign alone, because it is the one mistake in Excel that produces two hundred wrong rows and no error message.

All six run on the same 200 rows, on purpose. By session six they know the file well enough to see when an answer is wrong — which is the only reason the module's mistakes are visible at all. Five of the six sessions are caught out by the same two blank salaries, and the 52-lakh earner breaks something in four of them.

If only one thing lands

df["dept_id"].mean() returns 2.32. Valid arithmetic, meaningless answer — there is no average department. Everything tomorrow builds on that absurdity. Do not rush past it.

This session has now been delivered. The recording runs 78 minutes and the running order was: import and pandas → dictionary → head → columns → statistics intro → descriptive and inferential → DataFrame → loc → read_csv → tail → shape → info → describe → std → median → value_counts → groupby. The descriptive-versus-inferential explanation was correct — “descriptive means you are sure, inferential means you are assuming” — and the value_counts framing (“you cannot take the mean of a department, but you can count them”) already lands the day 2 hook. Four functions were missed; they are listed in the function section below.

Before you walk in

  1. Open a terminal and run every command in this script once. Twenty minutes. It is the difference between demonstrating and discovering live.
  2. Have employees.csv in the folder you will run Python from. Check with import os; os.getcwd().
  3. Write the board blocks up before anyone arrives (below).
  4. Have the file open in a spreadsheet too, minimised. When someone cannot picture a DataFrame, showing them the same file as a grid takes ten seconds and settles it.

Open, and set the room up

Establish who you are, name the mixed levels honestly, and give the sprint an end date. Six minutes, no code.

Stand away from the laptop. Nothing on screen yet.

Good morning, everyone. Before we start on today's content, two minutes on what is happening with these sessions, because some of you are wondering.

I am taking over the sessions from here. I have gone through everything that has been covered with you so far — all of it — so I know where you have reached. But I was not in the room for those sessions. So if I repeat something you have already done, tell me and I will move on. And if I assume something you have not covered, tell me faster, because that one is worse.

Second thing. There are two batches sitting in this room today. Some of you finished Pandas already. Some of you started NumPy last week and have not touched Pandas at all. I know that, and it is fine.

Here is how we handle it. Today I am going to teach eight commands. That is all. Eight. If you already know them, you will find today easy, and I am going to use you — you will be coaching the person next to you in the last fifteen minutes. If you have never seen them, by the end of today you will have used every one of them at least once.

And for the next six days, the July batch has one extra session each day to close the gap on NumPy and Pandas. From day seven, everybody is on exactly the same page and there are no extra sessions. Six days. There is an end date.

Say the date out loud. People work harder for a sprint that finishes than for a gap that might go on forever. The June batch also needs to hear why some of this week will feel like revision to them.

Now, today's actual subject. We are starting statistics. And I want to start by telling you what statistics is for, because if I open with formulas you will write them down and never use them again.

Transition: walk to the board, put your hand on the two lines you wrote before class, and go straight into the next block.
6 – 18

What statistics actually is

Install the descriptive / inferential split. Twelve minutes, still no code. This is the spine of the next ten sessions and it cannot be rushed.

Suppose you join a company on Monday as a data analyst. Your manager walks over and says: what is the average salary in this company?

What do you do? You open the employee file, you find the salary column, you add it all up and divide by how many people there are. Done. Fifteen seconds.

Now — is that answer certain? Could anybody argue with it?

Wait for someone to say no. If nobody does, ask directly: "Could I check your answer and get something different?"

No. It is exact. You had every single employee in that file, you did the arithmetic, and there is no argument to have. That is called descriptive statistics. You are describing data that you actually have in front of you.

Now the manager comes back and asks a second question: what is the average salary of every data analyst in India?

Stop and think about that one. Where is that file?

Genuinely pause here. Let the room work out that the file does not exist.

There is no file. Nobody has it. There is no database anywhere containing the salary of every analyst in this country, and there never will be. That number exists in reality — every analyst has a salary, so an average exists — but nobody can compute it.

And yet companies decide what to pay you based on that number. Salary surveys publish it every year. Job sites quote it. So how do they get it?

They ask a few thousand people. And from those few thousand, they make a careful claim about the whole country. That is inferential statistics — using the data you have to say something about the data you do not have.

And notice what has to change when you do that. The first answer was exact. The second answer can never be exact. It comes with a range, and a level of confidence, and a chance of being wrong. Learning to state that honestly is most of this course.

Point at the two lines on the board and read them out.

Descriptive: summarise the data you have. Inferential: make a claim about data you do not have.

These ten sessions walk from the left of that board to the right. Roughly the first half is descriptive — we get very good at describing what is in front of us. Then we cross over, and everything after that is about making claims under uncertainty.

Ask: "An exit poll on election day — descriptive or inferential?"
Inferential. They asked maybe twenty thousand people and made a claim about six hundred million voters. If someone says descriptive, ask them: "did they ask everybody?" That usually settles it.
Follow up: "The final result declared by the Election Commission — which one?"
Descriptive. Every vote was counted. That is a census, not a sample — and it is why the final result has no margin of error while the exit poll does. This pair is the cleanest illustration you have; use both.

One more thing before we touch a keyboard. Notice that the difference is not the amount of data. If I count all six hundred million votes, that is still descriptive — enormous, but descriptive. If I survey four hundred people and make a claim about ten million, that is inferential with a tiny dataset.

The difference is the claim you are making, not the size of the file. Hold onto that, because students get this wrong every year.

Transition: "Right. Now let us look at some actual data, because everything I just said is abstract until you see a table." Sit down at the laptop.
18 – 30

What a DataFrame is

Get the July batch from dictionaries to DataFrames. The June batch watches and is given something specific to look for. Twelve minutes.

Everything we do for the next three months happens inside one library, called Pandas. So let us start there.

For those of you who have not used it — Pandas gives you one thing, and that thing is a table. Rows and columns, exactly like a spreadsheet, except it lives in memory and you talk to it with code instead of a mouse. That table is called a DataFrame.

And the good news for the July batch is that you already know how to build one, you just do not know it yet. You have done dictionaries. Watch.

Type this
import pandas as pd

data = {
    "name":   ["Ramesh", "Mahesh", "Suresh"],
    "salary": [50000, 60000, 55000],
    "dept":   ["Sales", "Tech", "Sales"]
}

df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df)
What appears
name salary dept 0 Ramesh 50000 Sales 1 Mahesh 60000 Tech 2 Suresh 55000 Sales

Look at what happened. I gave it a dictionary — keys on the left, lists on the right — and it gave me back a table. The keys became the column headings. The lists became the columns.

That is the whole idea. A dictionary of lists is almost a table already. Pandas just makes it official and gives you a few hundred useful functions on top.

Pandas commands taught in this block
import pandas as pd
Loads the library. pd is the universal nickname — every tutorial, every answer on the internet uses it. Do not invent your own.
pd.DataFrame(dict)
Builds a table from a dictionary. Every list must be the same length, because they are becoming columns of one table and a table cannot have ragged columns.
print(df)
Displays it. In a notebook you can just type df on its own and it renders nicer.

One thing to notice, because somebody always asks. See that column on the far left with 0, 1, 2? I did not create that. Pandas added it.

That is called the index. It is the label for each row. If you do not give Pandas labels it just numbers them from zero. For now, that is all you need to know about it — it is a name tag on each row.

Do not go further into the index. loc versus iloc is a full block on another day and it will derail you here.
Then, so nobody is guessing
type(df)              # pandas.core.frame.DataFrame
type(data)            # dict

Different types. The dictionary is still a dictionary. Pandas made a new object out of it.

Now — June batch. You have seen all of this. Do not switch off, because I want you watching for something specific. In about twenty minutes I am going to run one command, and that single command is going to contain the entire syllabus for the next ten sessions. See if you spot it before I tell you.

That line genuinely keeps the experienced half engaged. It costs nothing and it stops them opening their phones.
Transition: "But nobody types data by hand. Real data arrives as a file. So let us open a real one."
30 – 42

Load the file, and look at it

Teach the four-command first-look ritual, arriving at dtypes — which sets up the session's punchline. Twelve minutes.

This is a file of two hundred employees from a company. I did not clean it. It is the kind of thing that actually lands in your inbox.

And I want to start with a rule that sounds obvious and that almost nobody follows. When a new dataset arrives, the first thing you do is not analysis. It is looking.

You would not sign a contract without reading it. Do not analyse a file you have not looked at. There are four commands, you run them in the same order every single time, and it takes about twenty seconds.

Type this — slowly, one line at a time
df = pd.read_csv("employees.csv")

df.head()

First command. read_csv, and the name of the file in quotes. That is it — the whole file is now in memory as a table.

Second, head. That gives you the first five rows. Why five? Because somebody who wrote Pandas decided five was a sensible default. You can ask for ten by putting ten in the brackets.

And look at what you learn in one second. What the columns are called. What kind of thing is in them. Whether the file loaded correctly at all. If you had the wrong separator, or the header row was wrong, you would see it here immediately.

Then
df.shape        # (201, 12)
df.columns
df.dtypes

shape gives you two hundred and one rows, twelve columns. Rows first, then columns — always that order, and you will use this constantly to check that an operation did what you expected.

Now notice something. head had brackets. shape does not. That is not a typo and it is not random.

Write on the board: brackets = it does something · no brackets = it already knows something. Leave it there for the rest of the module.

head() has brackets because it goes and does a job for you — it fetches rows. shape has no brackets because it is just a fact the table already knows about itself, sitting there waiting to be read.

You will get this wrong for about a week and then never again. If you type df.shape() you will get an error saying a tuple is not callable, and now you know what that means.

Pandas commands taught in this block
pd.read_csv("f.csv")
Reads a comma-separated file into a DataFrame. If the path is wrong you get FileNotFoundError — the most common error of today.
df.head(n)
First n rows, default 5. Has brackets — it does something.
df.tail(n)
Last n rows. Worth running too — junk and total rows hide at the bottom of files.
df.shape
A tuple of (rows, columns). No brackets — it is a stored fact.
df.columns
The column names. Useful when you cannot remember the exact spelling.
df.dtypes
The type of each column. object means text; int64 and float64 mean numbers.
Now the fourth one
df.info()

info gives you the types and something more valuable — how many values are actually present in each column.

Look at the age column. Two hundred non-null. And shape just told us there are two hundred and one rows. So one age is missing. Look at salary — a hundred and ninety-nine. Two salaries missing.

That subtraction is how you find missing data. You do not need a special command. Compare the count in info against the row count in shape, and the gap is your missing values.

Now the turn. Slow down, and change your tone — the next ninety seconds are the point of the whole session.

Right. Come back to dtypes for a second. I want you to look at one column.

There is a column called dept_id. Department ID. One for Sales, two for Tech, three for HR, four for Marketing. And Python has looked at it and decided it is int64 — a number.

So let me treat it like a number.

Type this
df["dept_id"].mean()
2.3233830845771144
Say nothing for a beat. Let it sit on the screen.

Two point three two.

The average department in this company is two point three two.

Now — what is two point three two? Sales is one. Tech is two. HR is three. What is two point three two? Is it a department? Can I go and sit in it?

Ask: "Did Python do anything wrong here?"
No. It was handed a column of numbers and asked for an average, and it computed one perfectly. The arithmetic is flawless. Push until someone says this out loud, because the next sentence depends on it.

Python did nothing wrong. It cannot tell the difference between a number that measures something and a number that is just a label. To Python, one two three four is one two three four.

The mistake was mine. I asked a meaningless question and got a meaningless answer, and nothing warned me. There was no error. No red text. Just a confident, useless number that I could have put straight into a report.

Knowing which columns you are allowed to average is your job. Not the computer's. And that sentence is the whole of tomorrow's session.

Ask: "Give me another column in this file where the mean would be meaningless."
emp_id — the average employee ID is 1100.1, which identifies nobody. If someone offers join_date, that is a thoughtful answer worth two minutes: you can average dates and it occasionally makes sense, but it is rarely what anyone wants.
Transition: "Hold that thought. I am going to show you one more command, and June batch — this is the one I told you to watch for."
42 – 58

describe() — the whole module in one line

The centrepiece. Sixteen minutes: reveal the summary, hunt two real bugs with it, and plant the mean-versus-median question that Day 3 answers.

Type this
df.describe()
The two columns to talk about
age salary count 200.0 199.0 mean 38.2 95648.4 std 16.6 364031.9 min -4.0 33085.0 25% 28.0 59003.5 50% 37.0 68647.0 75% 47.0 80599.5 max 210.0 5200000.0

June batch — this is the one. This single command is the syllabus for the next ten sessions, already computed, sitting on the screen.

Let me read it to you, top to bottom, and tell you which session each row belongs to.

Count. How many values are actually there. Two hundred ages out of two hundred and one rows. A hundred and ninety-nine salaries. That is missing data, and handling it is a session on its own.

Mean. The average. Day three is built on this row — and on when it lies to you.

Std. Standard deviation. How spread out the values are. Same day — day three covers centre and spread together, because you should never report one without the other.

Min and max. Smallest and largest.

Twenty-five per cent, fifty per cent, seventy-five per cent. Those are the quartiles. The fifty per cent row is the median. Those three plus min and max are called the five-number summary, and that is day four.

So you have not learned statistics yet. But you are already reading it. Every number in this output is a topic we are going to spend ninety minutes on.

Now stop teaching and start hunting. Change posture — lean in at the screen as though you are inspecting it for the first time.

But before all that, this output does something more immediately useful. Look at the age column. Just look at it for a moment and tell me if anything is wrong.

Wait for them to find it. Do not point.
Minimum age −4. Maximum age 210. Somebody will spot one of them within about fifteen seconds. If nobody does after thirty, say "look at the minimum" and wait again. Do not tell them. Finding it themselves is worth ten times being shown.

Minus four years old. And two hundred and ten years old.

Now think about what just happened. I did not write a loop. I did not write a filter. I did not inspect two hundred rows by hand. I typed one command on a file I had never opened and it handed me two data quality problems.

That is why you look before you analyse. If you had gone straight to computing the average age, you would have got a number, it would have looked fine, and it would have been wrong — and nothing would have told you.

Then the salary column — a different kind of problem
df["salary"].mean()      # 95648
df["salary"].median()    # 68647

Same column. Same hundred and ninety-nine people. And two completely different answers about what a normal salary looks like here.

Ninety-five thousand, or sixty-eight thousand. The gap is twenty-seven thousand rupees — the first number is thirty-nine per cent higher than the second.

So if your manager asks what people earn at this company, which one do you say? Because one of these two numbers is lying to you, and you need to know which.

Do not answer it. Write both numbers in the corner of the board. This is Day 3's opening and it works far better if it has been hanging in the air for two days.

I am not going to tell you today. Look at the maximum salary in that output though — fifty-two lakh. Keep that in the back of your mind and we will come back to it.

Ask the June batch: "When you handled missing salaries, you were told to fill with median rather than mean. Anybody remember why?"
Whoever answers has taught day three for you. It also hands the experienced half a moment of expertise in front of the new half, which is exactly what you want in a merged room. If nobody remembers, say "you will by Thursday" and move on.
Pandas commands taught in this block
df.info()
Column names, types, and non-null counts. Compare against shape to find missing data.
df.describe()
Eight summary statistics for every numeric column. Numeric only by default — pass include="object" for the text columns.
Transition: "That was all eight numbers at once. Now let me show you how to ask for them one at a time, because that is what you will actually do most days."
58 – 70

One column, and five numbers from it

Teach column selection and the individual statistics. Reinforce that text columns take different tools. Twelve minutes.

Everything so far worked on the whole table. Most of the time you want one column. Here is how you pull one out.

Type this
df["salary"]

Square brackets, and the column name in quotes. That is the pattern, and you are going to type it ten thousand times.

What comes back is one column with the row labels attached. Pandas calls that a Series. A DataFrame is the whole table; a Series is a single column out of it. That is the only distinction you need today.

And once you have a column, you hang a dot on the end and ask it for things.

Type these one at a time, saying each out loud
df["salary"].mean()      # 95648.4   the average
df["salary"].median()    # 68647.0   the middle value
df["salary"].std()       # 364031.9  how spread out
df["salary"].min()       # 33085.0
df["salary"].max()       # 5200000.0

Notice these are the same numbers describe already gave us. Nothing new has been computed. describe is a convenience that runs all of them at once — but when you want one number to put in a variable, this is how you get it.

The pattern is always the same. Table, square brackets, column name, dot, what you want. Say that with me once.

Genuinely have them say it. In a mixed-level room, a shared phrase gives the July batch something to hold onto when they lose the thread later.
Then quantiles
df["salary"].quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
0.25 59003.5 0.50 68647.0 0.75 80599.5

Quantile takes a list of positions between zero and one. Nought point five is the median. Nought point seven five means the value that seventy-five per cent of people are below.

Read those three numbers as a sentence: half this company earns between fifty-nine thousand and eighty thousand six hundred. That is a much more useful statement than any single average, and it is one line of code.

Now a text column
df["department"].value_counts()
Sales 65 Tech 49 HR 45 Marketing 42

For text you cannot ask for a mean. What you ask for is how often each value appears, and that is value_counts.

Sixty-five people in Sales, forty-two in Marketing. One line, and you know the shape of the organisation.

Now watch what happens if I forget which kind of column I am dealing with.

Break it on purpose
df["department"].mean()
This raises a TypeError. Let the red text sit on screen. Do not scroll past it.

There is the error. Pandas refuses, because you cannot average the words Sales and Tech.

But hold on — twenty minutes ago I averaged dept_id and it worked perfectly. Same information. Departments. One version errors and one version hands me two point three two.

The only difference is that one was stored as words and one was stored as numbers. When it is words, Pandas protects you. When somebody has coded it as one two three four, nothing protects you at all.

That is the trap, and tomorrow we learn the rule that gets you out of it.

Pandas commands taught in this block
df["col"]
Pulls out one column. What comes back is a Series.
.mean() .median() .std()
Average, middle value, spread. Numeric columns only.
.min() .max()
Smallest and largest. These do work on text — alphabetically.
.quantile([...])
Pass a list of positions from 0 to 1. 0.5 is the median.
.value_counts()
Counts each distinct value. The tool for text columns. Add normalize=True for percentages.
Transition: "So far everything has been about the whole file. Now the two commands you will use more than any others — asking questions about part of it."
70 – 80

Filtering and grouping

The only genuinely new mechanic for the July batch. Show it in two separate steps before combining. Ten minutes.

Almost every real question is about a subset. Not "what is the average salary" but "what is the average salary in Tech". So you need to be able to keep some rows and throw away the rest.

I am going to show you this in two steps, because if I do it in one line it looks like magic.

Step one — ask the question
df["salary"] > 80000
0 False 1 True 2 False 3 True ... Name: salary, Length: 201

Look carefully at what came back. Not a number. Not a list of salaries. Two hundred and one Trues and Falses.

I asked one question — is the salary above eighty thousand — and Pandas asked it of every single row at once and gave me back every answer. Row zero, no. Row one, yes.

Step two — use the answers
df[df["salary"] > 80000]

Now I take that entire column of yes-and-no answers and put it inside the table's square brackets. And Pandas keeps only the rows where the answer was yes.

Read the line out loud from the inside out: salary greater than eighty thousand — that is the question. Wrap it in df square brackets — that means keep those rows.

It looks strange for about two days and then it becomes the most natural thing in the world. You will write this line more than any other line in your career.

Two conditions at once
df[(df["salary"] > 80000) & (df["department"] == "Tech")]
# 29 rows

Twenty-nine people in Tech earning over eighty thousand.

Two rules here, and you are going to break both of them this week, so let me say them clearly.

One. Use the ampersand, not the word "and". The word "and" expects one true-or-false, and you are handing it two hundred and one of them. It will throw an error about the truth value being ambiguous, and now you know what that message means.

Two. Brackets around every single condition. Not optional. The ampersand binds tighter than the greater-than sign, so without brackets Python groups it wrongly and the whole thing breaks.

Ampersand instead of "and". Brackets around each condition. Write both down.

Then grouping
df.groupby("department")["salary"].mean()
HR 56705 Marketing 73954 Sales 66535 Tech 189754

One line, and I have four answers instead of one. Read it left to right: group by department, take the salary column, give me the mean. Pandas splits the rows into four piles, computes the average inside each pile, and stacks the results.

Now look at the numbers. HR fifty-six thousand. Sales sixty-six. Marketing seventy-three. Tech one lakh eighty-nine thousand.

Ask: "Is Tech really paid three times better than HR at this company?"
Let them think. The answer is no — the fifty-two lakh earner sits in Tech and has dragged that one group's average into nonsense. Point back at the max row in describe(). Do not resolve it further — say "day three" and move on. You now have the mean-versus-median hook planted twice from real data.
Pandas commands taught in this block
df["col"] > value
Asks a question of every row at once. Returns a column of True/False called a mask.
df[ mask ]
Keeps only the rows where the mask said True.
& and |
And / or. Never the words. Brackets around every condition.
df.groupby("c")["v"].mean()
Split into groups, compute per group, combine. The single most useful line in Pandas.
Transition: "That is all eight. Now you type them, because watching me type is not the same as knowing them."
80 – 90

Lab and close

Pair them explicitly. One June student with one July student at each machine, and say the roles out loud — the July student types, the June student coaches and does not touch the keyboard.

Last ten minutes. Pair up — if you have done Pandas before, sit with somebody who has not.

And here are the rules. The person who has not done Pandas is the one typing. If you already know this, your job is to talk, not to grab the laptop. Explaining it is going to do more for your revision than watching me would have.

Four tasks on the screen. Get through what you can.

On screen
1.  Load the file. Report its shape.

2.  Run describe(). Find one impossible value
    and say which column it is in.

3.  Report the mean AND median salary.
    Which would you put in a report to your manager?

4.  groupby department and find the highest paying one.
    Then tell me whether you believe it.
Circulate. Expect FileNotFoundError at least twice — it is almost always the working directory. Have them run import os; os.getcwd() and move the file.

Question four is a trap and I will tell you now so you are ready for it. The highest paying department is Tech, on paper. Anybody who tells me "Tech, but I do not trust that number because one person is distorting it" has understood everything I taught today.

Two minutes left. Stop the lab and close standing up, at the board.

Two things before you go.

First — every single thing we typed today was descriptive statistics. Averages, spreads, counts, groupings. You were doing statistics for the last hour and I only used the word twice. It is not a new subject. It is a name for what you were already doing.

Second — I left two questions unanswered on purpose, and they are both on the board. Why is the average department two point three two? And why are the mean and median salary twenty-seven thousand rupees apart?

Tomorrow we answer the first one. And the answer turns out to be a rule that decides, for every column you will ever work with, which statistics you are actually allowed to compute. See you then.

Every function in this session, explained

All 23 functions with a plain definition, a worked example and the real output. Four of them were not covered in the recorded delivery and are marked below.

What the recording missed

Series was never taught. The word appears twice in 78 minutes, both times as “TV series” in the Netflix analogy. Students have been using DataFrames without knowing what a single column is.
Also absent: iloc (loc was taught alone), mode, and unique / nunique. All four are below, and together they need about twelve minutes.

1. import pandas as pd
Definition
Brings the pandas library into your notebook and gives it the short name pd.
How it works

Written once at the top. Everyone writes pd — it is a convention, not a rule.

Type this
import pandas as pd print(pd.__version__)
You get
2.3.3
Watch out for
If this errors, pandas is not installed. Install it before class, not during.
2. pd.Series() — ONE column
Definition
A Series is a single column of data with a label on every row.
How it works

Give it a list. Pandas adds the row labels 0, 1, 2 automatically. That left-hand column is the index, not your data.

Type this
s = pd.Series([72000, 95000, 58000]) print(s) print() print('just the values:', s.values) print('the index :', list(s.index))
You get
0 72000 1 95000 2 58000 dtype: int64 just the values: [72000 95000 58000] the index : [0, 1, 2]
Watch out for
This was not covered in the recorded session. Teach it BEFORE DataFrame — a DataFrame only makes sense once they know what one column is.
3. Series with your own labels
Definition
You can name the rows instead of using 0, 1, 2.
How it works

Pass an index list of the same length. Now you look values up by name.

Type this
s = pd.Series([72000, 95000], index=['Rahul', 'Priya']) print(s) print() print(s['Rahul'])
You get
Rahul 72000 Priya 95000 dtype: int64 72000
Watch out for
This is the bridge from dictionary to Series — both look things up by a key rather than a position.
4. Series and DataFrame — the relationship
Definition
A DataFrame is many Series joined side by side, sharing one index.
How it works

Show it directly. Pull one column out of the table and check its type.

Type this
print(type(df['salary'])) print(type(df[['salary']])) print() print('columns in the table:', df.shape[1])
You get
<class 'pandas.core.series.Series'> <class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'> columns in the table: 12
Watch out for
One pair of brackets gives a Series. Two pairs give a DataFrame. That single difference confuses students for weeks — show it, do not just say it.
5. pd.DataFrame() from a dictionary
Definition
Builds a table. Each key becomes a column name.
How it works

This is how the recorded session introduced it, and it works well because they already know dictionaries.

Type this
data = {'name': ['Rahul', 'Priya', 'Amit'], 'salary': [72000, 95000, 58000]} d = pd.DataFrame(data) print(d)
You get
name salary 0 Rahul 72000 1 Priya 95000 2 Amit 58000
Watch out for
Every list must be the same length. Unequal lists raise an error.
6. pd.read_csv()
Definition
Loads a CSV file from disk into a DataFrame.
How it works

Give it the file name. The most used function in the whole library.

Type this
df = pd.read_csv('../employees.csv') print(type(df)) print(df.shape)
You get
<class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'> (201, 12)
Watch out for
Check your own path before class. If the notebook sits elsewhere, this line fails in front of the room.
7. head() and tail()
Definition
The first or last few rows.
How it works

Five rows by default. Put a number inside to change it.

Type this
print(df.head(3)) print() print(df.tail(2))
You get
emp_id dept_id name department city education rating \ 0 1001 3 Rahul Sharma HR Hyderabad Masters Poor 1 1002 4 Karthik Kumar Marketing Bangalore Diploma Poor 2 1003 2 Karthik Reddy Tech Bangalore Masters Good experience age height_cm salary join_date 0 4 53.0 169.5 47764.0 2018-01-03 1 13 57.0 169.5 86052.0 2024-07-02 2 1 56.0 166.5 62990.0 2025-03-04 emp_id dept_id name department city education rating \ 199 1200 2 Kavya Singh Tech Chennai Masters Average 200 1021 1 Anita Patel Sales Pune Masters Average experience age height_cm salary join_date 199 5 47.0 168.1 66075.0 2024-02-05 200 5 51.0 171.7 59760.0 2025-06-05
Watch out for
Always the first thing you run on a new file. Never assume you know what is inside it.
8. shape
Definition
How many rows and how many columns.
How it works

Gives a pair: (rows, columns).

Type this
print(df.shape) print('rows :', df.shape[0]) print('columns:', df.shape[1])
You get
(201, 12) rows : 201 columns: 12
Watch out for
No brackets. df.shape() is an error, and it is the most common typo in this session.
9. columns
Definition
The list of column names.
How it works

Use it to check spelling before typing a column name.

Type this
print(list(df.columns))
You get
['emp_id', 'dept_id', 'name', 'department', 'city', 'education', 'rating', 'experience', 'age', 'height_cm', 'salary', 'join_date']
10. dtypes
Definition
The data type held in each column.
How it works

object means text. int64 and float64 are numbers.

Type this
print(df.dtypes)
You get
emp_id int64 dept_id int64 name object department object city object ... experience int64 age float64 height_cm float64 salary float64 join_date object Length: 12, dtype: object
Watch out for
A column of numbers showing as object means something non-numeric is hiding in it. This was not covered in the session and is worth adding.
11. info()
Definition
Column names, how many values are filled, and the data types, all at once.
How it works

The single most useful first look at a file.

Type this
df.info()
You get
<class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'> RangeIndex: 201 entries, 0 to 200 Data columns (total 12 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 emp_id 201 non-null int64 1 dept_id 201 non-null int64 2 name 201 non-null object 3 department 201 non-null object 4 city 201 non-null object 5 education 201 non-null object 6 rating 201 non-null object 7 experience 201 non-null int64 8 age 200 non-null float64 9 height_cm 201 non-null float64 10 salary 199 non-null float64 11 join_date 201 non-null object dtypes: float64(3), int64(3), object(6) memory usage: 19.0+ KB
Watch out for
Point at the Non-Null Count. Where it is lower than the row count, values are missing. That is the whole reason to run it.
12. describe()
Definition
Summary statistics for every numeric column.
How it works

Count, mean, standard deviation, min, max and the quartiles.

Type this
print(df[['age', 'experience', 'salary']].describe().round(1))
You get
age experience salary count 200.0 201.0 199.0 mean 38.2 7.8 95648.4 std 16.6 4.5 364031.9 min -4.0 0.0 33085.0 25% 28.0 4.0 59003.5 50% 37.0 8.0 68647.0 75% 47.0 12.0 80599.5 max 210.0 15.0 5200000.0
Watch out for
It also averages emp_id and dept_id, which is meaningless. That is the day 2 hook, so let it happen and do not explain it yet.
13. isnull().sum()
Definition
Counts the missing values in each column.
How it works

isnull() marks every cell True or False. Summing counts the Trues.

Type this
print(df.isnull().sum())
You get
emp_id 0 dept_id 0 name 0 department 0 city 0 .. experience 0 age 1 height_cm 0 salary 2 join_date 0 Length: 12, dtype: int64
Watch out for
Run this straight after info(). It gives the same information but as a number you can act on.
14. loc[] — select by NAME
Definition
Picks rows and columns using labels.
How it works

Write df.loc[rows, columns].

Type this
print(df.loc[0, 'name']) print() print(df.loc[0:2, ['name', 'salary']])
You get
Rahul Sharma name salary 0 Rahul Sharma 47764.0 1 Karthik Kumar 86052.0 2 Karthik Reddy 62990.0
Watch out for
loc INCLUDES the last row. 0:2 gives three rows, not two.
15. iloc[] — select by POSITION
Definition
Picks rows and columns using numbers only.
How it works

Write df.iloc[rows, columns].

Type this
print(df.iloc[0, 2]) print() print(df.iloc[0:2, 0:3])
You get
Rahul Sharma emp_id dept_id name 0 1001 3 Rahul Sharma 1 1002 4 Karthik Kumar
Watch out for
iloc EXCLUDES the last position. 0:2 gives two rows. The session covered loc but never iloc — add it, because the difference is examinable.
16. mean()
Definition
The average of a numeric column.
How it works

Add everything up, divide by how many.

Type this
print(round(df['salary'].mean()))
You get
95648
Watch out for
It quietly skips missing values, so the count behind it may be lower than the row count.
17. median()
Definition
The middle value when the column is sorted.
How it works

Half the rows are above it, half below.

Type this
print(round(df['salary'].median()))
You get
68647
Watch out for
Mean is 95,648 and median is 68,647. Put both on the board together — the gap is day 3.
18. mode()
Definition
The most common value. The only average that works on text.
How it works

Returns a Series, because there can be more than one most-common value.

Type this
print(df['department'].mode()[0]) print(df['rating'].mode()[0])
You get
Sales Poor
Watch out for
Not covered in the recorded session. Worth adding, because it is the only one of the three that works on a text column.
19. std()
Definition
Standard deviation — how spread out the values are.
How it works

Roughly, the typical distance from the mean.

Type this
print(round(df['salary'].std()))
You get
364032
Watch out for
The value here is huge because one person earns 52 lakh. Note it and move on; the explanation is day 3.
20. min(), max(), sum(), count()
Definition
The other basic summaries of a column.
How it works

count() counts only the filled values, not the missing ones.

Type this
print('min :', df['salary'].min()) print('max :', df['salary'].max()) print('sum :', df['salary'].sum()) print('count:', df['salary'].count(), 'of', len(df), 'rows')
You get
min : 33085.0 max : 5200000.0 sum : 19034033.0 count: 199 of 201 rows
Watch out for
The gap between count() and len(df) is exactly the number of missing salaries.
21. value_counts()
Definition
Counts how many times each value appears in a column.
How it works

The correct summary for a text column, where mean and median make no sense.

Type this
print(df['department'].value_counts())
You get
department Sales 65 Tech 49 HR 45 Marketing 42 Name: count, dtype: int64
Watch out for
The session explained this well: you cannot take the mean of a department, but you can count them. Keep that framing.
22. unique() and nunique()
Definition
The distinct values, and how many there are.
How it works

Run these before grouping by a column, to see what you are about to group into.

Type this
print(df['city'].unique()) print('distinct cities:', df['city'].nunique())
You get
['Hyderabad' 'Bangalore' 'Chennai' 'Pune'] distinct cities: 4
Watch out for
Not covered in the session. Useful because it catches spelling variations before they become separate groups.
23. groupby()
Definition
Splits the table into groups, then summarises each group.
How it works

Say what to group by, choose a column, then say how to summarise it.

Type this
print(df.groupby('department')['salary'].mean().round(0))
You get
department HR 56705.0 Marketing 73954.0 Sales 66535.0 Tech 189754.0 Name: salary, dtype: float64
Watch out for
Split, apply, combine. The session reached this at 70 minutes — if you are short on time, this is the block to protect.

Questions you will get, with answers to say

Why not just use Excel for all this?

"Excel is genuinely better for a quick look and for handing something to someone who does not code. It falls over on three things. Files too big to open. Work you have to repeat every month — in Excel you redo the clicks, here you change one filename. And proving what you did six months ago; a script is a written record, a spreadsheet is not."

Why does shape have no brackets but head() does?

"Brackets mean it goes and does something. No brackets means it is a fact the object already knows. head() fetches rows for you. shape is just sitting there being true."

What is the difference between describe() and info()?

"info tells you about the structure — names, types, how many values are present. describe tells you about the numbers themselves. Use info to find missing data, describe to find impossible data."

Why is the standard deviation of salary 3.6 lakh?

"Because one person earns fifty-two lakh. Standard deviation measures distance from the average, and that one value is enormously far from everything else. Same reason the mean and median are so far apart. Day three."

Can I use single quotes instead of double?

"Yes, Python does not care. Pick one and be consistent."

Why did describe() skip the text columns?

"Because a mean of the word Sales does not exist. If you want a summary of the text columns, pass include='object' and you get counts and the most frequent value instead."

Something statistical you genuinely cannot answer

Say: "Good question, I will confirm it tonight and open with it tomorrow." Then actually do it. With a batch that does not know you yet, following through on that builds more credibility than a confident guess that turns out to be wrong.

If things go sideways

  • July batch drowning around minute 70 — drop groupby and keep filtering. Filtering is needed on day two; grouping is not needed until day six.
  • June batch visibly bored — start the lab early and make them coaches. Do not add advanced material; splitting your attention loses the other half.
  • Running long — cut the dictionary-to-DataFrame block at 18–30. They can meet DataFrames purely through read_csv.
  • Running short — run describe() on height_cm and experience and ask how those columns differ in shape from salary. Previews day four at no cost.
  • FileNotFoundError — the working directory, almost every time. import os; os.getcwd(), then move the CSV there.
  • You lose your place — go back to df.describe(). Everything today connects to it, so it is always a safe place to restart from.

The script above is self-contained. These are reinforcement only — the last two are really tomorrow's material.
