Questions you will get

“What is the difference between a bar chart and a histogram?”

“A bar chart has one bar per category — four departments, four bars. A histogram has one bar per range of numbers, because there are no categories to use. That is why histogram bars usually touch and bar-chart bars do not. It is a real interview question, so learn the one sentence.”

“Who decides where one bin stops and the next begins?”

“Python does, once you tell it how many bins you want. It takes the lowest value and the highest value, and chops that range into equal slices. That is why we counted HR's experience into four groups of four years — zero to three, four to seven, and so on. Equal width slices, automatically.”

“Should I always remove outliers before drawing?”

“No — and be careful here. Draw it with them first, because that is how you find out they exist. Then decide. If it is a data-entry error, like an age of minus four, remove it. If it is a real person who genuinely earns 52 lakh, it is real and you report it separately rather than deleting it. Removing a number because it is inconvenient is not analysis.”

“How many bins should I use?”

“There is no correct answer, and anybody who gives you one is oversimplifying. Try twenty, try thirty, look at both. What you must not do is try ten different values and keep the one that supports the story you wanted — that is the same mistake as running twenty tests and reporting the one that worked.”

“The line in the box — is that the mean?”

“No, the median. Almost everybody assumes mean, so remember it by what the box is made of: the box is built from quartiles, and the median is the middle quartile. It is all quartiles, no averages anywhere in that picture.”

“Why does the box plot show dots but the histogram does not?”

“Because the box plot has a rule for what counts as an outlier — 1.5 times the IQR — and the histogram does not. A histogram just shows you where everybody is and lets you judge. That is the trade: the box plot decides for you, the histogram shows you more detail.”

“My box plot is one flat line.”

“You passed it a column with an extreme value in it, so everything else got compressed, or you passed it a column that is not numbers. A box plot of department cannot work, because quartiles of a name do not exist.”

“Why did we do all that statistics if one line of code draws it?”

“Because the line of code does not tell you what it means. Anybody can type plt.boxplot. Knowing that the dots are the 1.5 IQR rule, that the line is the median, and that a long upper tail means the mean is unreliable — that is what you have and the person who only learnt the command does not.”

Data Visualisation day 3 · merged class · 90 minutes · full script

Comparing,
and Relating

Bar charts done properly — including the ordering trap and the column that should never be averaged. Then one small change to day one's picture turns it into a scatter plot, and 0.079 becomes 0.607.

2.32seen, not computed
1axis changed
0.079→ 0.607
3errors, one chart

The scatter plot is not a new chart

On day one they drew every age as a dot, with position in the file along the bottom — an x axis that meant nothing. Swap that for a second real column and the same picture becomes a scatter plot. One change, and a slope appears. Build it that way and nobody has to learn a new chart today.

Before you walk in

  1. Fix the ordering problem they noticed on day one. value_counts() sorts by frequency. For department that helps; for rating it destroys the meaning. That difference is statistics day 2 deciding a chart for them.
  2. Explain .astype(str), do not slip it in. Without it the dept_id bars are spaced by value like a number line. It is a one-line fix with a real reason, and silently typing it is exactly the habit the class has complained about.
  3. Introduce the scatter as day one's chart with one axis changed. Show the two pictures side by side. It costs two minutes and it means scatter plots arrive as a small change rather than a new topic.
  4. The 0.079 to 0.607 demo is the payoff. Give it twenty minutes. Draw it raw, diagnose, remove two rows, redraw, recompute. That is statistics day 7 finally making sense.
  5. Then age against salary, and say nothing. Three data errors appear in one picture, and one of them is in a column nobody was asking about. Let the room find all three.

Understand this yourself first

Three things: the ordering rule, why astype(str) is needed, and the one sentence that makes a scatter plot obvious.

Part one · bar charts, and the two things that go wrong
Sorted by size, or sorted by meaning?

value_counts() always sorts biggest first. For department that is helpful — the question is usually “which is biggest”, and sorted bars answer it instantly.

For rating it is destructive. Poor, Average, Good, Excellent have a natural order, and sorting by frequency scrambles it into Poor, Good, Excellent, Average — which reads as though Average is worse than Excellent.

Nominal — no natural order — sort by size. Ordinal — a natural order — keep the meaning order, always. Statistics day 2, deciding a chart.
The fix, and why it is a new idea

df["rating"].value_counts()[order] asks for the counts back in the order of a list you wrote. They have never indexed a Series with a list before. It is one line, and it deserves a sentence rather than being typed past.

Why dept_id needs .astype(str)

dept_id holds 1, 2, 3, 4. If you hand those to plt.bar as numbers, matplotlib treats the bottom ruler as a number line and positions each bar at its value — so the ruler shows 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 and the bars sit at measured distances apart.

.astype(str) turns them into the text “1”, “2”, “3”, “4”. Now matplotlib treats them as four names and spaces them evenly, like the department chart.

That is the whole lesson of dept_id appearing as a chart decision: the column looks numeric and is not. You have to tell the chart so, exactly as you had to tell yourself so on day one of statistics.
Part two · the scatter plot, as one change to a picture they already have
They drew one on day one without being told

On day one they plotted every age as a dot. Along the bottom was position in the file — row 1, row 2, row 3. That axis carried no information at all; it was only there to spread the dots out so the two strays could be seen.

Swap that axis for a second real column and the same picture becomes a scatter plot. Each dot is still one person. Only the question changed — from “what do these values look like?” to “do these two things move together?”

day one y = age, x = which row. A cloud with two strays.
today y = salary, x = years of experience. A slope.
The demonstration that makes the session

On statistics day 7 they got Pearson 0.079 and Spearman 0.61 on these two columns and you told them one extreme salary was the reason. Today: draw it raw, remove two rows with the fences they already have, draw it again, and Pearson comes back 0.607 — agreeing with the Spearman they got three weeks ago.

Age against salary, which finds three errors at once

They met the −4 and the 210 on day one. The 52 lakh is new to this picture. The point today is not that the data is dirty — they know that. It is that a chart you drew for a different reason handed you a problem in a column you were not asking about.

The session, minute by minute

Everything in a speech box is meant to be said more or less as written. Everything in a grey box is a direction for you, not words to say.

0 – 14

The question you asked on day one

Answer the ordering question properly, and teach one new line to do it.

On day one somebody asked why Sales came first in our bar chart, when it was third in the list I typed by hand. I said we would deal with it today.

Set up, and the chart from day one
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("employees.csv")

counts = df["department"].value_counts()
plt.bar(counts.index, counts.values)
plt.title("Employees per department")
plt.ylabel("Number of employees")
plt.show()

value_counts() always sorts biggest first. And here that is genuinely useful. If the question is “which department is biggest”, the sorted chart answers it before you have finished reading the title.

Now watch the same behaviour on a different column.

The same command, on rating
print(df["rating"].value_counts())
rating Poor 58 Good 51 Excellent 49 Average 43 Name: count, dtype: int64
“What is wrong with that order?”
Poor, Good, Excellent, Average. The ratings have a natural order and this scrambles it — a chart in this order reads as though Average is worse than Excellent.

Poor, Good, Excellent, Average. That is nonsense as an order.

These four have a meaning order — Poor, then Average, then Good, then Excellent. And sorting them by how often they occur throws it away.

This is day two of statistics deciding a chart for you. Department is nominal — no natural order, so sorting by size is fine. Rating is ordinal — it has an order, and you must keep it.

The fix is one line, and it contains an idea they have not met. Do not type past it.
Force the meaning order
order = ["Poor", "Average", "Good", "Excellent"]
counts = df["rating"].value_counts()[order]

print(counts)
rating Poor 58 Average 43 Good 51 Excellent 49 Name: count, dtype: int64

Look carefully at that second line, because there is something in it you have not seen.

value_counts() gives back the four counts. Then I put a list inside square brackets after it.

That says: give me those counts back, in the order of this list. I wrote the order I wanted, and asked for the results arranged that way.

Now the chart reads left to right from worst to best, and anybody can follow it.

The rule, and it is a real interview answer.

Nominal — no natural order — let it sort by size. It helps.
Ordinal — a natural order — write the order down and force it. Always.
Thirty seconds on the sideways version. It is only a readability fix.
When the labels are too long
counts = df["department"].value_counts()
plt.barh(counts.index, counts.values)
plt.title("Employees per department")
plt.xlabel("Number of employees")
plt.show()

barh. Use it when the category names are too long to sit under vertical bars without overlapping.

One thing to watch: the two rulers swap jobs. The counts are now along the bottom, so they go on xlabel, not ylabel. People get that wrong constantly.

14 – 24

2.32, finally drawn

Close the hook that opened the module — and explain the one odd line.

One more bar chart, and this one goes back to the very first day of statistics.

Remember dept_id? The column of numbers that turned out to be department names in disguise.

First try it the obvious way
counts = df["dept_id"].value_counts().sort_index()
print(counts)

plt.bar(counts.index, counts.values)
plt.show()
dept_id 1 65 2 49 3 45 4 42 Name: count, dtype: int64

One new thing there. sort_index() means put them back in order of the label — 1, 2, 3, 4 — instead of by size. We want them in their own order here, not biggest first.

Now look at the chart that came out.

Look at the bottom ruler on the left. One point zero. One point five. Two point zero.

Matplotlib was handed four numbers, so it did what you do with numbers — it built a number line and placed each bar at its value.

But there is no department one point five. We do not want a number line. We want four labels.

One word fixes it
plt.bar(counts.index.astype(str), counts.values)

plt.title("dept_id")
plt.xlabel("dept_id")
plt.ylabel("Number of employees")
plt.show()

print("the 'average' dept_id:", round(df["dept_id"].mean(), 2))
the 'average' dept_id: 2.32

.astype(str) turns the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 into the text “1”, “2”, “3”, “4”.

Now matplotlib sees four names instead of four numbers, and spaces them evenly — exactly like the department chart.

And that is the whole lesson of this column, showing up again as a chart decision. It looks numeric and it is not. You had to tell yourself that on day one of statistics. Today you had to tell the chart.

“Point at 2.32 on that chart for me.”
They cannot. It sits in the gap between bar two and bar three, and there is nothing there. Much stronger as a request than as a statement.

Four bars. Four departments. There is no order between them — department two is not “more” than department one.

And the average is two point three two. Show me where that is.

It is in the gap. There is nothing there. A valid calculation describing nothing at all.

That was the first thing I showed you in this entire module. Now you can see that it is.

24 – 34

A chart you have already drawn

The scatter plot arrives as one change, not as a new topic.

Put day one's age picture back on screen. They will recognise it immediately.

Everything so far today has been one column at a time. Now a different kind of question altogether: do two things move together?

And the chart for it is not new. You drew one on day one without me telling you what it was.

Think back to the age picture. Every person was a dot. Up the side was their age.

But what was along the bottom?

“On day one, what did the bottom ruler measure?”
Position in the file. Row one, row two, row three. It meant nothing at all — it was only there to spread the dots out so the two strays could be seen. Get them to say that out loud; the next sentence depends on it.

Position in the file. Row one, row two, row three.

That axis carried no information. Nobody cares whether somebody is the fortieth row of a spreadsheet. It was only there to spread the dots out.

So here is the whole idea for the next half hour. What if we put something real along the bottom instead?

On the left, salary against position in the file. A shapeless cloud, because the bottom ruler means nothing.

On the right, exactly the same salaries — but the bottom ruler is now years of experience.

Same dots. Same heights. One axis changed, and a shape appeared.

That picture on the right has a name. It is a scatter plot, and it is the chart for “do these two move together?”

A scatter plot is not a new chart. It is day one's picture with a meaningful x axis. One dot is still one person — now placed by two of their columns instead of one.
34 – 58

A number that moves

The biggest payoff in the module. Twenty minutes, and do not hurry it.

Draw it raw first — deliberately
plt.scatter(df["experience"], df["salary"])

plt.title("Experience against salary")
plt.xlabel("Years of experience")
plt.ylabel("Salary")
plt.show()

print("correlation:", round(df["experience"].corr(df["salary"]), 3))
correlation: 0.079

plt.scatter takes two columns. The first goes along the bottom, the second up the side. That is the only difference from everything else we have typed.

“We have seen this problem before. What is happening?”
Same as yesterday's histogram — the 52 lakh earner. One dot forces the side ruler to five million and flattens everybody else into a line. They should get this in seconds now.

Same problem as yesterday. One person at fifty-two lakh, so the side ruler stretches that far and everybody else is a flat smear.

And look at the correlation. Zero point zero seven nine. That says almost no relationship between experience and salary.

Does that sound right to you? Does experience really have nothing to do with pay?

We saw this exact number on day seven of statistics. Pearson gave 0.079, Spearman gave 0.61, and I told you the outlier was the reason. Today we prove it.

Remove two rows, with the fences you already have
sal = df["salary"].dropna()
q1, q3 = sal.quantile(0.25), sal.quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1
low, high = q1 - 1.5*iqr, q3 + 1.5*iqr

clean = df[(df["salary"] >= low) & (df["salary"] <= high)]

plt.scatter(clean["experience"], clean["salary"])
plt.title("Experience against salary")
plt.xlabel("Years of experience")
plt.ylabel("Salary")
plt.show()

print("correlation now:", round(clean["experience"].corr(clean["salary"]), 3))
correlation now: 0.607
Put the two numbers side by side on the board. This is the moment the session exists for.
On the board
experience against salary

   with every row      correlation = 0.079     "no relationship"
   with 2 rows gone    correlation = 0.607     "a solid relationship"

   the data did not change. two rows out of 199 did.

   and on statistics day 7, SPEARMAN gave us 0.61 on the raw file.
   spearman was right all along. it ignores the outlier by design.

Zero point zero seven nine, to zero point six zero seven. Two rows out of a hundred and ninety-nine. Nothing else changed.

And look back at day seven. Spearman gave us zero point six one on the raw file — the same answer we have just got the hard way.

Spearman was right all along, because it works on order rather than distance, so one huge value cannot drag it.

Three weeks ago I asked you to take that on trust. There it is.

Now the trend line. Four lines of code and three of them are new — so say plainly which parts to copy and which to understand.
Add a line of best fit
import numpy as np

plt.scatter(clean["experience"], clean["salary"])

m, b = np.polyfit(clean["experience"], clean["salary"], 1)
xs = np.array([clean["experience"].min(), clean["experience"].max()])
plt.plot(xs, m*xs + b, color="red")

plt.title("The same picture, with a trend line")
plt.xlabel("Years of experience")
plt.ylabel("Salary")
plt.show()

Three lines there, and I want you to copy them rather than understand them today. Let me tell you what each one does, and then we move on.

np.polyfit finds the straight line that fits best through the dots. It hands back two numbers — how steep the line is, and where it starts.

xs is just two numbers: the smallest experience and the largest. A straight line only needs two points.

And plt.plot draws a line between them.

What matters is what the line is. That is the straight line correlation was measuring all along. When we said 0.607, we meant the dots sit fairly close to that line.

Do not go further than that. The maths behind polyfit is least squares and it belongs to a regression course. “The line of best fit, and correlation says how close the dots are to it” is the right amount for a fresher.
58 – 74

A chart you drew for a different reason

The most practical habit in the module, taught by letting them find it.

Type it, show it, say nothing. Let the room work.
Type this, then look
plt.scatter(df["age"], df["salary"])

plt.title("Age against salary")
plt.xlabel("Age")
plt.ylabel("Salary")
plt.show()
“How many things are wrong with this data? Find them all.”
Three. Age −4 far left and age 210 far right — they met both on day one. The new one is the 52-lakh salary at the top. Do not accept the first answer.

Three problems, in one picture, in about one second.

Two of them you already know — minus four and two hundred and ten. We found those on day one, when we drew the age column on its own.

But now look at what this chart just did.

I asked it about age against salary. I was not looking for bad data at all. And it handed me a problem in the salary column, for free.

That is the habit. You do not go hunting for broken data. You draw the thing you were going to draw anyway, and the broken data finds you. Which is why you draw before you analyse, not after, to decorate the report.
Ten minutes on their own. The second one requires a decision rather than a command.
Their turn
# 1. bar chart of the "education" column
#    careful: Diploma, Bachelors, Masters has an ORDER.
#    write the order down and force it, like we did with rating.

# 2. scatter plot of height_cm against salary
#    what do you expect to see? draw it, then compute the correlation.
#    were you right?
The second one comes back near zero, and that is the point. Height and salary are unrelated — the correlation is about −0.04 and the scatter is a shapeless cloud, the same shape as the left-hand picture from the bridge earlier. Students who have only ever been shown charts that reveal something need to see what nothing here looks like. Same lesson as the chi-square p of 0.94.

Close, and the pattern so far

Four charts, four questions
WHAT I WANT TO KNOW                        CHART

how many in each category?                 bar
what does this one column look like?       histogram
what is the middle, spread, outliers?      box plot
do these two columns move together?        scatter


the first three show ONE column.
only the scatter shows TWO.

Four charts. Four different questions. That table is most of what this module is.

Tomorrow we draw every one of them again — in one line each, instead of five. The library is called seaborn, and once you have seen it you will not go back.

But you needed this first. Seaborn is built on top of matplotlib, and every title, label and show() you have learnt this week still works exactly the same way tomorrow.

The four lines. If everything else goes, keep these.
1.  NOMINAL data  -> let it sort by size. it helps.

       counts = df["rating"].value_counts()[order]

counts = df["department"].value_counts()

Poor 58 Good 51 Excellent 49 Average 43

Questions you will get

“What does putting a list in square brackets after value_counts() actually do?”

“It picks the results out in the order you asked for. value_counts() gives you four counts labelled Poor, Average, Good, Excellent. Handing it a list of those four names says ‘give them back to me in this order’. If you misspell one, you get an error — which is useful, because it means you cannot silently lose a category.”

“Why did the dept_id chart need .astype(str) but the department one did not?”

“Because department was already text. dept_id is numbers, and matplotlib treats numbers as positions on a ruler rather than as names. .astype(str) is you telling the chart that these digits are labels, not quantities — which is exactly the thing that column has been teaching us since day one.”

“So should I always delete outliers before finding the correlation?”

“No — you should always look first, then decide, then say what you decided. Here it was one data point distorting a real relationship, so removing it was right. If it had been a genuine high earner and the question was about total payroll, removing it would have been wrong. The unforgivable thing is removing it quietly.”

“Why did Spearman get it right when Pearson did not?”

“Because Spearman works on order, not distance. To Spearman the 52-lakh earner is simply the highest paid person — it does not matter whether they earn 52 lakh or 52 crore, they are still number one. Pearson uses the actual distance, so an enormous value drags it. That is why we taught both.”

“A correlation of 0.607 — is that good?”

“It is a solid relationship, and be careful with the word good. It means experience explains a fair part of salary and other things explain the rest — department, city, how well somebody negotiated. A correlation being high does not mean you have found the cause. That was day seven and it has not changed.”

“My scatter plot is just a solid blob. I cannot see anything.”

“Too many dots on top of each other. Add alpha=0.5 to make them see-through, so where dots pile up it looks darker. With a few hundred rows that is enough; with a million you would use a different chart entirely.”

“Why not just delete the −4 age quietly? It is obviously wrong.”

“Because you do not know why it is there. If somebody typed 4 as −4 that is one fix. If the export tool writes −4 whenever a value is missing, then every −4 in the file means missing, and there may be thousands of them in the real database. Find out what it means before you decide what to do with it.”

“Can I draw three columns at once?”

“Yes, and you will tomorrow. Seaborn lets you colour the dots by a third column with one extra word, and suddenly you can see experience, salary and department in a single picture. That is the main reason it is worth learning.”

Every chart from this week, rewritten in a single line. Then the two things matplotlib could not do easily — a third column for free, and every correlation at once.

Why seaborn comes now and not on day one

Three days of writing five lines per chart is what makes sns.histplot(data=df, x="salary") land as relief. Same reason a CSV read by hand makes read_csv land. And it is honest: seaborn sits on top of matplotlib, so everything they already know still runs.

Before you walk in

  1. Open by rewriting a chart they already have. Put the matplotlib version and the seaborn version side by side on screen. Five lines becomes one. No explanation needed — the comparison is the argument.
  2. Say plainly that seaborn is not a replacement. It is matplotlib with the common charts pre-written. plt.title() and plt.show() still work, unchanged, because underneath it is matplotlib.
  3. hue is the reason to learn seaborn. One extra word puts a third column into any chart. Doing that in matplotlib takes a loop. This is the genuinely new capability, not the shorter syntax.
  4. The heatmap is the biggest single payoff. Six correlations in one picture. They spent a whole statistics session computing correlations one pair at a time.
  5. Warn about the heatmap trap before you draw it. A correlation heatmap silently drops every text column. Students conclude a column “has no correlation” when it was never in the calculation.

Understand this yourself first

There is almost nothing new here conceptually — which is the point. Two things worth being precise about: what seaborn actually is, and how to read a heatmap.

Part one · what seaborn is, and what it is not
It is a shortcut layer, not a different library

Seaborn does not draw anything itself. It calls matplotlib for you, with sensible defaults already chosen. That is why plt.title(), plt.xlabel() and plt.show() all still work on a seaborn chart — underneath, it is a matplotlib chart.

Say this once, clearly: you have not wasted three days. Everything from this week still applies. Seaborn writes the common charts for you; matplotlib is still what finishes them.
The one pattern that covers every seaborn chart

Nearly all of them take the same three things: the DataFrame, which column goes along the bottom, and which goes up the side.

data= the whole DataFrame. Not a column — the table.
x= the column name, in quotes, that goes along the bottom.
y= the column name up the side. Some charts need only x.
hue= optional. A third column, shown as colour.

Once they have that, every chart in this session is one line with a different function name.

hue is the real reason to switch

Shorter syntax is convenience. hue is capability. Colouring a scatter plot by department in matplotlib means looping over the departments and plotting each separately. In seaborn it is one word, and the legend appears on its own.

Part two · the correlation heatmap
Every pair at once, in colour

On statistics day 7 they computed correlations one pair at a time. A heatmap computes every pair in the table and colours each cell by its value. Four numeric columns give sixteen cells, of which six are the pairs that matter.

How to read it in three steps
the diagonal Always 1.00 — every column against itself. Ignore it.
the two halves Mirror images. Experience against salary is the same number as salary against experience. Read one half only.
the colour Strong one way, strong the other way, or nothing. The number is printed in the cell; the colour is there so your eye finds it first.
The trap, and it catches people

.corr() silently ignores every non-numeric column. Department, city, education and rating simply do not appear. A student sees a heatmap without department in it and concludes department does not correlate with salary — when it was never tested.

Say it before you draw it, not after. Missing from a heatmap means not measured, never no relationship. And they already know the right tool for department against salary: statistics day 13, the two-sample t-test.

The session, minute by minute

Everything in a speech box is meant to be said more or less as written. Everything in a grey box is a direction for you, not words to say.

0 – 16

The same chart, one line

Show the comparison. Do not explain first.

For three days you have written five lines for every chart. Today I show you the same charts in one line.

Before you feel cheated — you have not wasted three days, and I will show you why in a moment.

Set up
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

df = pd.read_csv("employees.csv")

sns. Same idea as pd and plt — the nickname everyone uses. Do not invent your own.

And notice we still import matplotlib. That is not a mistake.

Put the two versions on screen together. The comparison does the arguing.
Day one's chart, both ways
# what you wrote on day one
counts = df["department"].value_counts()
plt.bar(counts.index, counts.values)
plt.title("Employees per department")
plt.ylabel("Number of employees")
plt.show()

# the same chart, today
sns.countplot(data=df, x="department")
plt.show()

One line instead of four. And look — it labelled both rulers on its own.

It could do that because I handed it the whole table and told it which column to use. It knows the column is called department, so it writes that under the chart. Matplotlib only ever got two anonymous lists, so it had nothing to label them with.

That is the difference in one sentence. Matplotlib takes numbers. Seaborn takes a table and a column name.

And you have not wasted three days. Seaborn does not draw anything itself — it calls matplotlib for you with the settings already chosen. That is why plt.show() still works on the line above. Underneath, it is a matplotlib chart.
The pattern — on the board, all session
sns.SOMETHING( data=df, x="column", y="column" )

  data=   the whole DataFrame. not a column. the TABLE.
  x=      the column NAME, in quotes, along the bottom
  y=      the column NAME up the side  (some charts need only x)

then plt.title(...) and plt.show() exactly as before.
16 – 38

This week's charts, rewritten

Fast. Three charts, three one-liners. They know what all of them mean already.

Move quickly here — nothing is conceptually new. The time belongs to hue and the heatmap later.
Tuesday's histogram
sal = df["salary"].dropna()
q1, q3 = sal.quantile(0.25), sal.quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1
low, high = q1 - 1.5*iqr, q3 + 1.5*iqr
clean = df[(df.salary >= low) & (df.salary <= high)]

sns.histplot(data=clean, x="salary", bins=20)
plt.show()
Tuesday's box plots, four at once
sns.boxplot(data=clean, x="department", y="salary")
plt.show()

Compare that with Tuesday. On Tuesday we had to build a list of four groups by hand and then pass labels separately.

Here I named two columns. x is what splits the boxes, y is what gets measured. Seaborn did the grouping itself.

“How did it know to make four boxes?”
It looked at the department column, found four distinct values, and made one box for each. That is what handing over the whole table buys you.
Yesterday's scatter
sns.scatterplot(data=clean, x="experience", y="salary")
plt.show()

Three charts. Three lines. Everything you learnt this week about what these charts mean is unchanged — only the typing got shorter.

Now the part that is not just shorter typing.

38 – 58

A third column, for one word

The actual reason to learn seaborn. This is capability, not convenience.

Every chart we have drawn shows one or two columns. A scatter shows two — experience and salary.

What if I want to see a third? What if I want to know whether the relationship between experience and salary is the same in every department?

In matplotlib that is a loop. In seaborn it is one word.

Add one word
sns.scatterplot(data=clean, x="experience", y="salary", hue="department")

plt.title("Experience against salary, by department")
plt.show()

hue. It means colour.

One word, and now every dot is coloured by which department that person is in. And seaborn built the legend for you — you did not ask for it.

Now the chart is answering a harder question. Not just “does experience relate to salary”, but “is it the same story in every department?”

“Look at the colours. Where do the Tech dots sit compared with the HR dots?”
Tech sits higher for the same experience. Which is what the day-13 t-test told them numerically — p of roughly zero between Tech and HR. Same finding, now visible.

On day thirteen of statistics we ran a test comparing Tech and HR salaries and got a p-value of basically zero. We said the difference was real.

Here it is, in colour. The Tech dots sit above the HR dots at the same level of experience.

This is why seaborn is worth the twenty minutes. Not the shorter syntax — the third column. hue works on almost every seaborn chart, and it turns a two-column picture into a three-column one for free.
Ten minutes on their own. This is where the word gets fixed in memory.
Their turn
# 1. sns.boxplot of salary by department, with hue="education"
# 2. sns.countplot of department, with hue="rating"
# look at both. which one is actually readable?
The second one is deliberately too busy. Four departments times four ratings is sixteen bars and it becomes hard to read. hue is powerful and it is easy to overuse. Let them discover the limit rather than being told it — that is tomorrow's session starting.
58 – 78

Every correlation at once

The biggest payoff. Warn about the trap before drawing, not after.

On day seven of statistics we computed correlations. One pair at a time. Experience against salary. Then age against salary. Then the next pair.

There is a chart that does all of them at once.

First, the numbers
num = clean[["experience", "age", "height_cm", "salary"]].corr()
print(num.round(2))
experience age height_cm salary experience 1.00 0.05 0.00 0.61 age 0.05 1.00 0.06 0.11 height_cm 0.00 0.06 1.00 -0.04 salary 0.61 0.11 -0.04 1.00

.corr() on several columns gives every pair at once. That is already useful — but it is a wall of numbers and your eye has nowhere to start.

Now colour it
sns.heatmap(num, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="RdBu_r", center=0)

plt.title("Correlation heatmap")
plt.show()
Walk the three arguments, then read the chart. Do not skip center=0 — it is the one that makes the colours honest.

Three arguments and they are all worth knowing.

annot=True — annotate. Print the actual number inside each square. Without it you get colour and no values, which looks impressive and tells you nothing precise.

fmt=".2f" — the number format. Two decimal places. Without it you get long ugly decimals.

center=0 — put the middle of the colour scale at zero, so no relationship is the pale colour, and strong-positive and strong-negative are the two ends. Without it the colours are misleading.

Now read it, and there are only three things to know.

The diagonal is always 1.00 — every column against itself. Ignore it entirely.

The two halves are mirror images. Experience against salary is the same number as salary against experience. Read one half only.

And then look for the strong colours. Experience and salary, 0.61. Everything else is near zero.

Say this before anybody asks. Look at which columns are missing. No department. No city. No education. No rating. .corr() silently ignores every column that is not a number. Missing from a heatmap means not measured — it never means no relationship. And for department against salary they already know the right tool: the two-sample t-test from day thirteen.
“Height and salary is −0.04. Does that mean tall people earn less?”
No — and this is the day-seven lesson again. −0.04 is nothing. It is noise, and with 197 rows you would expect small values like this even if the two were completely unrelated. A correlation near zero means no straight-line relationship, not a weak negative one.
78 – 90

Close, and which library when

The honest answer to “which one should I use?”
USE SEABORN                         USE MATPLOTLIB

the common charts                   anything unusual
anything needing hue                fine control of one detail
heatmaps                            and ALWAYS for the finishing:
several groups at once                title, labels, show


you do not choose between them.
seaborn draws it, matplotlib finishes it. every time.

You will use both, in the same cell, all the time. Seaborn draws the chart and matplotlib puts the title on it. That is not a compromise, it is how everybody works.

The seaborn cheat sheet — everything from today
import seaborn as sns

sns.countplot(data=df,  x="department")            # bar of counts
sns.histplot(data=df,   x="salary", bins=20)       # histogram
sns.boxplot(data=df,    x="department", y="salary")# box plots, grouped
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="experience", y="salary")

    ... add  hue="department"  to almost any of them

sns.heatmap(df.corr(), annot=True, fmt=".2f", center=0)
                                    # annot = print the numbers
                                    # center=0 = pale means "no relationship"

then, always:  plt.title(...) ; plt.show()

Tomorrow is the last session, and it is the one that matters most in an interview.

Not a new chart. The question of which chart to use — and how the same honest numbers can be drawn to tell a lie.

The four lines. If everything else goes, keep these.
1.  seaborn does not replace matplotlib. it SITS ON IT.
    plt.title() and plt.show() still work. always will.

2.  matplotlib takes NUMBERS.  seaborn takes a TABLE and COLUMN NAMES.
    that is why seaborn can label the axes by itself.

3.  hue="column" is the real reason to switch.
    a third column, one word, legend included.

4.  a heatmap silently drops every text column.
    MISSING means NOT MEASURED. it never means "no relationship".

Questions you will get

“If seaborn is shorter, why did we spend three days on matplotlib?”

“Because seaborn is matplotlib with the common charts pre-written. Every title, label and show() you learnt is still what finishes a seaborn chart. And the day you need something seaborn does not have, you are not stuck. It is the same reason we read a CSV by hand before using read_csv.”

“Do I still need plt.show()?”

“Yes. Seaborn builds a matplotlib chart, so the rules are identical — nothing appears until show(), and everything else goes before it.”

“Why data=df and then the column name in quotes? Why not just pass the column?”

“Because the name is how it labels the axis. If you hand it a bare column it has values but no name to print. Passing the table plus the name is what buys you the free labels — and it is what makes hue possible, since hue is just a third column it looks up in the same table.”

“My heatmap has no department in it.”

“Correct, and important. .corr() only works on numbers, so every text column is silently dropped. It does not mean department is unrelated to salary — you proved on day thirteen that it is strongly related. It means correlation is the wrong tool for a category, and a t-test is the right one.”

“My chart looks different from yours — different colours, gridlines appeared.”

“Seaborn sets a style when it loads, so charts drawn after importing it look different even if they are matplotlib charts. It is cosmetic, nothing is broken. sns.set_theme() controls it if you care, and for now you should not.”

“Can I use hue on a histogram?”

“Yes, on nearly everything. Whether it is readable is a different question — four overlapping histograms is usually a mess. That is the judgement we start on tomorrow: a chart that is technically correct and impossible to read is still a failed chart.”

“Which one do companies use?”

“Both, together, in the same cell — and then Power BI or Tableau for anything a manager will look at. Python charting is for you, while you explore. The dashboard the business sees is usually built somewhere else, which is the module after this one.”

Data Visualisation day 5 · merged class · 90 minutes · full script · closes the module

Choosing,
and Lying

No new chart today. The decision table that tells you which one to reach for — and then the same honest numbers, drawn twice, telling two opposite stories.

1table, four questions
2charts, same data
0numbers changed
4ways to mislead

The most useful session in the module

Everything before today was technique, and Power BI will do most of it for them. This session does not transfer away — choosing the right chart and spotting a dishonest one works in every tool, and it is the part an interviewer can actually test in five minutes.

Before you walk in

  1. The decision table is the deliverable. Build it the same way as the which-test table on statistics day 13 — question first, chart second. They should leave able to pick a chart from a sentence.
  2. Run the truncated-axis demo as a vote. Show the misleading one alone, ask how much bigger Tech is than HR, let them commit to a number out loud, then show the honest one. Being caught is the lesson.
  3. Do not moralise about it. Most misleading charts are made by people who were not trying to mislead. Frame it as “how to not do this by accident” and it lands far better.
  4. The percentage-point trap is the same one from day 13. They have met it on p-values; it appears again on charts. Repeat it — freshers get caught by this in their first month.
  5. Close the module and hand over properly. Power BI and Tableau come next. Say what carries across, which is almost all of today, and what does not.

Understand this yourself first

Two things: the table, and the four ways a chart misleads. The truncated axis is the one that actually happens most.

Part one · the decision table, built from the question
Start from the sentence, not the library

The mistake every beginner makes is starting at “which function do I call?”. The working order is: what is the question, what kind of columns do I have, then which chart.

How many in each category? One category column → bar chart
What does this column look like? One number column → histogram
Middle, spread and outliers? Several groups? A number, optionally split by a category → box plot
Do these two move together? Two number columns → scatter
How does this change over time? A date and a number → line

Five rows. That covers essentially everything a fresher analyst is asked for.

Why the line chart gets one row and no session

It is the same code as everything else — plt.plot with a date along the bottom. The only thing worth teaching is when: a line implies the points connect continuously, so it belongs to time and to nothing else. Joining four departments with a line would be nonsense, because there is nothing between HR and Marketing.

Part two · the four ways a chart misleads
1. The truncated y-axis — by far the most common

Start the vertical ruler near the top of the data instead of at zero and small differences become enormous. Nothing in the data is falsified. Every number is correct. The picture simply lies about proportion.

For bar charts, the y-axis must start at zero. The whole point of a bar is that its length encodes the value — cut the bottom off and the length means nothing. For line charts this is not a rule, because a line encodes change rather than size.
2. The pie chart

People are poor at comparing angles and good at comparing lengths. Two slices of 23% and 26% are almost impossible to tell apart; two bars are trivial. A pie is defensible for two or three slices that clearly make a whole, and bad for anything else.

3. Percentage points against relative change

8% to 11.5% is 3.5 percentage points and also a 43.75% relative increase. Both true. They sound wildly different, and a chart labelled “43% improvement” next to two bars of 8 and 11.5 is technically honest and practically deceptive. They met this exact trap on statistics day 13.

4. Cherry-picked range

Choosing where a time axis starts and stops can turn a decline into a rise. Harder to demonstrate with this dataset, so name it and move on — recognition is enough.

The session, minute by minute

Everything in a speech box is meant to be said more or less as written. Everything in a grey box is a direction for you, not words to say.

0 – 22

The table, built from questions

The one thing they must leave with. Build it from the sentence backwards.

Four days, four charts. Today no new chart at all.

Today is the question you will actually be asked, in an interview and on the job: somebody hands you a dataset and a question. Which chart?

And I want you to notice that the wrong way to start is “which function do I call”. That is never where you begin.

Build the table by asking them, row by row. Do not put it up finished — they have earned every row and will remember it better if they supply it.
Read each question out and take the answer from the room.
“How many employees in each department?”
“What do salaries look like?”
“Which department pays most, and how spread out is it?”
“Does experience affect salary?”
Bar, histogram, box plot, scatter. They will get all four. The value is in them hearing that the question chose the chart, not the library.
The table — on the board, and it stays up
WHAT IS THE QUESTION?                        WHAT DO I HAVE?          CHART

how many in each category?                   1 category column        BAR
what does this column look like?             1 number column          HISTOGRAM
middle, spread, outliers?                    1 number (+ category)    BOX PLOT
do these two move together?                  2 number columns         SCATTER
how does this change over time?              a date + a number        LINE


the QUESTION picks the chart. never the other way round.

Five rows. That is genuinely most of what a data analyst draws.

And notice the middle column, because it is the part people forget. The chart depends on what kind of columns you have. Categories or numbers. That is day two of statistics, still deciding things for you five weeks later.

The line chart is the one row they have not drawn. Ten minutes, and the lesson is when, not how.

One row there we have not done — the line chart. It is the same code you already know, so let us do it quickly and spend the time on when to use it.

A line chart, in the code you already know
df["join_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["join_date"])
per_year = df.groupby(df["join_date"].dt.year).size()

plt.plot(per_year.index, per_year.values)

plt.title("Employees who joined each year")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("How many joined")
plt.show()

One new function. pd.to_datetime tells pandas that this text column is really a date, which then lets you ask it for .dt.year. Without that step the join dates are just strings and you cannot group by year.

plt.plot is the line. Everything else is what you have written all week.

“Could I draw the four departments as a line chart instead of bars?”
You can, and you must not. A line says the points connect — that there is something in between. There is nothing between HR and Marketing. A line over time makes sense because March really does sit between February and April.
Line charts are for time, and essentially nothing else. The line is a claim that the space between two points means something. Over time that is true. Over categories it is a lie your chart is telling for you.
22 – 46

The same numbers, two opposite stories

Run it as a vote. Let them be wrong out loud before you explain anything.

This is the centrepiece. Show ONLY the misleading chart first. Cover the other one. Get a number out of them before you reveal anything.

I have the average salary for each of our four departments. Real numbers, from our file, nothing invented.

Here is the chart.

Show this one on its own
means = clean.groupby("department").salary.mean()

plt.bar(means.index, means.values)
plt.ylim(56000, 83000)          # start the ruler near the top
plt.title("Average salary by department")
plt.show()
“Roughly how many times bigger is the Tech bar than the HR bar? Give me a number.”
The room will say things like ten times, or twenty, or “HR is basically nothing”. Write two or three of their answers on the board before you show the second chart. Do not skip this — the wrong answer in their own handwriting is what makes the point.
Now put both up together.
The honest one is one word different
plt.bar(means.index, means.values)
plt.ylim(0, 90000)              # start at ZERO
plt.title("Average salary by department")
plt.show()

print(means.round().astype(int))
department HR 56705 Marketing 73954 Sales 66535 Tech 82419 Name: salary, dtype: int64

Tech is eighty-two thousand. HR is fifty-six thousand. Tech is about one and a half times HR.

Not ten times. Not twenty. One and a half.

And look carefully at what I did. I did not change a single number. Both charts show exactly the same four values. The only difference is where the vertical ruler starts.

On the first one I started it at fifty-six thousand. So HR's bar had almost nothing left above the line, and it looked like HR earns nothing.

For a bar chart, the y-axis starts at zero. Not usually. Always.

The whole idea of a bar is that its length is the value. Cut the bottom off and the length stops meaning anything — you have kept the shape of a bar chart and thrown away the thing that made it one.
Do not moralise here. Most charts like this are made by people who were not trying to deceive anybody — a tool picked the axis automatically, or somebody zoomed in to “show the difference more clearly”. Frame it as how not to do this by accident and the lesson lands. Frame it as fraud and they tune out.
“So is a truncated axis always wrong?”
For bars, yes. For a line chart, no — a share price moving between 1,010 and 1,040 would be a flat line from zero and you would see nothing. A line shows change; a bar shows size. That is the distinction worth remembering.
46 – 64

Three more ways, quickly

Pie, percentage points, cherry-picking. Name them, show one, move on.

Three more, and these are quicker.

The pie chart
counts = df["department"].value_counts().sort_index()

plt.pie(counts.values, labels=counts.index, autopct="%1.0f%%")
plt.title("Pie")
plt.show()

Look at the pie. Tech and HR — which is bigger? You have to concentrate. Now look at the bars. It takes no effort at all.

The reason is simple: people are bad at comparing angles and good at comparing lengths.

A pie is acceptable for two or three slices that obviously add up to a whole. For anything more, use bars. And if you ever see a pie with twelve slices, somebody has made a decorative object, not a chart.

Now the percentage-point trap. They met this on statistics day 13 — say so, because the repetition is the point.
On the board
a signup page goes from  8.0%  to  11.5%

   3.5 PERCENTAGE POINTS      11.5 - 8
   43.75% RELATIVE INCREASE   (11.5 - 8) / 8 x 100

both are TRUE. they sound completely different.

a chart titled "43% improvement" above two bars of 8 and 11.5
is technically honest and practically misleading.

SAY WHICH ONE YOU MEAN. in the title, not in a footnote.

We met this exact trap on day thirteen of statistics, on the A/B test. It is back, because a chart title is where it usually happens.

Three and a half percentage points, or a forty-three percent increase. Both true. And whichever one you put in the title is the one people will remember.

Last one, and I will only name it. Cherry-picking the range.

If a number fell for two years and then rose for six months, you can draw the six months and show a rise, or draw the whole thing and show a fall. Both from the same file. Neither is a false number.

When you see a chart, look at where the time axis starts, and ask why it starts there.

64 – 80

Their turn, and a checklist

Practice picking, not drawing. This is what tomorrow's interview asks.

Read each one out. Let them answer before you confirm. Two minutes each.
Which chart? No code — just the answer and why
1.  "Which city do most of our employees live in?"

2.  "Are our salaries mostly clustered, or spread out?"

3.  "Do people with more experience earn more?"

4.  "Did hiring go up or down over the last ten years?"

5.  "Is Tech's pay more consistent than Sales' pay?"

6.  "What share of employees has each education level?"
Take each answer from the room before confirming.
1 bar — one category column. 2 histogram — the shape of one number column. 3 scatter — two number columns. 4 line — a date and a count. 5 box plot — the word consistent means spread, and box plots compare spread side by side. 6 bar, and expect an argument — “share” tempts people into a pie. Three levels is the one case a pie is defensible; bars are still easier to read.
The checklist — before any chart leaves your laptop
[ ]  does it have a TITLE that says what it shows?

[ ]  are BOTH axes labelled, with units if there are any?

[ ]  if it is bars, does the y-axis start at ZERO?

[ ]  did I choose the chart from the QUESTION,
     or because it was the one I knew how to draw?

[ ]  would somebody who has never seen this data
     understand it without me standing next to them?


five checks. thirty seconds. it is the difference between
an assignment that gets read and one that gets returned.
80 – 90

Closing the module

Name the arc, and hand over to the BI tools honestly.

Five sessions. Let me tell you what you actually have.

You can draw four charts and you know which question each one answers. You can do it in matplotlib the long way and in seaborn the short way. You can put a third column in with hue. And you can look at somebody else's chart and tell whether it is honest.

That last one is the part that will not go away.

What carries into Power BI and Tableau — and what does not
CARRIES OVER, COMPLETELY

  which chart for which question        <- the whole of today
  y-axis starts at zero, for bars
  title and axis labels, always
  nominal sorts by size, ordinal keeps its order
  plot before you analyse
  pie charts are usually the wrong answer

DOES NOT CARRY OVER

  plt.bar, sns.histplot, the syntax        <- the tool does it now
  bins, figsize, tick rotation


you are about to learn a tool that draws for you.
what you learnt this week is WHAT TO ASK IT FOR.

Next module is Power BI, and it will draw these charts by dragging a column onto a canvas. You will not type plt.bar again for a while.

That is fine, and it is why I spent today on choosing rather than on drawing. The tool changes. The question “which chart answers this, and is it honest” does not.

And you will still use Python for exploring — for the first look, before anybody else sees it. That is what these five days were really for.

The four lines. If everything else goes, keep these.
1.  the QUESTION picks the chart. never the library.
      category counts -> BAR      one number column -> HISTOGRAM
      spread + outliers -> BOX    two numbers -> SCATTER
      over time -> LINE

2.  bars start at ZERO. always.
    a bar's LENGTH is the value - cut it off and it means nothing.

3.  people compare LENGTHS well and ANGLES badly.
    that is the whole case against the pie chart.

4.  8% -> 11.5% is 3.5 PERCENTAGE POINTS and a 43.75% RELATIVE rise.
    both true. say which one you mean, in the title.

The session, as a run sheet

Everything in order. Five steps, every code block, every board item written out. If you lose your place, this page alone is enough.

10 – 22

The decision table

Land this: build it by asking, row by row. Do not put it up finished. The question picks the chart, never the library.

Ask these four, take the answers from the room

"how many employees in each department?"    -> BAR
"what do salaries look like?"               -> HISTOGRAM
"which dept pays most, and how spread out?" -> BOX PLOT
"does experience affect salary?"            -> SCATTER
Then the table, and it stays up:
1 category column → BAR · 1 number column → HISTOGRAM · number + category → BOX PLOT · 2 number columns → SCATTER · date + number → LINE

The middle column is the one they forget: what kind of columns do I have? That is statistics day 2, still deciding things five weeks later.

The line chart — the only row they have not drawn

df["join_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["join_date"])
per_year = df.groupby(df["join_date"].dt.year).size()

plt.plot(per_year.index, per_year.values)
plt.title("Employees who joined each year")
plt.xlabel("Year"); plt.ylabel("How many joined")
plt.show()
One new function: pd.to_datetime turns the text column into a real date, which is what makes .dt.year possible.

Then ask: “could I draw the four departments as a line?” — you can, and you must not. A line claims the space between two points means something. True for time. A lie for categories.
222 – 46

The same numbers, two stories

Land this: the centrepiece. Show only the misleading chart. Get a number out of them and write it on the board before you reveal the honest one.

Show this one alone

means = clean.groupby("department").salary.mean()

plt.bar(means.index, means.values)
plt.ylim(56000, 83000)
plt.title("Average salary by department")
plt.show()
Ask: “roughly how many times bigger is Tech than HR? Give me a number.” Expect ten times, twenty, “HR is nothing”. Write two or three answers up. Do not skip this step.

Then the honest one — one word different

plt.ylim(0, 90000)
print(means.round().astype(int))
HR 56705 Marketing 73954 Sales 66535 Tech 82419
Tech is about 1.5× HR. Not ten. Not twenty.

Not one number changed. Only where the ruler starts.

The rule: for bars the y-axis starts at zero, always — a bar's length is the value, so cutting the bottom off throws away the only thing that made it a bar.
Do not moralise. Most of these are made by accident — a tool auto-picked the axis, or somebody zoomed in to “show it more clearly”. Frame it as how not to do this by accident.

Expect: “always wrong?” — for bars yes; for a line no, a share price between 1,010 and 1,040 would be flat from zero. Line shows change, bar shows size.
346 – 64

Three more, quickly

counts = df["department"].value_counts().sort_index()
plt.pie(counts.values, labels=counts.index, autopct="%1.0f%%")
plt.show()
Ask: “on the pie — Tech or HR, which is bigger?” They have to concentrate. On bars it is instant.

The reason: people compare lengths well and angles badly. A pie is fine for 2–3 slices that make a whole. Twelve slices is a decorative object, not a chart.
The percentage-point trap — back from statistics day 13:
8% → 11.5% is 3.5 percentage points AND a 43.75% relative increase. Both true. Say which one you mean, in the title, not a footnote.
Cherry-picking — name only: pick the last six months and show a rise, pick ten years and show a fall. Same file. Look at where the time axis starts, and ask why.
464 – 80

Which chart? — no code

Land this: practise picking, not drawing. This is exactly what an interview asks. Take each answer from the room first.

1. "which city do most employees live in?"
2. "are salaries clustered or spread out?"
3. "do people with more experience earn more?"
4. "did hiring go up or down over ten years?"
5. "is Tech's pay more consistent than Sales'?"
6. "what share has each education level?"
1 bar · 2 histogram · 3 scatter · 4 line · 5 box plot — “consistent” means spread · 6 bar, and expect an argument — “share” tempts them into a pie.

The checklist — on the board

[ ] a TITLE that says what it shows?
[ ] BOTH axes labelled, with units?
[ ] if bars, does y start at ZERO?
[ ] did the QUESTION pick the chart, or did I pick
    the one I knew how to draw?
