580 – 90

Close the module

CARRIES INTO POWER BI / TABLEAU     DOES NOT CARRY

which chart for which question      plt.bar, sns.histplot
y starts at zero, for bars          bins, figsize, ticks
title and labels, always
nominal by size, ordinal in order
plot before you analyse
pies are usually the wrong answer
The handover, said plainly: “the next tool draws for you. What you learnt this week is what to ask it for.”

And Python charting stays useful for exploring — the first look, before anybody else sees it.

Questions you will get

“Is a truncated y-axis always dishonest?”

“For bars, treat it as always wrong — the length is the value. For a line, no: a share price moving between 1,010 and 1,040 drawn from zero is a flat line showing nothing. The rule follows from what the ink means. Bars encode size, lines encode change.”

“Are pie charts banned then?”

“Not banned — usually beaten. Two or three slices that clearly add to a whole is fine. Past that, bars are easier to read and you lose nothing. If a manager asks for a pie, give them a pie and put the numbers on it.”

“How do I know what the interviewer wants when they say ‘visualise this’?”

“Ask them what question they want answered. That is not dodging — it is the correct first move and they are often testing whether you make it. Then say your reasoning out loud: ‘salary is one numeric column and I want its shape, so a histogram.’ The reasoning is what is being marked.”

“If Power BI does all of this, why learn Python charting?”

“Two reasons. Nearly every analyst job description asks for it, so it is a screening filter before anybody looks at the rest of you. And it is what you use to explore — the first look at a file, before you know what the dashboard should even contain. Power BI is for what you show other people.”

“What if two charts both work for a question?”

“Common, and fine. Salary by department could be box plots or bars of the averages. Box plots show spread, bars show only the middle. Pick the one that shows what the question needs, and be able to say why you picked it — that sentence is worth more than the chart.”

“Should I put the numbers on the chart as well?”

“For a handful of bars, yes — it costs nothing and removes all argument. For a scatter with two hundred dots, obviously not. The test is whether a reader would otherwise have to guess a value off the axis.”

“We never made a dashboard.”

“Deliberately. A dashboard is several charts arranged for somebody else to use, and the tool for that is Power BI, which is next. Building one in Python is possible and almost nobody does it. What you needed first was to know which charts belong on it.”

Excel day 1 · merged class · 90 minutes · full script · opens the module

The Same File,
With No Code

They have worked on employees.csv for more than twenty sessions and have never once seen it. Today they open it — and two of the things they hunted for with statistics and with charts are sitting on screen before they scroll.

201rows, all of them visible
=the whole idea
row 5the outlier, in plain sight
$the one that breaks everything

Open the file. Tell them not to scroll.

Row 5 is Lakshmi Kumar, Tech, salary 5,200,000. That is the one earner who destroyed their correlation — the reason Pearson came out at 0.079 instead of 0.607. Row 9 is Manoj Kumar, and the salary cell is empty. That is one of the two missing salaries they kept having to work around.

A whole statistics session went into the first one. A whole visualisation session went into drawing it. Here they are both on the first screen, and nobody typed anything. That is the argument for a spreadsheet, and it takes ninety seconds.

Before you walk in

  1. Open the file and say “do not scroll”. Row 5 and row 9 do the whole opening for you. If they scroll, they lose the moment — it only works because the screen has not moved.
  2. Save As .xlsx in the first five minutes, before any formula. A .csv file cannot store a formula. It stores only text. If they build the whole summary and then save, Excel keeps the answers and throws every formula away, and they will not find out until tomorrow. Do this step together, out loud, and do not move on until every laptop has done it.
  3. Say in minute one that Google Sheets and LibreOffice Calc both work. Every single thing in today's session — the grid, =, all seven functions, the dollar sign, autofill — is identical in all three. Nobody has to buy anything. Say it before somebody panics quietly for an hour.
  4. Write the twelve column letters on the board and leave them up all session. A to L, emp_id to join_date. You will be asked “which one is salary” ten times and the board answers it without stopping you.
  5. Budget twenty minutes for the dollar sign, and let the wrong answer happen on screen first. This is the one thing in Excel that goes wrong quietly. Do not warn them. Drag the broken formula down, let them see a column of nonsense, and then fix it. The fear is the lesson.
  6. Four shortcuts today and no more. Ctrl+↓, Ctrl+Home, double-click on the autofill square, and F4. On a Mac F4 is often taken by the system — if it does nothing, type the two dollar signs by hand and move on. Do not lose five minutes on a keyboard.

Understand this yourself first

Three things: what a cell actually holds and why that makes Excel worth a module after Python, how a reference works and what the dollar sign does to it, and what the formulas quietly skip. If you are shaky anywhere it will be part two, so read it twice.

Part one · what a cell holds, and why Excel comes after Python and not before
A cell holds one of two things

It holds a value — a number, a word, a date. Or it holds a rule for working out a value, and then it shows you the answer instead of the rule.

That is the entire idea of a spreadsheet, and the = sign is the switch between the two. Type 38 and the cell holds 38. Type =20+18 and the cell shows 38 but holds the rule. Click it and the formula bar at the top shows you the rule.

Why the rule being stored matters

Because the rule gets re-run on its own. Change a salary in column K and every cell whose rule mentions that salary works itself out again immediately. Not when you ask. Immediately.

In their Python work, the opposite is true. df["salary"].mean() runs once and gives a number. Change the file and that number is now wrong and nothing tells you — you have to remember to run it again.

This is the whole difference, and it is not the mouse.

A script is a set of instructions you run. A spreadsheet is a set of rules that are always running. That is why a business that has had Python for twenty years still has every number it cares about in a spreadsheet — somebody can change one cell and watch the answer move.
The same property is the danger, and you must say so

Nothing on the sheet records that the cell was changed. There is no log. One typo in one cell changes every number on the sheet, silently, and the person reading the sheet tomorrow has no way to know. Real companies have lost real money to exactly this.

So the honest summary is: a spreadsheet is faster to change and much harder to trust. A script is slower to change and leaves a record of exactly what it did.

The hard limits, so you can answer the question straight
rows
1,048,576. That is the maximum, and it is not a setting you can raise. Their file has 201. A real web log has five million, and Excel simply cannot open it.
columns
16,384, the last one lettered XFD. Nobody reaches this.
speed
Fine to about a hundred thousand rows with simple formulas. Past that it starts to freeze on every edit, because every rule on the sheet re-runs on every change.
so
Excel for data a human is going to read. Python for data a human cannot. That is the honest split, and it is also the answer in an interview.
Part two · the reference, the colon, and the dollar sign
A reference
definition
A reference is the address of a cell: the column letter followed by the row number.
how it works
Writing K2 inside a formula means “go and fetch whatever is in cell K2 right now”. It does not copy the number. It points at it.
example
Salary is column K and the first employee is on row 2, so =K2 in any empty cell shows 47764.
=K2 -> 47764
watch out for
Row 1 is the header, not an employee. K1 is the word salary. The 201 employees live on rows 2 to 202.
The colon
definition
A colon between two references means through — everything from the first cell to the last, inclusive.
how it works
I2:I202 is 201 cells: I2, I3, I4, all the way down to I202. One short piece of text instead of 201 addresses.
example
Age is column I, so the average age of everybody is
=AVERAGE(I2:I202) -> 38.175
which is the same 38.2 they got from pandas in the first visualisation session.
watch out for
They will write I:I for “the whole column”, which includes the header. AVERAGE happens to skip the word age so the answer comes out right anyway — which is exactly why it is dangerous. Teach I2:I202.
Relative is the default, and that is on purpose

Copy a formula from one cell to another and Excel moves the references with it. A formula in M2 that says =K2-100 becomes =K3-100 when you copy it to M3.

This sounds like a bug. It is the single most useful thing Excel does. It is what lets you write one formula and fill 201 rows with it, because what the formula really means is not “K2”, it is “the salary on my own row”.

The dollar sign
definition
A $ in front of a letter or a number freezes that part, so copying the formula does not move it.
how it works
$Q$10 means column Q, row 10, and nothing will change it. Copy that formula anywhere on the sheet and it still points at Q10.
example
The average salary is going to live in one cell, Q10. Every one of the 201 rows has to subtract that same cell.
M2: =K2-$Q$10 -> -47884.41 M3: =K3-$Q$10 -> -9596.41 M4: =K4-$Q$10 -> -32658.41
The K moved down a row each time. The Q10 did not move at all. That is the whole point.
watch out for
Half-locks exist — Q$10 freezes only the row, $Q10 only the column. Do not teach them today. They are for filling a grid in two directions, which is day five. Today: either both dollars or neither.
What the broken version looks like, and why it is worse than a crash

If they write =K2-Q10 with no dollars and drag it down, row 3 asks for Q11, row 4 asks for Q12, and so on down the sheet. There is no error. Excel does exactly what it was told.

Q11 happens to hold the median salary, 68647, so row 3 produces 17405 — a number that looks completely plausible. Q12 onwards are empty cells, and an empty cell in arithmetic counts as zero, so every row after that just shows the salary itself back again.

Nothing went red. Nothing said error.

One row right, one row plausibly wrong, and then two hundred rows of the salary column copied. This is the failure they have to be able to recognise on sight, because it is the one that gets into real reports.
Part three · blanks, text, and what the formulas quietly skip
COUNT and COUNTA are not the same function
COUNT
Counts cells that hold a number. Text does not count. A blank does not count.
COUNTA
Counts cells that hold anything at all — numbers, words, dates. Only a truly empty cell is skipped.
so
=COUNT(C2:C202) on the name column gives 0, because a name is not a number. That surprises everybody once and then never again.
Why that pair is the most useful thing in this session

Put the two side by side on columns that should agree, and the gap tells you what is missing.

=COUNTA(C2:C202) -> 201 names nothing missing =COUNT(I2:I202) -> 200 ages one missing =COUNT(K2:K202) -> 199 salaries two missing

201 rows. 200 ages. 199 salaries. They already knew those gaps existed, because pandas told them. This is the spreadsheet version of the same check, and it is two formulas.

A blank is not a zero, and AVERAGE knows the difference

AVERAGE skips blank cells completely. It does not count them and it does not treat them as zero. So the average salary divides by 199, not by 201.

=AVERAGE(K2:K202) -> 95648.41 divides by 199 (correct) =SUM(K2:K202)/COUNTA(C2:C202) -> 94696.68 divides by 201 (wrong)

A thousand rupees of difference, from two empty cells. And if anybody ever types a 0 into those two cells to “tidy them up”, the average becomes the second number permanently and nobody will notice.

There is also a function that counts them directly: =COUNTBLANK(K2:K202) gives 2. Worth thirty seconds, no more.

Formatting changes what you see, not what is there

=AVERAGE(I2:I202) gives 38.175. Click Decrease Decimal twice and the cell shows 38.2. The cell still holds 38.175. Every formula that points at it still uses 38.175.

This matters more than it sounds. Somebody will later show you two cells that both display 38.2 and refuse to add up, and the reason will be that one of them is really 38.175. Teach the sentence now: the number you see and the number that is there are two different things.
The two mistakes that will happen in the first ten minutes
no equals
They type AVERAGE(I2:I202) and the cell shows the text AVERAGE(I2:I202). Nothing is broken. There is no =, so Excel treated it as a word. The = is not decoration. It is the switch.
hashes
The cell fills with #####. The number does not fit in the column. Drag the line between the column headers, or double-click it. It is not an error.
One thing to say out loud, because it closes a loop from statistics

dept_id is column B. =AVERAGE(B2:B202) gives 2.32 — the same meaningless 2.32 that opened statistics day 2.

Excel does not know that dept_id is a label and not a quantity. Neither did pandas. No tool will ever ask you whether your question makes sense. Thirty seconds, and it tells them that moving to a friendlier tool has not made them safer.

The session, minute by minute

Everything in a speech box is meant to be said more or less as written. Everything in a grey box is a direction for you, not words to say.

0 – 12

Open it, and do not scroll

Twenty sessions on this file and they have never seen it. Two of its famous problems are on the first screen.

Laptops open. Everybody opens the same file. Say “do not scroll” before they touch the mouse — the whole opening depends on the screen not moving.

Find employees.csv on your laptop. The same file we have used since the first day of statistics. Double-click it. It will open in Excel.

Now take your hand off the mouse. Do not scroll.

What is on the screen — the columns that matter, as they really are
      A       C                 D          I     K         L
 1  emp_id  name            department  age   salary    join_date

 2  1001    Rahul Sharma    HR           53    47764    2018-01-03
 3  1002    Karthik Kumar   Marketing    57    86052    2024-07-02
 4  1003    Karthik Reddy   Tech         56    62990    2025-03-04
 5  1004    Lakshmi Kumar   Tech         41  5200000    2022-10-15
 6  1005    Arjun Sharma    HR           42    62556    2022-05-20
 7  1006    Sneha Reddy     Sales        25    47111    2023-10-26
 8  1007    Lakshmi Menon   HR           51    60925    2025-02-02
 9  1008    Manoj Kumar     HR           28   (empty)   2022-01-07

     columns B, E, F, G and J are on screen too - left out here only to fit.
Point at nothing. Just ask: “look at row five. What is that salary?”
Fifty-two lakh. That is the earner you have spent two sessions on. It is the reason your Pearson correlation came out at 0.079 instead of 0.607. Then: “now look at row nine.” The salary cell is empty — one of the two missing salaries. Wait for both. They will find them.

In statistics we spent a whole session on that one salary, and we could only find it through arithmetic — the mean was 95,648, the median was 68,647, and the gap between them told us something was wrong somewhere.

Last week we spent a whole session drawing it, so you could point at the dot.

Today you opened the file and it is on row five. Nobody typed anything.

Numbers summarise. Pictures show. A spreadsheet just puts the data in front of you.

That is not a small thing, and it is why this tool has survived forty years of better tools. Two hundred and one rows is a size a human being can actually look at.
Now the vocabulary, quickly. Four words, two minutes, then move.

Across the top, letters. Down the side, numbers. One box is a cell, and its name is the letter and the number together. K5 is the fifty-two lakh.

Click on it. Look at the top left — there is a small box showing K5. That is the Name Box. It always tells you where you are, and you can type an address into it to jump anywhere.

Row one is not a person. It is the header — the column names. Our people start on row two.

Four words on the board. That is the entire vocabulary for today.
  CELL        one box.  named by its column letter + row number.  K5
  NAME BOX    top left.  tells you where you are, and jumps you anywhere
  HEADER      row 1.  the column names.  NOT a person
  ROW COUNT   Ctrl + Down from A1  ->  A202,  minus the header  =  201
Two shortcuts, and the answer to “how many rows is this?”
  click A1  then  Ctrl + Down     jumps to the last filled cell in the column
  Ctrl + Home                     jumps back to A1 from anywhere
you land on A202

Row 202. Row one was the header, so that is 201 rows of data.

Two hundred and one. Not two hundred. You have seen 201 before — there is a duplicate row in this file, two copies of the same employee. We deal with that on Thursday.

Now the save step. Do not skip it and do not rush it. Wait until every laptop has done it.

One thing before we write a single formula. Go to File, then Save As. Change the type from CSV to Excel Workbook, which is .xlsx. Save it as employees.xlsx.

Here is why. A .csv file is plain text — you read one by hand in Python, you know exactly what is inside it. Commas and numbers. There is nowhere in that file to put a formula.

So if you spend the next hour building formulas and then save this as a CSV, Excel keeps the answers and throws every formula away. Open it tomorrow and all your work is gone, and the file will look fine, which is worse.

Expect “why did it ask me something when I pressed save?” Excel warns you when you save a workbook as CSV — that formulas and extra sheets will be lost. Show them that warning on purpose. It is the only time Excel tells you before destroying something, so it is worth recognising.
Column L may not look like the file. Depending on the laptop's region settings, Excel reads 2018-01-03 as a date and redisplays it as 03-01-2018, or leaves it as plain text. Either is fine and neither is wrong. Nothing in today's session touches join_date. If somebody asks, say “Excel guessed it was a date, we deal with dates properly later” and move on — do not start on date formats in the first ten minutes.
12 – 26

The equals sign

One idea, and the whole tool follows from it. A cell can hold a value, or a rule.

We need an empty cell to play in, well away from the data. Type A205 into the Name Box and press Enter. That is three rows below the last employee, where we cannot damage anything.

Type 38 and press Enter. The cell holds 38. Nothing interesting.

Now go back to it and type this instead.

Type it with the equals sign
=20+18
38

The cell shows 38. But click on it once and look at the formula bar — the long white strip above the letters.

The cell is not holding 38. It is holding the rule =20+18, and it is showing you what the rule works out to.

That is the entire tool. Every cell holds either a value, or a rule. And the equals sign is how you tell Excel which one you mean.

Somebody will type AVERAGE(I2:I202) without the equals sign in the next five minutes. Pre-empt it.
The cell will show the text AVERAGE(I2:I202), left-aligned, looking silly. Nothing is broken. There was no equals sign, so Excel read it as a word. Say the sentence: the equals sign is not decoration, it is the switch.

Now the useful version. Instead of typing numbers into the rule, we point at cells.

Still in A205 — point at a cell instead of typing a number
=K5
5200000

K5 is not the number five point two million. It is an address. The rule says “go and fetch whatever is in K5 right now”.

Hold on to the words right now. We come back to them in half an hour and they turn out to be the most important thing in this session.

One more piece of punctuation and then we can do real work. The colon.

Age is column I. The first person is on row 2 and the last is on row 202. So instead of writing two hundred and one addresses, I write the first one, a colon, and the last one.

I2:I202. Read the colon out loud as the word through. “I2 through I202.” Two hundred and one cells.

The first real formula of the module
=AVERAGE(I2:I202)
38.175
“Where have you seen that number before?”
38.2 — the average age, from the first visualisation session. Exact same number. Let somebody in the room say it rather than saying it yourself.

Thirty-eight point one seven five. That is the average age, and it is the same number pandas gave you, because it is the same arithmetic on the same file.

I want to be clear about what today is. You are not learning new statistics. You learned all of it already. Today you are learning to do it with a mouse, on a tool the people who ask you for numbers actually have open.

Quick formatting aside — sixty seconds, and it prevents a confusion that will come back in week two.

The −4 and the 210. They have met both before, in the visualisation session, where it took a chart to find them. Here two formulas did it. Also watch for somebody noticing 201 rows but only 200 ages — if they spot that themselves, stop and make a lot of it.

COUNTA counts cells that have anything in them. I pointed it at the name column, because every row has a name in it. 201.

COUNT — no A — counts cells that have a number in them. I pointed it at the age column. 200.

That is how you find missing data in a spreadsheet.

Count a column that is never empty. Count the column you care about. The gap is what is missing. You already did this in pandas with isnull().sum() — this is the same check, with two formulas and no library.
Try this live and let it surprise them. Put =COUNT(C2:C202) — COUNT, not COUNTA — on the name column. It gives 0. Not an error, not a crash: zero, because a name is not a number. One demonstration and nobody mixes up the two functions again.

Now the two that should have bothered you. MIN gives the smallest value in the column. MAX gives the largest.

The youngest person in this company is minus four years old. The oldest is two hundred and ten.

You met both of these last week. It took us a chart to find them. Today it took two formulas.

“201 rows, 199 salaries. How many salaries are missing, and can you prove it?”

95,648 average, 68,647 in the middle. You know those two numbers — the gap between them is the whole reason we learned about skew.

Now a question I want you to think about carefully. AVERAGE added up the salaries and divided. Divided by what? 199, or 201?

Put both on the sheet and compare them. Any two empty cells.
=AVERAGE(K2:K202)                 -- what we already have
=SUM(K2:K202)/COUNTA(C2:C202)     -- total, divided by all 201 rows
95648.41 divides by 199 (what AVERAGE does) 94696.68 divides by 201 (counting the blanks as nothing earned)

Nearly a thousand rupees apart, and both of them look perfectly reasonable.

AVERAGE skips empty cells completely. It does not count them, and it does not treat them as zero. So it divided by 199. That is the right behaviour, and it is the same thing pandas does.

A blank is not a zero.

An empty salary means we do not know. A salary of zero means this person earns nothing. Those are completely different facts. The day somebody types 0 into those two cells to tidy the sheet up, the average drops to 94,696 and stays there, and nobody will notice.

Two point three two. The average department number.

Department 2 is Tech and department 3 is HR. So 2.32 is somewhere between Tech and HR, which is not a sentence that means anything.

You remember this one. It is a label that happens to be written with digits, and averaging it means nothing at all.

Excel did not stop me. Excel does not know that dept_id is a name and not a quantity. Pandas did not stop you either.

No tool will ever ask you whether your question makes sense. That is still your job, and it is the only part of this course that no software will ever do for you.

44 – 56

The one thing a script cannot do

Why this tool exists, answered honestly — including the part that makes it dangerous.

This is the block that answers “sir, we already know pandas, why are we learning this”. Somebody is thinking it. Ask it for them.

Let me ask the question you are all too polite to ask. You can already do every one of those seven formulas in pandas, in one line each. So why are we spending two weeks on a spreadsheet?

It is a fair question and it has a real answer. Watch the screen.

Keep your summary block where you can see it. Now click on K5 — the fifty-two lakh salary.

Suppose we find out it was a typing mistake. Somebody typed an extra zero. The real salary is five lakh twenty thousand.

Type 520000 and press Enter. Do not look away from your summary block.

Before and after — one cell changed, nothing else touched
                    before          after

 salaries             199             199
 total salary    19034033        14354033
 average salary  95648.41        72130.82
 middle salary      68647           68647
“How many formulas did I re-run?”
None. They re-ran themselves, the instant the cell changed. And ask the second half too: “why did the middle salary not move?” Because 520,000 is still the largest salary in the file, so nobody changed places in the sorted order. The median only cares about position, which is exactly what they learned in statistics.

The average dropped by twenty-three thousand rupees because one person's salary changed. The total dropped by forty-seven lakh. And I did not run anything.

Now think about what that same change costs you in Python. Open the CSV. Edit the row. Save it. Run read_csv again. Run the mean again. Run the median again. Run every cell in the notebook again, in order, and hope you did not miss one.

A script is instructions you run. A spreadsheet is rules that are always running.

That is the real difference, and it has nothing to do with the mouse. It is why a company that has had Python for twenty years still keeps the numbers it actually argues about in a spreadsheet — because somebody in that meeting can change one cell and watch the answer move.
Now turn it around. Do not skip this half. It is what separates somebody who uses Excel from somebody who can be trusted with it.

Now the other side, and this is the part nobody teaches you.

I just changed a number that every single formula on this sheet depends on. Where does it say that I did that?

Nowhere. There is no record. No note, no mark on the cell, no list of changes. If I hand you this file tomorrow you will see 72,130 as the average salary and you will have no way at all to know that I edited it.

Your Python notebook would have shown it. The line that changed the salary would still be sitting there in the code, for anybody to read.

Say this plainly, because it is interview-grade. A spreadsheet is faster to change and much harder to trust. A script is slower to change and leaves a record of exactly what it did. Real companies have lost real money to a single wrong cell that nobody could see. You are going to use both tools for the rest of your career, and knowing which one a job needs is part of being good at this.

Put it back — Ctrl + Z. Your average should go back to 95,648.

Then the size limits, two minutes, because somebody always asks and it is a real interview question.

One more honest limit. A sheet stops at ten lakh forty-eight thousand five hundred and seventy-six rows. That is fixed. You cannot change it.

Our file has 201 rows, so we are fine. A month of website visits is five million rows, and Excel cannot open it at all. Pandas will not even notice.

Excel for data a human is going to look at. Python for data a human cannot.

That is the honest split, it is the answer if an interviewer asks you which is better, and it is why you are learning both.

That square is called the fill handle, and it is the most used thing in Excel. Put your mouse on it until the pointer turns into a thin black plus, then double-click it.

It fills all the way down to row 202 in one go, because column L next to it runs that far. Now stop. Say nothing. Let them look at what they got.

“Is that right? Look at row four. The salary is 62,990 and the gap from the average is also 62,990. Can that be true?”
No — it would only be true if the average salary were zero. From row 4 down, column M is just a copy of column K. And row 3 is worse: 17,405 looks completely believable and is wrong. Let them sit with it. Nothing went red. Nothing said error.

Nothing crashed. Nothing turned red. Excel did not complain once. And the whole column after row two is rubbish.

Let us find out why. Click on M3 and read the formula bar.

What the formula bar says in each cell
  M2    =K2-Q10        what I actually typed
  M3    =K3-Q11        both halves moved down one
  M4    =K4-Q12
  M5    =K5-Q13
  M6    =K6-Q14

Excel moved both addresses down. The K moved down, and the Q moved down with it.

And now look at what the Q is landing on. Q11 is the middle salary, 68,647 — so row 3 worked out 86,052 minus 68,647, which is 17,405. A real subtraction, of the wrong number.

Q12 is empty. Q13 is empty. Everything below Q11 is empty. And an empty cell in a subtraction counts as zero. Salary minus nothing is the salary. That is why the rest of the column is a copy of column K.

This is the single most dangerous thing in Excel, and it is not an error message.

One row right, one row plausibly wrong, two hundred rows of nonsense — and the sheet looks perfectly healthy. Learn to recognise a column that has quietly turned into a copy of its neighbour.
Now the correction. Explain why Excel moved the addresses before you explain how to stop it — otherwise they will think it was a bug, and it is the opposite.

Before we fix it, understand why Excel did that, because it is not a bug. It is the best thing about the tool.

When I wrote K2 on row 2, Excel did not store “K2”. It stored “the cell five to my left”. So on row 3 that means K3, and on row 152 it means K152.

And that is exactly what I wanted for the salary. Every row should use its own salary. Without that behaviour I really would be typing two hundred formulas.

The problem is the other half. The average salary is not different on each row. It is one cell, Q10, for everybody. And I have no way yet of telling Excel the difference.

That is what the dollar sign is for. A dollar sign means do not move this.

Go back to M2 and change the formula to this.

M2, corrected — two dollar signs, nothing else different
=K2-$Q$10

$Q means never change the letter. $10 means never change the number. So $Q$10 means Q10, always, no matter where you copy this.

The K moved down every row. The $Q$10 did not move at all. That is the whole idea.

Now look at the shape of the column. Scroll down it. Almost every number is negative.

I will give you the exact count, because it is worth hearing out loud. Of the 199 salaries in this file, 187 are below the average. Twelve people are above it.

Ninety-four per cent of this company earns less than the average salary of this company. That sentence sounds impossible and it is completely true, and you already know why — it is the fifty-two lakh earner on row 5 dragging the average up past almost everybody.

In statistics we proved that with a mean and a median twenty-seven thousand apart. Here you can scroll down it.

“How did you count the 187?” Say honestly that you used a formula they do not have yet — COUNTIF, which counts cells that pass a test. It arrives in the third session. Today the point is only that the column has a shape, and they can see it.
“Row 9 says minus 95,648. Manoj Kumar has no salary in this file. So what does minus 95,648 mean?”
Nothing. It is wrong. The cell is empty, and an empty cell in arithmetic becomes zero, so Excel worked out 0 minus 95,648. This is the trap worth more than anything else today, so give it the time.
Two different behaviours, and you need both.

AVERAGE, COUNT, SUM and the rest skip an empty cell. Plain arithmetic — plus, minus, times — turns it into zero.

So the same blank cell is ignored by one formula and counted as nothing-earned by the next one on the same sheet. Nobody tells you. You have to know.

Last thing in this block, and it will save you a lot of typing. You do not have to type the dollar signs by hand.

While you are writing a formula, click on the address and press F4. Excel puts both dollar signs in for you. Press it again and it cycles through the other combinations — ignore those for now, we need them in week two.

On a Mac F4 is often taken by the system and does nothing. Try fn+F4 once, and if that fails, type the two dollar signs by hand and move on. It is two characters. Do not lose five minutes of the session to a keyboard.

86 – 90

Close, and what comes next

Four things from today. If you forget everything else, keep these.

The four lines. Put them on the board and leave them up.
1.  a cell holds a VALUE or a RULE.
    the = sign is the switch between them.
    no = means excel reads it as a word, not a formula.

2.  a colon means THROUGH.
    I2:I202 is 201 cells, because row 1 is the header.

3.  copying a formula MOVES its addresses. that is the useful part.
    $Q$10 means "do not move this one". that is the part you forget.
    the broken version does not crash - it quietly copies
    the column next to it.

4.  a blank is not a zero.
    AVERAGE, COUNT, SUM  ->  skip it.
    plus, minus, times   ->  treat it as zero.

And look at what we did today without writing one line of code. We found a person who is minus four years old. We found a person with no salary. We found the fifty-two lakh earner. We proved one age and two salaries are missing. And we built a column of two hundred and one answers from one formula.

All of it on the file you have known for twenty sessions.

Thursday we stop looking and start fixing. Three things are waiting for us in this file and you have met all of them.

The duplicate. 201 rows, 200 employees — somebody is in there twice, and Excel has a button that finds them.

The minus four and the two hundred and ten. Thursday they turn red automatically, without you looking for them.

Aditya Gupta. Today I had to tell you he was on row 152. Thursday you will find him yourself, in about four clicks.

 8    60925      -34723.41
 9   (empty)    -95648.41       <-- ask about this one
Scroll the column and give them the count: 187 of the 199 are negative. Twelve people are above the average salary. Ninety-four per cent of the company earns less than the company average — and they already know why, it is row 5. Say you used COUNTIF, which is session three.
Row 9 is the big one. Manoj Kumar has no salary, so Excel did 0 minus 95,648. AVERAGE / COUNT / SUM skip a blank. Plus, minus and times turn it into zero. Same blank cell, two behaviours, on the same sheet, and nobody tells you.
F4 puts both dollars in while you are typing. On a Mac it is often dead — type the two characters by hand and move on. Fill-handle broken? Click M2, Ctrl+C, type M3:M202 in the Name Box, Enter, Ctrl+V.

Close

1.  a cell holds a VALUE or a RULE. the = is the switch.
2.  a colon means THROUGH. I2:I202 is 201 cells, row 1 is the header.
3.  copying MOVES the addresses - that is the useful part.
    $Q$10 means "do not move this one" - that is the part you forget.
    the broken version does not crash. it copies the next column.
4.  a blank is not a zero.
    AVERAGE / COUNT / SUM  ->  skip it
    plus / minus / times   ->  zero
Count the wins out loud: a person aged −4, a person with no salary, the 52 lakh earner, one age and two salaries proved missing, and 201 answers from one formula — and not one line of code.
Set up Thursday: the duplicate — 201 rows, 200 employees, and Excel has a button for it. The −4 and the 210 — they turn red automatically. Aditya Gupta — today you were told row 152, Thursday you find him in four clicks.

Ask them these before they leave

Thirteen questions, in order, with the answer under each one. Numbers 4, 8 and 9 are the three that matter. Take each answer from a different person.

A cell can hold one of two kinds of thing. What are they?
A value — a number, a word, a date. Or a rule for working out a value. If it holds a rule, it shows you the answer and keeps the rule.
My cell is showing the words AVERAGE(I2:I202) instead of a number. What did I do?
Left out the =. With no equals sign Excel read it as text. Nothing is broken. The equals sign is the switch between a value and a rule.
What does the colon mean in I2:I202, and why does it start at 2?
The colon means through — every cell from I2 down to I202, which is 201 cells. It starts at 2 because row 1 is the header, not a person.
What is the difference between COUNT and COUNTA?
COUNT counts cells holding a number. COUNTA counts cells holding anything at all. Only a truly empty cell is skipped by COUNTA.
I put =COUNT(C2:C202) on the name column and got 0. Is that an error?
No. It is the correct answer. There are 201 names and not one of them is a number, so COUNT counted nothing.
COUNTA on names gave 201 and COUNT on ages gave 200. What does that tell you, and what did you use to do in pandas?
One row has no age in it. Count a column that is never empty, count the column you care about, and the gap is what is missing. In pandas that was isnull().sum().
=AVERAGE(K2:K202) gave 95,648. It added up the salaries and divided — by 199 or by 201?
199. There are only 199 salaries in the file. AVERAGE skips the two empty cells completely. Dividing by 201 would have given 94,696.68, which is a different and wrong answer.
So is a blank cell the same as a zero or not?
It depends on the formula, and that is the whole trap. AVERAGE, COUNT and SUM skip a blank. Plain arithmetic — plus, minus, times — turns it into zero. Same cell, two behaviours, same sheet.
In =K2-$Q$10, what do the two dollar signs stop from happening?
They stop the address moving when the formula is copied. $Q locks the letter, $10 locks the number. Every row has its own salary, but all 201 rows share one average.
I dragged =K2-Q10 down with no dollar signs and column M turned into a copy of column K. Why was there no error message?
Because nothing illegal happened. Excel moved both addresses down, so row 4 asked for Q12, which is empty, and an empty cell in a subtraction is zero. Salary minus nothing is the salary. It did exactly what it was told.
The cell shows 38.2. What is actually in it?
38.175. Decrease Decimal changed what you are shown, not what is stored. Every formula pointing at that cell still uses 38.175.
I changed one salary and a dozen numbers on the sheet changed with it. Where is it recorded that I did that?
Nowhere. There is no log and no mark on the cell. That is why a spreadsheet is faster to change and much harder to trust than a script.
I built the whole summary and saved the file as .csv. What have I lost?
Every formula. A CSV is plain text and has nowhere to put a rule — it keeps only the answers that were showing. And the file will look completely fine, which is the worst part.

Questions you will get

“Why are we learning Excel when we already know pandas?”

“Two reasons, and both are real. First, it recalculates on its own. Change one cell and every answer that depends on it moves immediately — in Python you have to remember to run it again. Second, it is what the person asking you for the number already has open. Nobody in a sales meeting is going to open your notebook. You will be sent a spreadsheet and asked for an answer by lunchtime, and that is a normal week in this job.”

“I don't have Microsoft Excel. Can I use Google Sheets?”

“Yes, and LibreOffice Calc too. Every single thing in today's session is identical in all three — the grid, the equals sign, all seven functions, the colon, the dollar sign, the fill handle. The only difference is the saving step: Google Sheets saves itself, so you can skip it. When we reach pivot tables the buttons sit in slightly different places, and I will show both.”

“My cell is full of #####.”

“That is not an error. The number is too wide for the column. Double-click the line between the two column letters at the top and it will widen to fit. Nothing is lost — the number is still in there.”

“My formula is showing as text even though I typed the equals sign.”

“Two causes. Either that cell was formatted as Text before you typed — set it back to General on the Home tab, then press F2 and Enter to retype it. Or somebody pressed Ctrl+`, which turns on Show Formulas for the whole sheet. Press it again and everything comes back.”

“Should we just delete the −4 and the 210?”

“Not until you know why they are there, and that answer has not changed since we were in Python. If one person typed 4 as −4, that is one fix on one row. If the system writes −4 whenever an age is missing, then every −4 means missing and there could be thousands of them in the real database. Find out what it means first. Thursday we make them visible, and after that we decide.”

“F4 does nothing on my laptop.”

“On most Macs it is taken by the system. Try fn+F4 once, and if that does nothing, type the two dollar signs yourself. It is two characters and it is exactly the same result. Do not spend your evening on this.”

“Why write I2:I202? Can I not just say the whole column I:I?”

“You can, and today it would even give the right answer, because AVERAGE ignores the word age in the header. But that is luck, not a rule. COUNTA(C:C) would count the header and tell you there are 202 people. Say exactly what you mean — the people are on rows 2 to 202.”

“Could Excel open a file with fifty lakh rows?”

“No. A sheet stops at 10,48,576 rows and that is fixed — it is not a setting. Our file has 201 so we are nowhere near it. A month of website visits is five million rows and Excel will not open it at all, while pandas will not even notice. Excel for data a human is going to look at. Python for data a human cannot. That is the honest answer in an interview too.”

“Is this the same as Power BI?”

“No, and they are not competing. Excel is where you work on the data — clean it, calculate on it, check it. Power BI is where you show it to somebody who will never touch the numbers. Power BI comes after this module, and most of what you learn here carries straight over.”

=            # tells excel "this is a RULE, not a value"
no =         # excel reads it as TEXT. the commonest mistake in the room

I2:I202      # the colon means THROUGH. 201 cells, because row 1 is the header
$Q$10        # the dollars mean DO NOT MOVE when this formula is copied

# ---- THE EIGHT FUNCTIONS FROM TODAY ----
=COUNTA(C2:C202)       # 201        counts anything that is not empty
=COUNT(I2:I202)        # 200        counts NUMBERS only
=COUNTBLANK(K2:K202)   # 2          counts empty cells
=SUM(K2:K202)          # 19034033   adds them up
=AVERAGE(K2:K202)      # 95648.41   the mean
=MEDIAN(K2:K202)       # 68647      the middle one
=MIN(I2:I202)          # -4         the smallest
=MAX(I2:I202)          # 210        the largest

# 1  A BLANK IS NOT A ZERO

#
# 2  WHAT YOU SEE IS NOT WHAT THE CELL HOLDS

Excel day 2 · merged class · 90 minutes · full script · pays back three promises from day 1

Cleaning, With the
Sheet Looking Back

On day 1 two formulas told them the youngest person in this company is minus four years old, and then refused to say who. Today they find him in four clicks. Then they sort one column on its own, and two hundred true rows become two hundred false ones — with every single statistic on the sheet unchanged.

2 clicksand the −4 and the 210 have names
row 202the second Anita Patel
3 cellsevery blank in the file, selected at once
K alonethe sort that destroys the file

Rehearse the one-column sort before you walk in. It is the whole session.

Select only column K, the salary column, and sort it smallest to largest. Excel will stop you with a box called Sort Warning. It offers Expand the selection, which is already chosen and is the correct answer. You have to pick “Continue with the current selection” on purpose. If you click the default, nothing breaks, and the lesson is gone.

What happens next is the point. Every salary in the file is still in the file. The total is still 19,034,033 and the average is still 95,648.41, because the same 199 numbers are still sitting in the same column. Nothing turns red. Nothing says error. And every row is now a lie. Rahul Sharma on row 2 is being paid Aditya Gupta's salary.

Then Ctrl + Z, once, immediately. That is the only way back, and this is the one mistake in this module that no number on the sheet can ever tell you about.

Before you walk in

  1. Make a spare copy of the file first, and tell them to do the same. Today has three buttons that delete things — Remove Duplicates, Text to Columns and Replace All. Copy employees.xlsx and call the copy employees-day2-backup.xlsx. If a laptop ends up wrecked, they open the backup instead of losing the session.
  2. Say “Ctrl + Z” in minute one and write it on the board. Everything today is undoable if you press it straight away. Everything today is permanent if you save and close first. That is the whole safety rule and it takes ten seconds.
  3. Clear columns M and N at the start, and keep P and Q. M and N hold yesterday's two practice columns and they will get in the way when rows start moving. Select M1:N202 and press Delete. Do not touch the summary block in P and Q — watching those numbers change themselves when you delete a row is the best free demonstration in the session.
  4. Name the three promises in minute one. Day 1 ended by promising them three things: the duplicate row, the −4 and the 210 turning red on their own, and finding Aditya Gupta without being told where he is. All three get paid back today. Say so before you start, so they know what they are collecting.
  5. The row count changes from 202 to 201 in the middle of the session. After Remove Duplicates there are 200 people and the last row is 201, not 202. Say it out loud the moment it happens and write the new number on the board, or you will spend the last half hour correcting ranges one laptop at a time.
  6. This file is clean on spaces and spelling, and the last block makes a mess on purpose. There is not one leading space anywhere in it, and every department, city, education and rating value is spelled exactly one way. So the TRIM block types five fake rows at the bottom of the sheet. Say “I made these five rows up” out loud, twice, or somebody will go home and hunt for row 206.
  7. Five shortcuts today and no more. Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+L for the filter, Ctrl+G for Go To, Ctrl+H for Replace, and the Name Box for jumping. Every one of them also has a button on a ribbon tab, and on a Mac the button is the safer route. Do not lose five minutes to a keyboard.

Understand this yourself first

Three things: what sorting and filtering actually do to the file, which of today's five buttons change your data and which only change what you are looking at, and why this particular file has nothing to clean. The second one is the part you will be asked about all session, so read it twice.

Part one · a row is only held together by sitting in a row
There is no glue

Row 2 is Rahul Sharma. His emp_id, his department, his age and his salary are one person only because those twelve values are sitting next to each other. Nothing inside the file links them. There is no key, no pointer, no record.

That is why sorting is dangerous and filtering is not. Sorting moves values. If you told Excel to move whole rows, the twelve values travel together and the person survives. If you told Excel to move one column, that column slides past the other eleven and the person is destroyed.

Excel does exactly what you selected. That is the entire story of this session.

Select the whole table and sort — 201 people change places. Select one column and sort — 201 people get somebody else's salary. Both are called Sort, both sit under the same button, and only one of them tells you afterwards.
Excel does warn you, and that is the uncomfortable part

Select one column inside a block of data and press Sort, and Excel shows a box called Sort Warning:

Excel found data next to your selection. Since you have not selected this data, it will not be sorted. (o) Expand the selection <-- already chosen. the right answer. ( ) Continue with the current selection

So the real lesson is not “Excel let me destroy my data”. The real lesson is the warning was there and somebody clicked past it, which is how it actually happens in an office. Teach them to read that box instead of closing it.

Sort
definition
Sort rewrites the file in a new order. It is not a view. The rows really move.
how it works
Select the table, Data → Sort, pick a column and a direction. Tick My data has headers so row 1 stays on top instead of being sorted in with the people.
example
Sort the whole table by age, smallest to largest.
row 2 Aditya Gupta -4 <-- the MIN from yesterday, with a name row 201 Lakshmi Singh 210 <-- the MAX from yesterday, with a name
watch out for
Blank cells always go last. Smallest to largest or largest to smallest, it makes no difference — an empty cell is pushed to the bottom either way. One age is missing in this file, so after an age sort the very last row is the person with no age, not the 210.
and
There is no unsort button. Once you sort, the order the file arrived in is gone. Ctrl+Z brings it back, and so does sorting by emp_id — the ids in this file run 1001, 1002, 1003 straight down the rows. That is what an id column is for.
Filter
definition
A filter hides rows. It is a pair of glasses, not a knife. Nothing is deleted and nothing moves.
how it works
Data → Filter puts a small arrow on every header. Open an arrow and Excel shows you every distinct value in that column, built by reading the column. Untick what you do not want.
example
Filter department to HR. The status bar at the bottom left says
45 of 201 records found
and the row numbers down the left turn blue and start skipping — 2, then 8, then 15. The missing numbers are the rows that are still there.
watch out for
Your formulas ignore the filter completely. With only 45 rows showing, Q1 still says 201 and Q10 still says 95,648.41. That is the proof that nothing was deleted, and it is also the thing that catches people out. There is one function that does respect a filter, SUBTOTAL, and it is not today.
and
Copying a filtered range copies only the visible rows. That is usually what you wanted, and it surprises everybody the first time.
Part two · five buttons, and exactly what each one destroys
The one table that answers every question you will get today

Before anything else, know which of today's tools touch your data and which only touch what you are looking at. Almost every hand that goes up is really asking this.

sort
Changes the data. Rows really move, permanently.
filter
Changes nothing. Rows are hidden. Formulas still see them.
cond. formatting
Changes nothing. It only adds colour. Every number is exactly as it was.
go to special
Changes nothing. It only selects cells. What you do next is up to you.
remove duplicates
Deletes rows, and does not show you which ones first.
text to columns
Writes over the column to its right, with no warning at all. The most destructive button in the module.
replace all
Rewrites cells. On the whole sheet, unless you selected a range first.
Remove Duplicates
definition
Deletes rows that are repeats of a row higher up the sheet. It keeps the first one it meets and deletes the rest. It does not ask you which to keep.
how it works
Select the table, Data → Remove Duplicates. You get a list of all twelve columns with tick boxes. The ticks decide what the word duplicate means. All twelve ticked = only rows that match on all twelve counts.
example
On this file, all twelve ticked:
1 duplicate values found and removed; 200 unique values remain.
201 rows became 200. emp_id 1021, Anita Patel, was in the file twice — on row 22 and again on row 202.
watch out for
Tick fewer boxes and you delete real people. There are only 20 first names and 10 last names in this whole file — two hundred possible names for two hundred and one people. Names must repeat in here. Tick only name and Excel will happily delete somebody who simply shares a name with somebody else.
Conditional formatting
definition
A rule attached to a range: “colour this cell if it passes this test”. It is not paint.
how it works
Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules, then Greater Than, Less Than, Between, Duplicate Values. Excel re-checks the rule every time the cell changes.
example
Two rules on I2:I202 — less than 0, and greater than 100. Out of 201 ages, exactly two cells light up:
I152 -4 Aditya Gupta I179 210 Lakshmi Singh
Nothing else. And nobody went looking.
watch out for
It is a rule, so it un-colours itself too. Type 29 over the −4 and the red disappears on its own. That is the day 1 idea — rules that are always running — applied to colour instead of to a number.
and
Colour is not a filter. The two red cells are still 27 rows apart and you still have to scroll to them. Colour tells you that something is wrong. A filter tells you where.
Go To Special → Blanks
definition
Selects every empty cell inside the range you have highlighted. It changes nothing — it only puts your cursor on all of them at once.
how it works
Select the data range. Then Home → Find & Select → Go To Special, or Ctrl+G then the Special button. Tick Blanks. OK.
example
On the 200-row file it selects exactly three cells:
K9 salary Manoj Kumar K44 salary Pooja Rao I93 age Sanjay Menon
Yesterday two COUNT formulas told them how many were missing. This tells them where.
watch out for
Select the data first, not the whole sheet. Press Ctrl+A and then Go To Special and Excel selects a million empty cells and freezes for a moment. Select A1:L201 and it finds three.
Text to Columns
definition
Splits one column of text into several columns, cutting at a character you choose — usually a space or a comma.
how it works
Data → Text to Columns, then Delimited → Next, tick Space → Next. On step 3 there is a Destination box. That box is the whole safety story.
example
Column C is name, and all 201 names are exactly two words. Split C with the destination set to $S$2:
S T 2 Rahul Sharma 3 Karthik Kumar 4 Karthik Reddy
Column C is untouched, because the output went somewhere empty.
watch out for
Leave the destination at $C$2 and you lose the department column. The second half of every name is written straight into column D, 201 times, with no warning and no prompt. Ctrl+Z brings it back — if you noticed.
Part three · why this file has nothing to clean, and the numbers that move today
I checked the file, and it is clean

There is not one cell in employees.csv with a space at the front or the back. The department column holds four values and no more. The city column holds four. Education holds three. Rating holds four. Every one of them is spelled exactly one way, every time.

So TRIM has nothing to trim, PROPER has nothing to fix, and Find & Replace has nothing to find. Pretending otherwise would mean inventing dirt and telling them it was there, and they would never find it again.

So the last block of the session types five dirty rows by hand, at row 206, and cleans those.

Say out loud that you made them up. Interviewers do ask about TRIM — it is one of the most asked Excel text functions there is — so it earns its minutes. But it earns them honestly, on data you built in front of them, not on a lie about their own file.
TRIM, PROPER, UPPER, LOWER
TRIM
Removes spaces from the front and the back, and squeezes any run of spaces in the middle down to one. It does not remove all spaces.
PROPER
Capital letter at the start of every word, small letters for the rest of it. UPPER makes it all capitals, LOWER all small.
example
The five made-up rows, and a LEN to prove the invisible space is real. LEN counts the characters in a cell.
A208 looks like Anita Patel 11 letters and a space = 11 characters =LEN(A208) 12 so there is a 12th character =TRIM(A208) Anita Patel =LEN(TRIM(A208)) 11 the 12th character was a space at the end
watch out for
These functions do not fix the original column. They build a clean copy in a new column. To finish the job you must Copy the clean column and Paste Special → Values over the old one, then delete the helper. Paste it normally and you paste the formulas, which then point at cells you are about to delete, and the whole column turns into #REF!.
Three numbers will move on their own today, and they are the best demo in the session

Yesterday's summary block is still sitting in P and Q, and it recalculates every time the file changes. When Remove Duplicates takes one row out, nobody retypes anything and three of those answers change by themselves:

before after why Q1 rows 201 200 one row gone Q2 ages 200 199 Anita Patel had an age Q8 salaries 199 198 Anita Patel had a salary

The two age extremes do not move — MIN is still −4 and MAX is still 210, because Anita Patel was neither. The averages shift very slightly, and there is no reason to read them out.

Say the sentence when it happens. “I deleted a row and three answers on the other side of the sheet corrected themselves. That is what we proved yesterday when we changed one salary and the whole summary block moved.” It costs ten seconds and it ties the two sessions together.
One honest limit on all of today's cleaning

Not one of today's buttons fixes the two broken ages. Sorting finds them. Red colouring points at them. A filter isolates them. None of them knows what the right answer is, and neither do we, because nobody has told us whether −4 means somebody typed it wrong or whether the system writes −4 when an age is missing.

Finding a problem and fixing a problem are two different jobs, and today is the first one.

This is the answer to “sir, should we just delete it”, and it has not changed since they were in Python. Make the problem impossible to miss, write down exactly what you found, and ask the person who owns the data. An analyst who guesses is worth less than one who asks.

The session, minute by minute

Everything in a speech box is meant to be said more or less as written. Everything in a grey box is a direction for you, not words to say.

Two minutes of housekeeping that saves half an hour, then name out loud the three things today owes them.

Here is why. Yesterday every single thing we did was a formula in an empty cell. If you got it wrong, you deleted the cell. Today we move rows, delete rows and write over columns. Three of the buttons we press actually destroy things.

And one key, which is the only safety rule you need all session. Ctrl and Z. Undo.

Everything today is undoable if you press it straight away. Everything today is permanent the moment you save and close. So if something looks wrong, do not sit and stare at it — press Ctrl Z first and work out what happened after.

Now scroll down. Row 1 stays on screen. You can see the column names from anywhere in the file.

You will be reading this file all session and you will stop asking me which column is which.

Now the frame for the session. Day 1 ended with three promises. Name all three before you start, so they know what they are collecting.

Last session ended with me owing you three things. I want to say all three out loud now.

One. This file has 201 rows and 200 employees. Somebody is in there twice. I told you Excel has a button that finds them.

Two. The minus four and the two hundred and ten. I said that today they would turn red by themselves, without anybody looking for them.

Three. Aditya Gupta. Yesterday I told you he was on row 152, and I admitted I cheated — I already knew. I said today you would find him yourself in about four clicks.

All three today. And one thing I did not promise you, which is the most important ninety seconds of this module: a way to break this file so badly that no number on the sheet can tell you it happened.

Yesterday was looking. Today is touching.

Every formula yesterday went into an empty cell and read the data without changing it. Everything today reaches into the data itself. That is a real step up in what you can do and a real step up in what you can wreck, and both halves are the lesson.

And of course it did not. The same one hundred and ninety-nine salaries are still sitting in the same column K. I did not add one, I did not delete one, I did not edit one. I only changed the order they are in. The total of a list does not care what order the list is in. Neither does the average. Neither does the median.

So think about what that means. Every statistic you know how to calculate — mean, median, minimum, maximum, standard deviation, correlation, every single one — is exactly the same on a file where every row is a lie.

Nothing turned red. Nothing said error. No formula will ever warn you. If I save this file now and close it, nobody on earth can tell this happened.

This is the worst thing you can do to a spreadsheet, and it is three clicks.

Yesterday's dangerous mistake — the missing dollar sign — at least left two hundred rows of visible nonsense on the screen. This one leaves a file that looks perfect. Every column valid, every total correct, every row wrong.

Nothing can put a salary back next to the right person once you have done this, because nothing in the file records which person it belonged to.

A filter hides rows, it does not delete them — and there are two ways to prove that on screen. Then they collect promise number three.

After the last block the room is a bit shaken. Good. Filter is the safe tool and it is the one they will use most in their working life. Fourteen minutes.

That was the dangerous one. This one cannot hurt you at all, and it is the tool you will use every single day of this job.

“Only 45 rows on my screen. But Q1 still says 201. Did Excel delete the other hundred and fifty-six or not?”
No. And there are two proofs on the screen at once. The row numbers skip — 2, then 8, then 15 — and the missing numbers are the rows that are still sitting there. And =COUNTA(C2:C202) still counts 201 names, because a formula does not care what you are looking at.
A filter is a pair of glasses, not a knife.

Nothing is deleted. Nothing moves. You have changed what is on your screen and you have changed nothing else. That is why it is safe, and it is also why the number in your filtered view and the number in your formula can disagree with each other all day.

And you already know what you just did. In pandas that is value_counts. You have just done value_counts with a mouse, one value at a time. Next session you get COUNTIF, which puts all four of those numbers on the sheet at the same time and updates them when the data changes.

To clear a filter, open the arrow and tick Select All again. Or Data, then Clear — the funnel with a small red cross — which clears every filter on the sheet at once.

And Clear is not the same as turning the filter off. Clear shows all the rows and leaves the arrows there. Pressing Data, Filter again takes the arrows away completely. Two different buttons, and people mix them up for years.

None. That is the point and it is worth saying slowly. You did not search, you did not sort, you did not read a single row. You described what a wrong answer looks like, and the sheet found them. That is promise number two, paid.

Now I want to show you what conditional formatting actually is, because the name makes it sound like decoration and it is not.

Click on the red cell. Type 29 and press Enter.

The red went away on its own. I did not remove it. Nothing un-coloured it.

Because it was never a colour. It is a rule — “go red if you are less than zero” — and the cell is not less than zero any more, so it stopped being red.

Now press Ctrl Z. The minus four comes back, and so does the red.

This is yesterday's idea in a different costume.

Yesterday: a cell holds a value or a rule, and a rule re-runs itself whenever anything it depends on changes. Today: a colour can be a rule too, and it re-checks itself the same way. Same tool, same behaviour. A spreadsheet is a pile of rules that are always running.
Where the rules live, if somebody wants to change or delete one. Home → Conditional Formatting → Manage Rules. It lists both rules and which range each one covers. Clear Rules on the same menu removes them. Thirty seconds, so they know it is not permanent paint.
And the honest limit on colour. The two red cells are twenty-seven rows apart and you still have to scroll to find them. Colour tells you that something is wrong. A filter tells you where. Stop and understand what those tick boxes mean, because this is the only part of this button that can hurt you.

The ticks decide what the word “duplicate” means. All twelve ticked means “only delete a row if it matches another row on all twelve columns”. That is the safe answer and it is what we want.

Now imagine I tick only name. There are only twenty first names and ten last names in this whole file. Twenty times ten is two hundred possible names, for two hundred and one people. Names must repeat in here. So Excel would go down the file deleting everybody who shares a name with somebody above them, and it would not tell you who they were.
