Two hundred. Not two hundred and one.

Click A1 and press Ctrl and down arrow. You land on A201 now, not A202.

Write this on the board, because it changes for the rest of the session: our data is now rows 2 to 201. Two hundred people. From here on, when I say select the data, it is A1:L201.

Now the free demonstration. Point at the summary block in column Q. They have not touched it since yesterday.
Nobody retyped anything. Three answers corrected themselves.
                         before    after

 Q1    rows                201      200     one row gone
 Q2    ages                200      199     Anita Patel had an age
 Q8    salaries            199      198     Anita Patel had a salary

 Q5    youngest             -4        -4     unchanged - she was not the -4
 Q6    oldest              210       210     unchanged - or the 210
“How many of those formulas did you retype?”
None. Same as yesterday when they changed one salary and the whole block moved. A spreadsheet is rules that are always running — say the sentence again, because this is the second time they have watched it happen and the first time it was on a row they deleted.

And one more thing, which is the honest version of what you just did. Those department counts we read off the status bar twenty minutes ago are now wrong by one.

Sales 65, Tech 49, HR 45, Marketing 42. One of those four is now one lower, because one of those rows was Anita Patel twice.

You were counting rows. You thought you were counting people. Those are the same number only in a clean file, and nobody hands you a clean file.

Clean first. Count second. In that order, always.

Every number anybody got out of this file in the last twenty sessions — the average age, the average salary, the correlation, every chart — was computed on 201 rows for 200 people. None of it was badly wrong. All of it was slightly wrong, and nothing told anybody.
Remove Duplicates keeps the first one it meets and deletes the rest. It does not ask you which copy to keep. Here both copies are identical so it makes no difference — but one day you will have two rows for the same customer with different addresses, and then the order your rows are in decides which address survives. That is why we coloured them and looked at them first.
Expect: “could I have just ticked emp_id?” Yes, and here it would have given the same answer, because an id is supposed to be unique. That is a real and often better choice — but only when you know what the column is for. All twelve is the answer when you do not know.
And yes, Ctrl+Z undoes Remove Duplicates and brings the row back. But it deleted a row without showing you which one, and that is the habit to be nervous about, not the undo.
58 – 72

Find every blank at once, and split a column in two

Two buttons, seven minutes each. One shows them where the missing values are. The other is the most destructive button in the module, and they learn the safe way first.

Yesterday you proved this file is missing one age and two salaries, with two COUNT formulas. 201 names, 200 ages, 199 salaries.

What those formulas could not tell you is where. Here is the button that does.

Select the data first — A1:L201 in the Name Box. This matters, and I will show you why in a minute.

Go To Special. Two routes — use the ribbon one if the keyboard fights you.
  keyboard    Ctrl + G      ->  then the  [ Special ]  button
  ribbon      Home  ->  Find & Select  ->  Go To Special

  then        (o) Blanks      and  OK
Three cells are now selected, all at once
  K9      salary    Manoj Kumar      HR
  K44     salary    Pooja Rao        ...
  I93     age       Sanjay Menon     ...

     press Enter or Tab to walk your cursor from one to the next.
     the Name Box at the top left tells you which one you are on.
“Yesterday's formulas said one age and two salaries were missing. Does that match?”
Exactly. Two salary cells and one age cell. And one of them is K9, Manoj Kumar — the empty cell they spotted on the very first screen of day 1, before anybody scrolled. The count told them how many. This tells them who.

And here is the other name on that list, which I want you to notice. Sanjay Menon. You met him forty minutes ago — he was the very last row when we sorted by age, pushed to the bottom because his age cell is empty.

Two completely different tools, one sort and one Go To Special, and they both pointed at the same man. That is what it feels like when your checks agree.

Now the useful bit. All three cells are still selected. Do not fill them in — mark them.

All three cells are still selected. So I can do one thing to all three at once.

Go to Home, click the Fill Colour button — the little paint pot — and pick yellow.

Three cells, one click, and now anybody who opens this file can see exactly what is missing and where. And I have not changed one value. That is yesterday's sentence again: the number you see and the number that is there are two different things. I changed what you see. There is still nothing in those cells.

Now. With all three selected I could type a number and press Ctrl and Enter, and Excel would put it in all three cells at the same time.

Do not. Think about what you would be typing.

A zero in a salary cell says this person earns nothing. That is a lie, and you proved yesterday that it drags the average down and stays there and nobody notices. A zero in an age cell is worse — it says somebody was born this year.

We do not know what belongs in those three cells. So we mark them, we write down exactly which three cells they are, and we ask whoever owns this data. That is the answer in an interview and it is the answer in a job.

Finding a problem and fixing a problem are two different jobs, and today is the first one.

Everything in this session makes problems impossible to miss. Not one thing in this session decides what the right answer is, because that is not a spreadsheet question. An analyst who guesses is worth less than one who asks.
Why selecting the range first mattered. Do Go To Special → Blanks with just one cell selected, or after pressing Ctrl+A, and Excel looks at a much bigger area — it will select a very large number of empty cells and sit there for a second. Select A1:L201 and it finds three. Go To Special only ever looks inside what you selected.
Second half — Text to Columns. Teach the danger before the demonstration, because this is the one button today where the damage is silent and 201 rows wide.

Last tool. This one splits one column into two, and it is the most destructive button we touch today, so we are going to do it the safe way from the start.

Column C is name, and every name in this file is two words — a first name and a last name, with a space between them. I want them in separate columns.

Before we start, look at what is beside column C. Column D is department. Hold on to that.

Select the names, not the header, then open the wizard
  type  C2:C201  into the Name Box and press Enter

  then  Data  ->  Text to Columns
The wizard. Three steps, and step 3 is the one that matters.
  Step 1 of 3     (o) Delimited          our names are split by a space
                  ( ) Fixed width
                  Next

  Step 2 of 3     Delimiters:  [x] Space    [ ] Tab  [ ] Comma  [ ] Semicolon
                  [ ] Treat consecutive delimiters as one
                  the Data preview at the bottom now shows TWO columns
                  Next

  Step 3 of 3     Destination:   $S$2      <-- CHANGE THIS. it says $C$2.
                  Finish

That Destination box on step 3 is the whole safety story of this button.

Excel offers to put the answer back where the names came from, $C$2. The first names would land in C, which is fine. And the last names would land in the column to the right of it.

Which is column D. Which is department.

Two hundred departments, overwritten with surnames. No warning. No prompt. No red. Ctrl Z brings it back — if you noticed, and the thing about silent damage is that you do not.

So change it. Type $S$2 into the Destination box. Column S is miles away from everything and there is nothing to its right. Then Finish.

What is in S and T now, with column C untouched
        C                   S           T

 1   name                first name   last name     type these two by hand

 2   Rahul Sharma        Rahul       Sharma
 3   Karthik Kumar       Karthik     Kumar
 4   Karthik Reddy       Karthik     Reddy
 5   Lakshmi Kumar       Lakshmi     Kumar
 6   Arjun Sharma        Arjun       Sharma
 7   Sneha Reddy         Sneha       Reddy

Column C is exactly as it was. The split went somewhere empty, and that is the habit: never run Text to Columns into a column that has something to its right.

Now put labels in S1 and T1 by hand — first name and last name. No equals sign, they are just words.

Now check the work with yesterday's function. This is the best moment in the block — a check they already know, used on something new.

How do I know it worked for all two hundred rows and not just the six I can see? I am not scrolling two hundred rows.

Put this in any empty cell — V1 will do.

V1 — yesterday's function, checking today's work
=COUNTA(T2:T201)
200

Two hundred. Two hundred people, two hundred last names. Every single row split.

If that had said 197, then three names did not split, and I would go and find out why before using this column for anything.

That is yesterday's trick doing a completely new job. Count a column you expect to be full. If the number is not what you expect, something is wrong and you now know how many.

And one last thing with this new column, because it is a nice payoff. Turn the main filter off first — Data, Filter — because a plain sheet only allows one filter at a time.

Now click in T1 and press Data, Filter again. Open the arrow on last name.

Every surname in the company, read off a dropdown
  [x] Gupta    [x] Menon    [x] Patel    [x] Reddy    [x] Singh
  [x] Iyer     [x] Nair     [x] Rao      [x] Sharma   [x] Kumar

     ten. and the first name column has exactly twenty.

Ten surnames. Two hundred people. And you could not have asked that question an hour ago, because the surname was not a column — it was half of a word.

That is what reshaping data is for. You did not add information. You changed the shape, and a question that was impossible became a dropdown.

Why the split was so clean, and why you should not expect that again. All two hundred names here are exactly two words with exactly one space. In a real file somebody is called Rahul Kumar Sharma, and that splits into three pieces — the third one lands in column U, which here is empty and in a real sheet is somebody's data. And somebody else has two spaces by accident, which gives you an empty middle column unless you tick Treat consecutive delimiters as one on step 2. Always look at the Data preview on step 2 before pressing Next.
There is a second way, and it is worth sixty seconds. Type Rahul into an empty cell next to the first name, then press Ctrl+E. That is Flash Fill — Excel guesses the pattern from your one example and fills the rest. It is lovely and it is a guess, which is exactly why we taught the wizard first. Mention it, do not teach it.
72 – 84

A mess we make on purpose — TRIM, PROPER and Replace All

This file is clean. There is nothing in it to trim and nothing spelled two ways. So the mess gets typed in by hand, at row 206, and cleaned there. Say out loud that you made it up.

This is the only block today that can be cut. If the sort block ran long, skip it and give it to session 3, and say so to the room. If it runs, the five rows at 206 to 210 are invented — say that sentence twice, or somebody will spend an evening looking for row 206 in their own file.

One more group of tools, and I have to be straight with you about something first.

I went through this file properly. There is not one cell in it with a space at the front or the back. Every department is spelled one way. Every city is spelled one way. Every education and every rating, one way each — you proved that yourselves half an hour ago when every dropdown added up to 201.

So the three most famous cleaning tools in Excel have nothing to do in this file. And interviewers ask about them constantly.

So we are going to make the mess ourselves. I am about to type five rows that are not real. They are not in your file. I am inventing them. Say that back to me later if you remember nothing else.

Type these five rows by hand, starting at A206. Well below the data, with a gap.
         A                      B            C

 206   rahul sharma          tech         Bengaluru
 207  PRIYA IYER            HR           bangalore
 208  Anita Patel           hr           Bangalore
 209  sanjay  menon         Tech         BLR
 210  Kavya Rao             marketing    Bangalore

     row 206 has ONE SPACE before the r.
     row 208 has ONE SPACE after the final l.
     row 209 has TWO SPACES in the middle.
     row 210 is already fine - we need one clean row to compare against.

Look at that column of names. Row 206 and row 208 look completely normal. You cannot see a space. Nobody can see a space. That is the entire problem with this kind of dirt — it is invisible and it breaks everything quietly.

So the first job is to make it visible. There is a function that counts the characters in a cell. LEN.

E206, then fill down to E210
=LEN(A206)
206 13 207 10 208 12 209 13 210 9
“Row 208 says Anita Patel. Count it on your fingers — five letters, a space, five letters. That is eleven. So why does Excel say twelve?”
Because there is a twelfth character and it is a space at the end. LEN is how you prove an invisible problem is real. Row 206 is the same trick at the front — twelve characters of name and a thirteenth hiding before the r.

Now clean them. Two functions, and we are going to use them together in one go.

TRIM removes spaces from the front and the back, and squeezes any run of spaces in the middle down to a single one. PROPER puts a capital letter at the start of every word and makes the rest small.

And you can put one inside the other. Excel works out the inside one first and hands the answer to the outside one.

F206, then fill down. TRIM runs first, PROPER runs on its answer.
=PROPER(TRIM(A206))
And G206 to prove the spaces are gone
=LEN(F206)
A F E G 206 rahul sharma Rahul Sharma 13 12 207 PRIYA IYER Priya Iyer 10 10 208 Anita Patel Anita Patel 12 11 209 sanjay menon Sanjay Menon 13 12 210 Kavya Rao Kavya Rao 9 9
“Three rows got shorter and two did not. Which two, and why?”
207 and 210 — they had no stray spaces to begin with. 207 only had the wrong capitals, and PROPER does not change the length. So TRIM leaves clean data completely alone, which is why it is safe to run on a whole column without checking first. And row 209 went from 13 to 12 with no space at either end — that is TRIM squeezing the double space in the middle down to one.
Now the PROPER trap. Sixty seconds and it is worth every one of them, because it is the reason the next tool exists.

So PROPER fixes capital letters. Let us use it on the department column, which is also a mess in my made-up rows. tech, HR, hr, Tech, marketing.

Try it on two of them and read the answers carefully
=PROPER(B206)      tech        ->  Tech      correct
=PROPER(B210)      marketing   ->  Marketing correct
=PROPER(B207)      HR          ->  Hr        WRONG
=UPPER(B208)       hr          ->  HR        correct, but only for HR
=LOWER(B209)       Tech        ->  tech      correct, and useless

Look at the third line. PROPER turned HR into Hr.

It is doing exactly what it was told — capital at the start, small for the rest. It does not know that HR is two initials and not a word. No function knows what your data means. You have heard that sentence in this course before.

So there is no single function that can fix this one column, because it holds three ordinary words and one pair of initials. And that is exactly what the next tool is for.

Find & Replace. Teach the selection habit before the dialog, the same way you did for sorting.

Look at my made-up city column. Bengaluru, bangalore, Bangalore, BLR, Bangalore. Five rows, four spellings, one city. This is the most common dirt in real data and no function fixes it, because the computer has no way to know those are the same place. You have to tell it.

First, select the cells you want to change. C206:C210. This is the whole safety rule for this tool and we will see why in a minute.

Then Ctrl and H. Or Home, Find & Select, Replace.

Three replacements, one at a time. Read the count Excel reports each time.
  Find what:  BLR            Replace with:  Bangalore     -> 1 changed
  Find what:  Bengaluru      Replace with:  Bangalore     -> 1 changed

  now the awkward one. only row 207 is still wrong, and it is
  wrong only in its capital letter.

  Options >>   [x] Match case
  Find what:  bangalore      Replace with:  Bangalore     -> 1 changed
206 Bangalore 207 Bangalore 208 Bangalore 209 Bangalore 210 Bangalore

One city, one spelling, and now it would count as one thing in a filter dropdown instead of four.

And Match case is the box that made the last one possible. With it off, Excel does not care about capitals, which is usually convenient and is sometimes the difference between changing one cell and changing four.

“Why did I select those five cells before pressing Ctrl H?”
Because with nothing selected, Replace All runs on the entire sheet. Every column, all two hundred rows, plus the summary block and the split name columns. And it replaces inside words, not just whole cells — unless you tick Match entire cell contents, which is the other safety box in that dialog. Select first, always.
Replace All is the only tool today that changes data you are not looking at.

Sort tells you by moving things. Remove Duplicates tells you how many it removed. Text to Columns at least damages the column you can see. Replace All quietly edits cells on parts of the sheet you have scrolled past — which is why the selection, Match case and Match entire cell contents are three boxes worth reading every single time.
The other half of the TRIM job, and it is the half people forget. TRIM and PROPER did not fix column A. They built a clean copy in column F. To finish, you Copy column F, then Paste Special → Values over column A, then delete F. Paste it normally and you paste the formulas, which then point at the column you are about to delete, and the whole thing turns into #REF!. Show the Paste Special menu even if you do not do the paste — it is the single most useful right-click in Excel.
Now clean up, out loud. Deleting the invented rows is part of the lesson — it is the moment you say again that they were never real.

Last job. Click on the row number 206 on the far left, hold shift, click 210. Five whole rows selected. Right-click, Delete.

Then select columns E, F and G and delete those too.

And say it with me, because I want it to stick: those five rows were never in the file. I typed them in front of you because your file is clean and these three tools had nothing to do. Your file has two hundred rows, no stray spaces and no misspelled values, and that is not what the next file you are sent will look like.

84 – 90

Close, and what comes next

Five things from today. If you forget everything else, keep these.

The five lines. Put them on the board and leave them up.
1.  SELECT THE WHOLE TABLE, THEN SORT.
    one column sorted on its own = every row is a lie,
    and every total on the sheet is still correct.
    if excel offers to "expand the selection" - say yes.

2.  a filter HIDES rows. it does not delete them.
    proof: the row numbers skip, and COUNTA still says the old number.

3.  conditional formatting is a RULE, not a colour.
    describe what wrong looks like. the sheet finds it for you.
    change the cell and the colour corrects itself.

4.  before you delete anything, LOOK at it.
    colour the duplicates. select the blanks. then decide.
    remove duplicates keeps the FIRST one and asks you nothing.

5.  a blank is still not a zero.
    sorting pushes blanks to the bottom, both directions.
    and you still do not get to invent what belongs in them.

And look at what we did without one line of code, and almost without a formula.

We found out who is minus four years old and who is two hundred and ten. We found out who has no age and who has no salary, and exactly which three cells they are. We found a row that was in the file twice and took it out, and two hundred and one became two hundred. We turned a name into two columns and then asked a question we could not have asked before. And we broke the file so badly that no number on it could tell us.

Yesterday the file told you numbers. Today the file told you names.

Now say what you skipped. Naming the gaps makes the session trustworthy and it stops the clever student in the back from thinking they have found a hole in the course.
What today left out on purpose, and where it goes
sorting by two columns at once       the "Add Level" button in the Sort box.
                                    real and useful. you will meet it when
                                    you need it.

sorting by your own order           "Custom List" - Poor, Average, Good,
                                    Excellent instead of alphabetical.
                                    mentioned today, not taught.

sort and filter BY COLOUR           one sentence today. it works, it is
                                    not important yet.

Flash Fill  (Ctrl + E)              mentioned. it guesses, so you learn
                                    the wizard first.

Advanced Filter, dropdown lists     later in the module, or not at all.
(data validation)

COUNTIF  /  SUMIF  /  value_counts  next session. all of it.

Next session the sheet starts answering questions instead of just showing you things.

Today you filtered to HR and read 45 off the bottom of the screen. It is not on the sheet, it does not update, and you had to click four times to get it. Next session one formula puts all four department counts on the sheet at once and they fix themselves when the data changes. That is COUNTIF, and you already know it — it is value_counts.

And then IF, which is the first time a cell makes a decision instead of a calculation. “If this salary is above the average, write ABOVE, otherwise write BELOW.” Two hundred rows, one formula.

Bring the cleaned file. Two hundred rows, no duplicate, three yellow cells, and two red ones.

One sentence to leave them with, because it is the one an interviewer will ask for.

Sorting, filtering and colouring do not clean data. They make dirt impossible to miss. Deciding what the right value is was never a spreadsheet job, and the person who asks instead of guessing is the one who gets kept on.

The session, as a run sheet

Everything in order. Seven steps, every click, every board item, every number it should produce. If you lose your place, this page alone is enough.

Yesterday was looking. Today is touching. Every formula yesterday went into an empty cell. Everything today reaches into the data itself.

Ctrl+Z now. Check row 2 says Rahul Sharma, 47,764. And say it plainly: sorting by emp_id would NOT have saved you here. The rows were not reordered, they were torn apart, and nothing in the file records which salary belonged to whom. Undo, or reopen without saving. There is no third option.
On the board for the rest of the module: SELECT THE WHOLE TABLE, THEN SORT. A1:L202, every time. If Excel offers to expand the selection, say yes.

Filter — and they collect promise three

Land this: a filter hides rows and there are two proofs on one screen. Then stop talking and let them find Aditya Gupta.

The dropdown is the fastest spell-check in Excel. Excel built that list by reading 201 rows. One row saying tech in small letters would make it five items. This file has four, and four is correct — that is unusual.
row numbers go blue and skip: 2, 8, 15, ... status bar: 45 of 201 records found column Q: rows STILL SAYS 201
Ask: “45 rows on screen, Q1 says 201. Did Excel delete the other 156?” No — two proofs at once. The row numbers skip, and a formula does not care what you are looking at. A filter is a pair of glasses, not a knife.

They read the numbers off their own status bar, not off you. All four columns add up to 201, so nothing is missing from any of them. That is value_counts with a mouse. Then the honest warning: in twenty minutes one of those numbers goes down by one, because they are counting rows, not people.

Clear (funnel with a red cross) shows all rows and keeps the arrows. Data → Filter again removes the arrows. Two different things.

Promise three, paid. Ask why the row number still says 152 — because a filter hides, it does not move. That is the row you were handed yesterday, and you found it yourself.

Then the line that matters: nobody will ever pay you to work out an average. They will pay you to notice that a row cannot possibly be true.
CLEAR THE FILTER BEFORE YOU GO ON. Data → Clear, and walk the room. A filter left on will confuse both of the next two blocks.

If asked about two filters at once: age Less Than 0 plus department HR is still 1 of 201. Switch to Tech and it is 0 of 201 and the sheet looks empty — show that once on purpose so it does not frighten them at home.

Not two people with the same name — one row written into the file twice. A job ran twice, or somebody appended the same record again. Happens constantly.

And the red followed them through the sort — the colour was never attached to an address, it is attached to a value.

Now delete it — read the ticks out loud

A1:L202  ->  Data -> Remove Duplicates

1 duplicate values found and removed; 200 unique values remain.
The ticks decide what the word duplicate means. All twelve = only delete a row that matches on all twelve. Tick only name and you delete real people — 20 first names and 10 last names means 200 possible names for 201 people, so names must repeat.

Remove Duplicates keeps the FIRST one it meets and asks you nothing. Here both copies are identical so it does not matter — one day two rows for one customer will have different addresses, and then the row order decides. That is why you coloured them first.
ON THE BOARD, NEW NUMBER: the data is now rows 2 to 201. Two hundred people. Ctrl+↓ lands on A201. From here on the range is A1:L201. Say it out loud or you will correct ranges one laptop at a time for the rest of the session.

Nobody retyped a formula. Second time they have watched the summary block correct itself, and the first time it was because of a row they deleted.

Then the honest part: those department counts from twenty minutes ago are now wrong by one. Clean first, count second, always. Every number anybody got from this file in twenty sessions was computed on 201 rows for 200 people — not badly wrong, slightly wrong, and nothing told anybody.

Twenty first names in S. You added no information. You changed the shape, and an impossible question became a dropdown.

And a double space gives an empty middle column unless you tick Treat consecutive delimiters as one. Look at the step 2 preview every time. Flash Fill (Ctrl+E) gets one mention and no more — it guesses.

A mess we make on purpose — the cuttable block

Land this first: “I am about to type five rows that are not real. They are not in your file.” Say it twice. This file has no stray spaces and nothing spelled two ways — they proved it themselves when every dropdown added up to 201. If you are short of time, cut this block and give it to session 3.

         A                   B           C

 206      rahul sharma       tech        Bengaluru     space BEFORE the r
 207    PRIYA IYER           HR          bangalore

210   Kavya Rao            Kavya Rao         9    9
Ask about row 208: “five letters, a space, five letters is eleven. Why does Excel say twelve?” LEN is how you prove an invisible problem is real.

Then ask which two rows did not shrink — 207 and 210, because they had no stray spaces. TRIM leaves clean data completely alone, which is why it is safe on a whole column. And 209 shrank with no space at either end — that is TRIM squeezing the double space in the middle.
=PROPER(B206)   tech       ->  Tech       correct
=PROPER(B210)   marketing  ->  Marketing  correct
=PROPER(B207)   HR         ->  Hr         WRONG
=UPPER(B208)    hr         ->  HR
=LOWER(B209)    Tech       ->  tech
PROPER turns HR into Hr. It is doing exactly what it was told — it does not know HR is two initials and not a word. No function knows what your data means, which is a sentence they have heard in this course before. So no single function fixes that column, and that is what the next tool is for.

Find & Replace — select first, always

select C206:C210 FIRST     then  Ctrl + H

BLR        ->  Bangalore                       1 changed
Bengaluru  ->  Bangalore                       1 changed
bangalore  ->  Bangalore   [x] Match case      1 changed
Ask: “why did I select five cells first?” With nothing selected, Replace All runs on the whole sheet — every column, the summary block, the split name columns — and it replaces inside words unless you tick Match entire cell contents. Replace All is the only tool today that changes data you are not looking at.
The half people forget: TRIM and PROPER did not fix column A, they built a clean copy in F. Copy F, Paste Special → Values over A, then delete F. Paste normally and you paste the formulas, which then point at the column you are deleting → #REF! everywhere.
Then delete rows 206–210 and columns E, F, G, and say it again: those five rows were never in the file. Your file is clean, and the next file you are sent will not be.
784 – 90

Close

1.  SELECT THE WHOLE TABLE, THEN SORT. one column alone = every row
    is a lie, and every total on the sheet is still correct.
2.  a filter HIDES rows. the row numbers skip and COUNTA does not move.
3.  conditional formatting is a RULE, not a colour. it corrects itself.
4.  before you delete anything, LOOK at it. remove duplicates keeps
    the FIRST one and asks you nothing.
5.  a blank is still not a zero. sorting pushes blanks to the bottom
    both ways, and you still do not get to invent what belongs there.
Count the wins out loud: who is −4 and who is 210, who has no age and no salary and exactly which three cells, a row removed so 201 became 200, a name turned into two columns and a question asked that was impossible an hour ago — and a file broken so badly that no number on it could tell us. Yesterday the file told them numbers. Today it told them names.
Say what you skipped, so the gaps are yours and not theirs: sorting by two columns (Add Level), Custom List order, sort and filter by colour, Flash Fill, Advanced Filter, data validation. Mentioned, not taught, on purpose.
Set up session 3: today they read 45 off the status bar — it is not on the sheet, it does not update, and it took four clicks. COUNTIF puts all four department counts on the sheet at once and they fix themselves. That is value_counts. Then IF — the first time a cell makes a decision instead of a calculation. Bring the cleaned file: 200 rows, no duplicate, three yellow cells, two red ones.

Ask them these before they leave

Thirteen questions, in order, with the answer under each one. Numbers 1, 3 and 9 are the three that matter. Take each answer from a different person.

I selected only the salary column and sorted it. What did I just do to the file?
Slid one column past the other eleven. Every person now has somebody else's salary. Nothing was deleted and nothing is red — and the total, the average and the median are all exactly the same as before, because the same numbers are still in the same column.
So how do you get the file back after a one-column sort?
Ctrl+Z, straight away, or close the file without saving. Sorting by emp_id will not help — the rows were not reordered, they were torn apart, and nothing in the file records which salary belonged to which person.
Does a filter delete the rows it hides? Give me two proofs from your own screen.
No. One: the row numbers turn blue and skip — 2, 8, 15 — and the missing numbers are the rows still sitting there. Two: =COUNTA(C2:C201) still counts every name. A formula does not care what you are looking at.
Sort the whole table by age, smallest first. Which row is at the very bottom, and why is it not the 210?
The person with no age at all — Sanjay Menon. Excel always puts blank cells last, in both directions. The 210 is on the last row that has a number in it, one above him.
Excel showed me a box called Sort Warning. What are the two choices and which one do I want?
Expand the selection — which is already chosen and is the one you want — and Continue with the current selection, which sorts your one column on its own and wrecks the file. Read that box. Do not close it.
In the Remove Duplicates box, what did you tick, and what would happen if you ticked only name?
All twelve columns, so a row is only a duplicate if it matches on all twelve. Tick only name and Excel deletes anybody who shares a name with somebody above them. There are 20 first names and 10 last names in this file — 200 possible names for 201 people — so names must repeat, and you would delete real people.
Two rows are duplicates. Which one does Excel keep, and when would that matter?
It keeps the first one it meets and deletes the rest. It never asks. Here both copies were identical so it made no difference — but the day two rows for one customer have different addresses, the order your rows happen to be in decides which address survives. That is why you colour them and look first.
201 rows became 200 and three numbers in column Q changed. Which three, and how many formulas did you retype?
rows 201→200, ages 200→199, salaries 199→198. And none — they corrected themselves, because a spreadsheet is rules that are always running. MIN and MAX did not move, because Anita Patel was neither the −4 nor the 210.
Conditional formatting turned two cells red. What did it change in the data?
Nothing at all. It only added colour. It is a rule — “go red if you are less than zero” — and it re-checks itself. Type 29 over the −4 and the red disappears on its own, because the cell stopped passing the test.
Go To Special → Blanks selected three cells. Which three, and what should you type into them?
K9 and K44, two missing salaries, and I93, one missing age. And you type nothing. A zero in a salary says this person earns nothing; a zero in an age says they were born this year. Mark them yellow, write down the three addresses, and ask whoever owns the data.
Column C is name and column D is department. What happens if I run Text to Columns on C and leave the Destination box alone?
First names stay in C and last names are written straight into D. Two hundred departments gone, with no warning and no prompt. Change the destination to an empty column — never split into a column that has something to its right.
I split the names into S and T. How do I check all 200 rows worked without scrolling?
=COUNTA(T2:T201). It should say 200 — 200 people, 200 last names. If it says 197, three names did not split and you now know how many to go and find. Yesterday's check, doing a new job.
=LEN(A208) says 12 and the cell looks like it says Anita Patel, which is eleven characters. And then TRIM gave me a clean name in another column — why is the job not finished?
The twelfth character is a space at the end, which nobody can see. And the job is not finished because TRIM did not fix the original column — it built a clean copy somewhere else. You have to Copy it and Paste Special → Values over the original, then delete the helper. Paste normally and you paste the formulas, and the whole thing turns into #REF!.

Questions you will get

“Why can't I just sort the one column I care about?”

“Because a row is only one person for as long as the twelve values stay side by side. There is nothing inside the file holding them together — no link, no key, nothing. Sort one column and that column slides past the other eleven, and now Rahul Sharma is being paid Aditya Gupta's salary. And the worst part is that every total on the sheet is still correct, because the same numbers are still in the same column. Select the whole table, every time. If Excel offers to expand the selection, say yes.”

“I sorted and now I cannot get the original order back.”

“There is no unsort button, and that catches everybody once. Ctrl+Z works if you do it now. After that, the only way home is a column that was already in order — and this file has one. emp_id runs 1001, 1002, 1003 straight down the rows, so sorting by emp_id smallest to largest puts the file back the way it was written. That is what an id column is for. Nobody ever reports on it and it is the only thing that can save you.”

“Is a filter the same as deleting? Where did my hundred and fifty-six rows go?”

“They are still there, behind the ones you can see. Look at the row numbers down the left — they went blue and they skip. Every number that is missing is a row that is still in the file. And your summary block has not moved either, because a formula does not care what you are looking at. That is the test: if the formula changed, something was deleted. If it did not, something was hidden.”

“Should we put zero in the three blank cells, or the average?”

“Neither, and not yet. A zero in a salary cell says this person earns nothing, which is a completely different fact from we do not know what they earn, and you proved yesterday that it drags the average down permanently and nothing warns you. Putting the average in is worse in a quiet way — the number stops being wrong and starts being invented, and nobody reading the file later can tell the difference. Mark the three cells, write the three addresses down, and ask whoever owns the data. That is the professional answer and it is the answer in an interview too.”

“My Remove Duplicates said zero duplicates found.”

“Then somebody has already run it, or your selection did not include the whole table. Press Ctrl+Home, type A1:L202 into the Name Box, and try again. And if it says 0 and your file still ends at row 202, check the My data has headers box — with it unticked Excel treats row 1 as an employee, which does not change the answer here but does change what it tells you.”

“Can I undo Remove Duplicates?”

“Yes. Ctrl+Z brings the row straight back. That is not the thing to be nervous about. The thing to be nervous about is that it deleted a row without showing you which one, and it told you the count afterwards. If you had ticked the wrong boxes it would have deleted thirty rows just as quietly and still only told you a number. Colour them first, look at them, then press the button.”

“Where is Go To Special on my laptop? Ctrl+G does nothing.”

“Use the ribbon and you never have to care: Home → Find & Select → Go To Special, on the far right of the Home tab. That route is the same on Windows and on a Mac and in every version. F5 usually opens the same Go To box if you prefer a key. Do not spend two minutes on a keyboard shortcut — the button is always there.”

“Does Google Sheets have all of this?”

“Almost all of it, under slightly different names. Data → Sort range, Data → Create a filter, Data → Data cleanup → Remove duplicates, Format → Conditional formatting, Data → Split text to columns, and TRIM, PROPER, UPPER, LOWER and LEN are identical. The one thing Sheets does not have is Go To Special. You find blanks there a different way — put a filter on the column and tick only (Blanks) in the dropdown, which gives you the same three rows. Same job, different door.”

“If our file is already clean, why are we learning TRIM?”

“Two honest reasons. One, it gets asked in interviews — TRIM and PROPER are two of the most asked text functions there are, and ‘our file did not need it’ is not an answer you can give in a room. Two, this file is the exception. A file with no stray spaces and nothing spelled two ways is rare, and the reason you could not find any dirt today is that I went and checked, not that dirt is unusual. That is why I typed those five rows in front of you instead of pretending they were yours.”

Excel day 3 · merged class · 90 minutes · full script · the session that pays for the module

Formulas That
Ask a Question

Every formula so far has worked on all the rows. Today one of them asks a question first and only counts the rows that answer yes — and the first thing it rebuilds is value_counts().

64in Sales, from a formula
198not 200. the blanks again
1,89,753a correct, useless average
2conditions, one answer

The whole day in one sentence

Up to now AVERAGE(K2:K201) has meant average everything. Today it becomes AVERAGEIF — average only the rows where something is true. That one change is the difference between a sheet that reports and a sheet that answers.

And it hands you the best mistake in the module. AVERAGEIF on the Tech department returns 1,89,753. The formula is perfectly correct. The answer is useless, and they already know exactly why.

Before you walk in

  1. Open the cleaned file from Thursday, not the original. It has 200 rows, so the data now runs 2 to 201, not 202. Every range on this page says 201. If somebody is on the old file their numbers will be one out all session and neither of you will know why.
  2. The summary block in P and Q should already read 200 / 199 / 198. It corrected itself when the duplicate went. Thirty seconds confirming that at the start saves twenty minutes of mismatched answers later.
  3. Teach IF before anything with the word COUNT in it. They need to see a condition on its own, on one row, before they see one buried inside a counting formula. The order matters more than it looks.
  4. Let the Tech average happen and do not warn them. AVERAGEIF on Tech returns 1,89,753 and it is the moment the session is built around. If you flag it in advance you have given away the answer and it becomes a demonstration instead of a discovery.
  5. Say the quotes rule once, early, and then point at it all day. Text in a condition needs quotes. A comparison needs quotes. A plain number does not. They will get this wrong four times before it sticks, and every one of those is a 0, not an error.
  6. COUNTIFS is the same function with more commas. Do not teach it as a new idea. Teach it as “the one you already know, asked twice”, and it costs you ten minutes instead of thirty.

Understand this yourself first

Three things: what a condition actually is to Excel, the quoting rule that causes every silent failure, and why the Tech average comes out the way it does. Part three is the session, so read it properly.

Part one · a condition is a question with a yes-or-no answer
Excel has been doing this quietly since day one

Type =K2>50000 into any empty cell. It returns TRUE or FALSE. Nothing else. That is a condition, and it is the whole building block.

Everything today is that one idea wrapped in something useful. IF picks between two answers depending on it. COUNTIF counts the rows where it came out TRUE. SUMIF adds up those rows. AVERAGEIF averages them.

The four shapes
IF
IF(test, what if yes, what if no) — works on one row at a time and returns a value.
COUNTIF
COUNTIF(where to look, what to look for) — works on a whole range and returns one number.
SUMIF
SUMIF(where to test, what to look for, what to add) — three parts, and the third is a different column from the first.
the trap
IF takes the test first. SUMIF takes the range first and the test second. The order is genuinely inconsistent and they will swap them.
Part two · the quotes, which cause every silent failure today
The rule, in three lines
COUNTIF(D2:D201, "Sales") text -> quotes COUNTIF(K2:K201, ">50000") a comparison -> quotes, the > INSIDE them COUNTIF(H2:H201, 10) a plain number -> no quotes needed

The one that catches everybody is the middle line. The greater-than sign goes inside the quotes, along with the number. ">50000" is a single piece of text that Excel reads as an instruction.

Pointing at a cell instead of typing the number

To compare against a cell — the average sitting in Q10, say — you cannot write ">Q10", because that is the literal text “greater than Q10”. You have to glue the two together with &:

=COUNTIF(K2:K201, ">"&Q10) correct =COUNTIF(K2:K201, ">Q10") gives 0, and no error
Both of those run. One is right and one returns zero. There is no red, no warning, no #VALUE!. This is the same shape of failure as the missing dollar sign on day 1 — a wrong answer that looks like a real answer, and it is worth saying out loud that this is now the second time.
What & actually does

It joins two things into one piece of text. ">"&Q10 becomes ">95829.66" before COUNTIF ever sees it. They do not need the theory, but they do need to know that the & is not decoration.

Part three · why the Tech average comes out at 1,89,753
The number, and why it is not a bug

=AVERAGEIF(D2:D201, "Tech", K2:K201) returns 1,89,753.54. Tech does not pay nineteen lakh. Nobody in Tech earns nineteen lakh.

There are 48 salaries in Tech. Forty-seven of them are between 56,727 and 1,16,894. The forty-eighth is 52,00,000 — Lakshmi Kumar on row 5, the same person they have been tripping over since statistics.

AVERAGEIF Tech, all 48 salaries 1,89,753.54 the same 47, without her 83,152.55
Why this is the most valuable thing on the page

Every previous mistake in this module was a mistake — a missing dollar sign, a one-column sort, a blank treated as a zero. You could fix the formula and the answer came right.

This one is different. The formula is correct. The range is correct, the condition is correct, the arithmetic is correct. And the answer is still useless, because one row in the data is nothing like the others.

A correct formula is not the same thing as a correct answer.

No software will ever tell you the difference. They first met this on day 1, when a perfectly correct average described a company containing somebody aged minus four. Today they meet it again in a formula they wrote themselves, and that is why the module keeps coming back to this file.
What to say when somebody asks what to do about it

Not “delete the row”. The honest answer is the one from statistics: report the median alongside the average, or report the average with the outlier named. The fix is in how you present the number, not in quietly changing the data.

There is no MEDIANIF in Excel. It genuinely does not exist. If somebody asks for it, say so plainly — it needs an array formula, and the clean way to get a median per department is a pivot table, which is session five. It is a good question and it deserves a straight answer rather than a workaround.

The session, minute by minute

Everything in a speech box is meant to be said more or less as written. Everything in a grey box is a direction for you, not words to say.

0 – 10

Check the file, and the question for today

Thirty seconds confirming the row count, then a question they can only answer by hand.

Everybody opens employees.xlsx — the cleaned one from Thursday, not the original. Check this before anything else. If somebody is on the old file their numbers will be one out all session.

Open Thursday's file. Look at your summary block in P and Q, and tell me the first three numbers.

rows 200 ages 199 salaries 198

Two hundred. Not two hundred and one, because the duplicate is gone. So our data now runs from row 2 to row 201.

Every formula today ends in 201. Write that on the corner of your screen.

“How many people are in Sales? You already know two ways to find out.”
Filter the department column and read the status bar. Or sort by department and count. Both work, and both are something you do with your hands. Let them say it, then ask the follow-up: “now how do you put that number in a cell, so it stays?” Nobody can.

Both of those work. And both of them are you, doing something, and then reading a number off the screen.

If the file changes tomorrow, you have to do it again. And you cannot put it in a report, because it is not in a cell.

Today every formula learns to ask a question first.

10 – 28

IF — the first formula that decides

A condition on one row, on its own, before it goes anywhere near a count.

Start with the condition completely bare. No IF around it yet — they need to see what a condition returns before they see what it is for.

Go to M1 and type a label: above or below. Then in M2, before we do anything clever, type this.

M2 — just the question, nothing around it
=K2>50000
FALSE

FALSE. Rahul Sharma earns 47,764, which is not more than fifty thousand.

That is a condition. You ask Excel a question that can only be answered yes or no, and it answers TRUE or FALSE. Nothing else.

Useful, and ugly. Nobody wants a report full of the word FALSE. So we wrap it in something that turns it into a real answer.

M2 again, this time wrapped in IF
=IF(K2>50000, "Above 50k", "Below 50k")
Below 50k
Three parts, on the board, and leave it up all session
  =IF(  the question  ,  what to put if YES  ,  what to put if NO  )

        K2>50000          "Above 50k"           "Below 50k"

  the question is the SAME condition you just typed on its own.
  IF only chooses between two answers based on it.

Three parts, separated by commas. The question, then what to put if the answer is yes, then what to put if it is no.

And notice the quotes around the two answers. They are text, so they need quotes. Keep looking at those quotes today — they are going to cause you trouble in about twenty minutes.

Now make it useful. Not a made-up fifty thousand, but a comparison against the real average sitting in the summary block. This is where the dollar sign comes back.

Fifty thousand is a number I invented. Let us compare against something real.

Your average salary is in Q10. Look at it — 95,829.66. That moved on Thursday when the duplicate went, and the formula corrected itself without being asked.

Now, every row has its own salary. But all two hundred rows share one average.

“So what do I need on the Q10, before I fill this down?”
The dollar signs. $Q$10. Second session in a row — and if somebody answers this without being prompted, that is the day 1 lesson landing.
M2, properly, then fill down to row 201
=IF(K2>$Q$10, "Above average", "Below average")
M2 Below average M3 Below average M4 Below average M5 Above average <-- the 52 lakh M6 Below average M7 Below average

Scroll down it. It is almost entirely Below average.

You saw this on day 1, when we drew the gap column and nearly every number came out negative. It is the same fact wearing different clothes.

In about half an hour you will be able to count these two words exactly, with one formula, and we will find out just how lopsided this company is.

Expect the blank rows, and answer it now rather than later. Row 9 is Manoj Kumar, who has no salary. His cell says Below average, because an empty cell in a comparison behaves like zero and zero is below the average. It is wrong, and nothing marks it as wrong. Third time this file has done that to them.
28 – 40

IFS — when two answers are not enough

Three bands instead of two. Twelve minutes, and resist going further.

IF gives you two answers. Real questions often have three.

Take experience, column H. Say under five years is Junior, five to nine is Mid, ten and above is Senior. That is three answers, and IF only has room for two.

N1 a label, then N2 — conditions in order, each with its answer after it
=IFS(H2>=10, "Senior", H2>=5, "Mid", H2>=0, "Junior")
N2 Junior (4 years) N3 Senior (13 years) N4 Junior (1 year) N5 Senior (11 years) N6 Mid (9 years) N7 Junior (3 years)

No nesting, no extra brackets. Just pairs: condition, answer, condition, answer, for as many as you need.

And the order matters more than anything else in this formula. IFS checks them top to bottom and stops at the first one that is true.

“Thirteen years. Is that greater than or equal to ten? Yes. Is it also greater than or equal to five?”
Also yes — and also greater than zero. All three conditions are true for that person. They get Senior because that one was written first and IFS stopped there. Make somebody say this out loud; it is the only idea in the block.
What happens if you write them the other way round
=IFS(H2>=0, "Junior", H2>=5, "Mid", H2>=10, "Senior")

   everyone is Junior. every single row.
   the first condition is true for everybody, so IFS never
   looks at the other two. no error. no warning.
Write the narrowest condition first.

Widest-first is not an error and does not look like one — it quietly returns the same answer for every row. If a column of 200 rows all says the same thing, that is the first thing to suspect.
IFS needs Excel 2019 or Microsoft 365. On an older copy it simply does not exist and you get #NAME?. The old way is nesting — =IF(H2>=10,"Senior",IF(H2>=5,"Mid","Junior")). Show it once, say it is what you will see in older files, and move on. Do not make them write it.
40 – 58

COUNTIF — and value_counts comes back

The question from minute five, answered in a cell. Then the blanks, one more time.

Back to the question I asked at the start. How many people are in Sales?

Not filter it and read a number off the bottom of the screen. Put the answer in a cell, so it is still there tomorrow and still right if the file changes.

Go to V1. Labels in V, formulas in W.
V1   Sales        W1   =COUNTIF(D2:D201, "Sales")
64

Two parts. Where to look — the whole department column. And what to look for — the word Sales, in quotes, because it is text.

Now do the other three.

V2 down to V4, same shape
V2   Tech         W2   =COUNTIF(D2:D201, "Tech")
V3   HR           W3   =COUNTIF(D2:D201, "HR")
V4   Marketing    W4   =COUNTIF(D2:D201, "Marketing")
V5   check        W5   =SUM(W1:W4)
Sales 64 Tech 49 HR 45 Marketing 42 check 200
“Why did I add that last row?”
Because 200 is the number of rows in the file. If the four counts add up to 200, every single person has been counted exactly once — no department was missed, nothing was spelled two different ways. If it came to 198, two people are in a department you have not listed. Teach the check, not just the count.

Four numbers, and they add to two hundred. Which means nothing is missing and nothing is double-counted.

Some of you have seen this exact output before. In pandas it was value_counts(), one line. Here it is four formulas and a check — and unlike value_counts, these four cells update themselves the moment somebody changes a department.

Now the numeric version, and the blank trap. Do not rush this — it is the third time the blanks have bitten them and the first time they can prove it.

Text is one thing. Now count a comparison — how many people earn more than the average?

And here is where the quotes get strange, so watch carefully. The greater-than sign goes inside the quotes.

W7 and W8 — note the ampersand
V7   above avg    W7   =COUNTIF(K2:K201, ">"&$Q$10)
V8   below avg    W8   =COUNTIF(K2:K201, "<"&$Q$10)
V9   check        W9   =W7+W8
above avg 12 below avg 186 check 198
“Twelve and one eighty-six. That is one hundred and ninety-eight. We have two hundred rows. Where are the other two?”
The two blank salaries. Manoj Kumar and Pooja Rao. A blank is not above the average and it is not below it — COUNTIF with a number test skips it entirely. Wait for them to find this. It is the third different way this file has taught them the same lesson.
Twelve people out of 198 earn more than the average salary of this company.

That is six per cent. Ninety-four per cent earn less than average. You told them that number on day 1 and they had to take your word for it — now they have counted it themselves, in two cells.

And look at what the check row did for us again. 198, not 200. The formula did not warn us — we caught it because we added the two numbers up and knew what the answer should be.

That is the habit. Every time you break a column into groups, add the groups back up.

The failure to show them, in a spare cell, so they recognise it later. Type =COUNTIF(K2:K201,">$Q$10") — with the Q10 inside the quotes and no ampersand. It returns 0. No error, no red, no warning. It is looking for salaries greater than the literal text “$Q$10”, and nothing matches. Second time this module a wrong answer has looked exactly like a real one.
58 – 74

SUMIF and AVERAGEIF — the answer that is wrong

Three columns instead of two, then the number the whole session is built around.

COUNTIF counts the rows that match. SUMIF adds up a number for those rows instead.

And it needs one more part, because the column you test and the column you add are not the same column. You test department and you add salary.

The three parts — put this on the board
  =SUMIF(  where to TEST  ,  what to look for  ,  what to ADD  )

           D2:D201            "Sales"             K2:K201
           department                             salary

  COUNTIF has two parts. SUMIF has three.
  the third one is the column you actually want the total of.
V11 down, total salary by department
W11   =SUMIF(D2:D201, "Sales",     K2:K201)
W12   =SUMIF(D2:D201, "Tech",      K2:K201)
W13   =SUMIF(D2:D201, "HR",        K2:K201)
W14   =SUMIF(D2:D201, "Marketing", K2:K201)
Sales 4264991 Tech 9108170 HR 2495026 Marketing 3106086

Tech is paying more than twice what Sales pays. But Tech only has 49 people and Sales has 64.

So totals are not comparable. We need the average per department. Same shape, one word different.

This is the moment. Let them type all four and read the output themselves. Say nothing.
V16 down — AVERAGEIF, same three parts
W16   =AVERAGEIF(D2:D201, "Sales",     K2:K201)
W17   =AVERAGEIF(D2:D201, "Tech",      K2:K201)
W18   =AVERAGEIF(D2:D201, "HR",        K2:K201)
W19   =AVERAGEIF(D2:D201, "Marketing", K2:K201)
Sales 66640.48 Tech 189753.54 HR 56705.14 Marketing 73954.43
Let them look at it. Then: “does the Tech number look right to you?”
No. Nearly nineteen lakh average, against about sixty to seventy thousand everywhere else. Somebody will say the formula is wrong. It is not. Let them check it against the other three — same formula, one word different, and those three are fine.

One lakh eighty-nine thousand. Tech does not pay that. Nobody in Tech earns that.

And the formula is right. Same formula as the other three. Same range, same column, correct arithmetic.

So who is doing this?

Wait. Do not answer it.
Somebody will get there: Lakshmi Kumar, row 5, Tech, 52,00,000. The same person from statistics, from the visualisation session, and from day 1 of this module. Let the room find her.
Prove it — take her out and run it again
AVERAGEIF Tech, all 48 salaries         189753.54
the same 47 people, without her          83152.55

one row in 200 moved the department average
by more than a lakh.
A correct formula is not the same thing as a correct answer.

Everything that has gone wrong in this module so far was a mistake — a missing dollar sign, a one-column sort, a blank read as a zero. You fixed the formula and the answer came right.

This one you cannot fix by fixing the formula. The formula is already right. The data has somebody in it who is nothing like the others, and no software on earth will tell you that.

So what do you actually do? You do not quietly delete her — she is a real employee and that is real money.

You report the median next to the average, which is exactly what you learned to do in statistics. Or you report the average and say out loud that one person is carrying it.

The fix is in how you present the number. Not in changing the data.

Expect “so is there a MEDIANIF?” and answer it straight. No. It does not exist in Excel. It is a fair question and the honest answer is that getting a median per department properly needs a pivot table, which is session five. Do not improvise an array formula at the board.
74 – 84

Two conditions at once — just add an S

Not a new idea. The same function, asked twice. Ten minutes.

Last thing, and it is the easiest of the day. A real question is rarely about one thing.

Not “how many in Sales”, but “how many in Sales have been here ten years or more”. Two conditions, one answer.

Add an S to the end of the function name and keep adding pairs.

The shape — and watch where the answer column moved
  =COUNTIFS(  range1, test1,  range2, test2  )

  =SUMIFS(  what to ADD  ,  range1, test1,  range2, test2  )
            ^^^^^^^^^^^
            in SUMIFS the thing you add comes FIRST.
            in SUMIF it came LAST. yes, really.
Try it
=COUNTIFS(D2:D201, "Sales", H2:H201, ">=10")
32

Thirty-two people in Sales with ten years or more. Half the department.

And the conditions are joined by AND, never OR. A row is counted only if it passes every test you listed.

Now the grid. This is the payoff for the whole session, and it previews the pivot table in session five without naming it yet.

Now watch what two conditions let you build. Set up a small grid — departments down the side, ratings across the top.

One formula, filled across and down. Note which half is locked.
=COUNTIFS($D$2:$D$201, $V23, $G$2:$G$201, W$22)

   $D$2:$D$201   the department column, locked completely
   $V23          the department name - column locked, row free
   $G$2:$G$201   the rating column, locked completely
   W$22          the rating name - row locked, column free
Poor Average Good Excellent total Sales 17 14 19 14 64 Tech 15 8 13 13 49 HR 12 9 11 13 45 Marketing 14 11 8 9 42 total 58 42 51 49 200
“Add the row totals. Now add the column totals. What do you get both times?”
200 both ways. Sixteen cells, one formula, and every single person counted exactly once. Same check as the department counts earlier, now in two directions.
The half-locks are the hard part and you said you would skip them on day 1. This is why they exist. $V23 keeps the department as you fill across; W$22 keeps the rating as you fill down. If anybody is stuck, let them write sixteen separate formulas — the grid is the point, not the shortcut. Fix it one to one while the rest move on.

Sixteen numbers, from one formula, and they add up correctly in both directions.

Hold on to this. In session five there is a tool that builds this entire grid by dragging two words, with no formula at all. You will appreciate it a great deal more having built it by hand first.

84 – 90

Close

The five lines. If everything else goes, keep these.
1.  a CONDITION is a question with a yes/no answer.
    =K2>50000 on its own returns TRUE or FALSE.
    everything today is that, wrapped in something useful.

2.  IF decides for ONE ROW.    COUNTIF / SUMIF / AVERAGEIF
    work on a WHOLE RANGE and give back one number.

3.  the quotes:
      "Sales"        text          -> quotes
      ">50000"       a comparison  -> quotes, > INSIDE
      ">"&$Q$10     vs a cell     -> join with &
    get this wrong and you get 0. not an error. ZERO.

4.  IFS stops at the FIRST condition that is true.
    narrowest first. widest first = every row the same answer.

5.  ALWAYS ADD THE GROUPS BACK UP.
    64+49+45+42 = 200   correct
    12+186      = 198   the two blank salaries, again

And the one that is not about Excel at all.

AVERAGEIF on Tech gave us one lakh eighty-nine thousand, and the formula was perfect.

You can write a formula correctly, point it at the right column, and still get an answer that would be a lie if you put it in a report. Excel will never tell you. Pandas never told you either. That part stays your job for the rest of your career.

Tuesday is the one every interview asks about. You have two sheets — a list of employees and a list of departments — and you need to pull information from one into the other.

That is VLOOKUP. It is the single most-asked Excel question for a fresher analyst, and it breaks in three specific ways that I am going to make happen on purpose.

The session, as a run sheet

Everything in order. Seven steps, every formula, every number it should produce. If you lose your place, this page alone is enough.

10 – 10

Check the file, and the question

Land this: everybody on Thursday's cleaned file. 200 rows, so data runs 2 to 201. Every range today ends in 201.

rows 200 | ages 199 | salaries 198
Ask: “how many people are in Sales?” — they say filter, or sort and count. Then the follow-up: “now put that number in a cell so it is still there tomorrow.” Nobody can. That is the session.
210 – 28

IF — the first formula that decides

Land this: show the condition bare before wrapping it. They need to see TRUE/FALSE on its own.

M2   =K2>50000                                          FALSE
M2   =IF(K2>50000, "Above 50k", "Below 50k")            Below 50k
M2   =IF(K2>$Q$10, "Above average", "Below average")   fill to 201
Three parts: the question, what if yes, what if no. Quotes on the text answers.

Ask before filling down: “what does Q10 need?” — the dollar signs. Every row has its own salary; all 200 share one average. Second session in a row.
Expect: row 9, Manoj Kumar, no salary, says Below average. Empty behaves like zero. Wrong, and nothing marks it wrong. Third time this file has done that.
328 – 40

IFS — three bands

N2   =IFS(H2>=10, "Senior", H2>=5, "Mid", H2>=0, "Junior")

     Senior 79 | Mid 65 | Junior 56
Ask: “13 years — is it >=10? yes. also >=5? also yes.” All three are true. They get Senior because it was written first and IFS stops at the first true one.

Write the narrowest condition first. Widest first and every row says Junior — no error, no warning.
If somebody gets #NAME? they are on Excel 2016 or older. Show the nested version once, do not make them write it.
440 – 58

COUNTIF, and the blanks again

W1   =COUNTIF(D2:D201, "Sales")          64
W2   =COUNTIF(D2:D201, "Tech")           49
W3   =COUNTIF(D2:D201, "HR")             45
W4   =COUNTIF(D2:D201, "Marketing")      42
W5   =SUM(W1:W4)                       200  <-- the check
Ask why the check row exists: four counts adding to 200 proves everybody was counted once. 198 would mean two people are in a department you did not list.

This is value_counts() — except these four cells update themselves.
W7   =COUNTIF(K2:K201, ">"&$Q$10)       12
W8   =COUNTIF(K2:K201, "<"&$Q$10)      186
W9   =W7+W8                            198  <-- not 200
Ask: “where are the other two?” — the two blank salaries. A blank is neither above nor below; COUNTIF skips it.

12 of 198 earn above average. Ninety-four per cent earn below it — you told them that on day 1 and now they have counted it.
Show the failure: =COUNTIF(K2:K201,">$Q$10") with Q10 inside the quotes returns 0. No error. Second time a wrong answer has looked like a real one.

SUMIF, AVERAGEIF — and the wrong answer

Land this: SUMIF has three parts — test range, what to look for, what to add. Then let the Tech average happen. Do not warn them.

=SUMIF(D2:D201, "Sales", K2:K201)       4264991
=SUMIF(D2:D201, "Tech", K2:K201)        9108170

Without her: 83,152.55 across 47 people. One row moved a department average by over a lakh.
The line: a correct formula is not the same thing as a correct answer. Every earlier error was a mistake you could fix. This one you cannot fix by fixing the formula.

What to do: report the median beside the average, or name the outlier. Not delete the row.

784 – 90

Close

1.  a CONDITION is a question with a yes/no answer
2.  IF = one row.  COUNTIF/SUMIF/AVERAGEIF = a whole range
