The line that is not about Excel: AVERAGEIF gave 1,89,753 and the formula was perfect. You can write a formula correctly and still get an answer that would be a lie in a report. Excel will not tell you. Pandas never did either.
Set up Tuesday: two sheets, and you need to pull information from one into the other. VLOOKUP — the single most-asked Excel question for a fresher, and it breaks in three ways we will cause on purpose.

Ask them these before they leave

Thirteen questions, in order, with the answer under each one. Numbers 5, 9 and 12 are the three that matter. Take each answer from a different person.

What does =K2>50000 return on its own, with no IF around it?
TRUE or FALSE. Nothing else. That is a condition, and everything today is that one thing wrapped in something useful.
What are the three parts of an IF?
The question, what to put if yes, what to put if no — separated by commas. Text answers need quotes.
What is the difference between IF and COUNTIF?
IF works on one row and gives back a value for that row. COUNTIF works on a whole range and gives back one number for all of it.
Why did =IF(K2>Q10, ...) go wrong when you filled it down, and what fixed it?
Q10 moved down with the formula, so row 3 compared against Q11. Dollar signs — $Q$10. Every row has its own salary; all 200 rows share one average.
Write the condition for “more than fifty thousand” inside a COUNTIF. Where do the quotes go?
">50000" — the greater-than sign goes inside the quotes, together with the number. It is one piece of text that Excel reads as an instruction.
Why does =COUNTIF(K2:K201,">$Q$10") return 0 instead of an error?
Because it is looking for salaries greater than the literal text “$Q$10”, and nothing matches. You need ">"&$Q$10 to join the sign to the cell's value. A wrong answer that looks like a real one.
Your four department counts are 64, 49, 45 and 42. Why did you add them up?
They come to 200, which is the number of rows. That proves every person was counted exactly once — nothing missed, nothing spelled two ways. Always add the groups back up.
Above average is 12, below average is 186. That is 198. Where are the other two rows?
The two blank salaries. A blank is not above the average and not below it — COUNTIF with a number test skips it entirely.
How many parts does SUMIF have, and what is the extra one?
Three. Where to test, what to look for, and what to add — because the column you test (department) is not the column you add (salary).
AVERAGEIF on Tech returned 1,89,753. Is the formula wrong?
No. The formula is perfectly correct. One person in Tech earns 52,00,000 and she drags the average up on her own. Without her it is 83,152 across 47 people.
So should you delete her row?
No. She is a real employee earning real money. Report the median beside the average, or report the average and name the outlier. The fix is in how you present it, not in changing the data.
In an IFS, somebody with 13 years passes all three conditions. Why do they come out as Senior?
Because IFS checks top to bottom and stops at the first true one. Senior was written first. Put the narrowest condition first — widest first and every row gets the same answer, with no error.
In COUNTIFS with two conditions, does a row need to pass both or just one?
Both. The conditions are joined by AND, never OR. A row counts only if it passes every test you listed.

Questions you will get

“Can I use COUNTIF with two conditions?”

“No — that is exactly what COUNTIFS is for. The S means more than one. Same for SUMIFS and AVERAGEIFS. And once you are used to them you can just always write the S version, even with one condition; it works perfectly well.”

“Why does SUMIF put the column to add at the end, but SUMIFS puts it at the front?”

“Because SUMIFS takes any number of condition pairs after it, so the thing you are adding has to come first or Excel would not know where the list stops. It is inconsistent and it catches everybody. Check the order every single time you write a SUMIFS.”

“Is there a MEDIANIF?”

“No. It does not exist in Excel, and that is a real gap — you just saw exactly why you would want one. Getting a median per department properly needs a pivot table, which is session five.”

“My COUNTIF says 0 and I know the value is there.”

“Three usual causes. The quotes are in the wrong place — the sign has to be inside them. Or you are comparing against a cell and left out the &. Or there is a trailing space in the data, so "Sales" does not match "Sales ". That last one is what TRIM was for.”

“Does COUNTIF care about capital letters?”

“No. "sales", "Sales" and "SALES" all count the same rows. That is usually helpful and occasionally not — if you genuinely need case to matter, it takes a different formula and it is rare enough that you should look it up when it happens.”

“Can I use a wildcard, like counting everybody whose name starts with A?”

“Yes. =COUNTIF(C2:C201,"A*") gives 33. The * means any number of characters, the same as it did in Find and Replace on Thursday. It works on text, not on numbers.”

“I got #NAME? on the IFS.”

“Your Excel is older than 2019, so that function does not exist there. The old way is putting one IF inside another. It gives the same answer and it is much harder to read, which is why they added IFS.”

“Could we do all of this in pandas instead?”

“Yes, and in fewer lines — value_counts and groupby do most of today in two. The difference is the same one as day 1: these cells recalculate themselves when the data changes, and the person you hand the file to can see the formula and check it. You will use both.”

“Why do we build the grid by hand if a pivot table does it?”

“So that when the pivot table gives you a number you do not trust, you know what it is doing underneath and can check one cell of it yourself. People who only know the button cannot debug it.”

Excel day 4 · merged class · 90 minutes · full script · the one interviews ask about

Pulling Data
From Another Sheet

VLOOKUP is the single most-asked Excel question for a fresher analyst. It is also the one that breaks most often, in three specific ways — and all three are going to happen on screen today.

4arguments, and all four matter
FALSEthe one you always type
#N/Anot a bug
43.8%of the bonus bill, one person

Build the second sheet in front of them, by hand

Everything so far has lived on one sheet. Today there are two, and the job is to pull a number out of the second one into the first. Type the second sheet live, four rows, in about a minute — if it arrives already made, half the room never understands what is being looked up in what.

The session lands on a real number. Rate the company's bonuses off the rating column and the bill comes to ₹17,81,426. Of that, ₹7,80,000 goes to one person — Lakshmi Kumar, row 5, again. Forty-four per cent of the entire bonus bill is one employee, and they will have computed it themselves.

Before you walk in

  1. Rehearse the broken version before the working one. Day 4 has the same shape as day 1 and day 3 — let it fail, let them look at it, then fix it. The three failures are the content. A session where VLOOKUP works first time teaches almost nothing.
  2. Say “FALSE, always” in minute fifteen and keep saying it. The fourth argument is optional, which is the single worst design decision in Excel. Leave it out and you get approximate matching, which returns wrong answers silently. They should type FALSE every time without thinking.
  3. Do not skip the #N/A block. Students see it as a failure and start deleting rows to make it go away. It is Excel saying this value is not in your lookup table, which is usually a real finding about the data.
  4. INDEX + MATCH is taught to answer one question, not as a second method. The question is “what if the thing I want is to the left of what I am looking up?” Introduce it there and it takes twelve minutes. Introduce it as an alternative and it takes forty and nobody remembers which argument goes where.
  5. Check who has XLOOKUP before you teach it. It needs Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021. On anything older it is #NAME?. Ask for a show of hands in minute seventy and teach it to whoever has it — but VLOOKUP is what the interview asks, so it keeps the main hour.
  6. Keep the two sheets visibly separate on screen. Name the second one bonus, and let them watch the formula build itself when you click across to it. The sheet name appearing in the middle of their formula is the moment the idea lands.

Understand this yourself first

Three things: what the four arguments actually mean, the three failures and why none of them produce an error, and why INDEX and MATCH exist at all. Part two is the session.

Part one · the four arguments, in plain words
1 — what
The value you are looking for. Usually a cell on the row you are standing on. G2, the rating.
2 — where
The block of cells to search in. And the thing you are looking for must be in its first column. This is the rule everything else follows from.
3 — which
How many columns across to count, once it finds the row. Not a letter. A number, counting the first column of the block as 1.
4 — how
FALSE means exact match only. TRUE, or leaving it out, means approximate. Type FALSE. Every time.
Say it as one sentence
=VLOOKUP( what I am looking for , where to look for it , how many columns across to bring back , FALSE )

The V stands for vertical — it searches down the first column of your block. There is an HLOOKUP that searches across a row instead, and you will meet it roughly never.

Part two · the three failures, and why none of them look like failures
Failure one — the block moves when you fill down

This is day 1 again. The lookup block is one fixed place, the same for all 200 rows. Fill a formula down without locking it and row 3 searches one row lower, row 4 two rows lower, and by row 6 the block has slid off the bottom of your four-row table entirely.

=VLOOKUP(G2, bonus!A2:B5, 2, FALSE) row 2 - correct =VLOOKUP(G3, bonus!A3:B6, 2, FALSE) row 3 - already wrong =VLOOKUP(G6, bonus!A6:B9, 2, FALSE) row 6 - block is empty

Rows at the top return the right answer. Rows further down return #N/A. The column half works, which is why people think the data is at fault rather than the formula.

Failure two — leaving out the fourth argument

=VLOOKUP(G2, bonus!$A$2:$B$5, 2) runs perfectly. No error. And it is doing approximate matching, which on an unsorted text column returns whatever it happens to land on.

This is the most dangerous default in Excel. The argument is optional, and the value it defaults to is the one you almost never want. There is no warning, no colour, no mark on the cell. The answer is simply wrong.
Failure three — somebody inserts a column

The third argument is a number, counted by hand. Insert a column into the middle of the lookup table and every formula pointing at it is now bringing back the wrong field — and the formula has not changed, so nothing suggests anything happened.

All three failures return a value or an #N/A. None of them says “you made a mistake”.

This is the third session running where a wrong answer has looked exactly like a real one. By now they should expect it — and that expectation is most of what this module is teaching.
Part three · why INDEX and MATCH exist
The one thing VLOOKUP genuinely cannot do

The value you look up has to be in the first column of the block. So VLOOKUP can only ever bring back something to the right of it.

Give somebody a table with name in column B and emp_id in column A, ask them to find the name for a given id, and VLOOKUP does it happily. Reverse it — find the id for a given name — and it cannot, because the name is to the right.

The two halves
MATCH
Gives you which position a value sits at in a list. MATCH("Tech", D2:D201, 0) returns a row number, not a value.
INDEX
Gives you the value at a position. INDEX(C2:C201, 3) returns the third name.
together
INDEX asks MATCH where to look. The two columns are named separately, so neither has to be left or right of the other.
the zero
MATCH has the same trap as VLOOKUP's fourth argument. The third argument must be 0 for an exact match. Type the zero.
And then XLOOKUP, which fixes all of it

One function. You name the lookup column and the return column separately, so direction stops mattering. It defaults to exact match, so the dangerous default is gone. And it has a built-in place to put the “if not found” answer, so you do not need IFERROR around it.

Teach it, but do not lead with it. It needs Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021, so some of the room will not have it, and the interview question is still VLOOKUP — because the files they will be handed were built by people who only had VLOOKUP.

The session, minute by minute

Everything in a speech box is meant to be said more or less as written. Everything in a grey box is a direction for you, not words to say.

0 – 12

Two sheets, and a number that is on the wrong one

Build the second sheet live. Make the problem obvious before naming the function.

Open the cleaned file. 200 rows, data runs 2 to 201. Then make a second sheet in front of them — the plus sign at the bottom of the window.

The company is paying bonuses this year, and the rule is simple. Your bonus depends on your rating.

Poor gets nothing. Average gets five per cent of salary. Good gets ten. Excellent gets fifteen.

Everybody's rating is already in our file, column G. But those four percentages are not. So let us put them somewhere.

Click the + at the bottom, rename the new sheet bonus, and type four rows
        A            B

 1   rating       percent
 2   Poor              0
 3   Average           5
 4   Good             10
 5   Excellent        15

Four rows. That is the whole second sheet.

Now back to the first sheet. Row two is Rahul Sharma, HR, rating Poor, salary 47,764.

I want his bonus percentage sitting next to him on this sheet. It is on the other sheet. How do I get it across?

“Two hundred rows. How would you do it by hand?”
Read the rating, go to the other sheet, find that rating, read the percentage, come back, type it. Two hundred times. Let somebody describe it out loud — the tedium is the argument for the function.

You read the rating. You go to the other sheet. You find that rating. You read the number next to it. You come back and type it in.

That is exactly what VLOOKUP does. Those five steps, as one formula.

12 – 32

VLOOKUP, one argument at a time

Build it slowly. Twenty minutes, and do not fill it down until the end.

Go to X1 on the main sheet and label it bonus pct. Then in X2 start typing, and stop after each comma while I explain it.

X2 — type it in four stages. Stop at every comma.
=VLOOKUP(G2,                                    1. WHAT am I looking for?  his rating

=VLOOKUP(G2, bonus!$A$2:$B$5,                   2. WHERE do I look?  the four rows

=VLOOKUP(G2, bonus!$A$2:$B$5, 2,                3. WHICH column do I bring back?

=VLOOKUP(G2, bonus!$A$2:$B$5, 2, FALSE)         4. HOW?  exact match only
0

Zero. Rahul is rated Poor, and Poor gets nothing. That is correct.

Now the four parts, because every one of them will catch you at some point.

On the board — leave this up all session
  G2                   WHAT.   the rating on this row

  bonus!$A$2:$B$5      WHERE.  the sheet name, then an exclamation mark,
                               then the block. LOCKED, because this block
                               is the same for all 200 rows.

  2                    WHICH.  a NUMBER, not a letter. count the first
                               column of the block as 1. rating is 1,
                               percent is 2. so: 2.

  FALSE                HOW.    exact match. always. type it every time.

The second argument is the one to look at twice. bonus! is the sheet name, then an exclamation mark, then the cells. And it has dollar signs on it.

You know why by now. Every row has its own rating, but all two hundred rows look it up in the same four cells. Third session in a row.

“Why is the third argument a 2 and not a B?”
Because it counts from the start of your block, not from the start of the sheet. The block begins at column A, so A is 1 and B is 2. If the block began at column D, then D would be 1. This catches people constantly.
Now fill it down. It will work. They should see it succeed once before you break it.
Double-click the fill handle
        G            X

 2   Poor             0
 3   Poor             0
 4   Good            10
 5   Excellent       15
 6   Excellent       15
 7   Poor             0

Two hundred lookups, done. Now turn it into actual money.

Y1 a label, then Y2, filled down
=K2 * X2 / 100
Y2 0.00 Poor Y3 0.00 Poor Y4 6299.00 Good, 10% of 62990 Y5 780000.00 Excellent, 15% of 52,00,000 Y6 9383.40 Excellent, 15% of 62556

Look at row five.

Seven lakh eighty thousand rupees. One person's bonus.

32 – 48

The three ways it breaks

All three live, in order, with a Ctrl+Z after each. Sixteen minutes.

Work on a spare copy of the column so the good one survives. Do each break, look at it, undo it.

That formula works. Now I am going to break it three times, because these are the three things that will actually go wrong on you, and none of them says “error”.

Break one — take the dollar signs off and fill down again
=VLOOKUP(G2, bonus!A2:B5, 2, FALSE)

   row 2   searches  bonus!A2:B5     0        correct
   row 3   searches  bonus!A3:B6     0        correct BY LUCK
   row 4   searches  bonus!A4:B7     10       correct BY LUCK
   row 5   searches  bonus!A5:B8     #N/A     the block has slid off
   row 6   searches  bonus!A6:B9     #N/A
   row 7   searches  bonus!A7:B10    #N/A
“The first three rows are right. Does that mean the formula is right?”
No. They are right because the value they wanted happened to still be inside the sliding block. Correct by luck is not correct. The block slid one row per row and ran out of table by row 5.

The top of the column is right and the bottom is broken, which is the worst possible shape for a mistake — because you look at the top, it looks fine, and you move on.

Ctrl+Z. Dollar signs go back on.

Break two — leave out the fourth argument entirely
=VLOOKUP(G2, bonus!$A$2:$B$5, 2)

   no FALSE. no error. the formula runs.
   and it is now doing APPROXIMATE matching on a text column
   that is not sorted - so it returns whatever it lands on.

Nothing turned red. Nothing complained. Excel let me leave out an argument and quietly chose a default for me — and the default is the one you almost never want.

Approximate matching has a real use and we will see it in ten minutes. But on a column of words that are not in order, it just returns something. Possibly the right thing. Possibly not.

Type FALSE. Every single time.

It is four extra characters and it is the difference between a formula that is right and a formula that is right by accident. If you learn one habit from today, learn this one.
Break three — go to the bonus sheet and insert a column
   right-click column B on the bonus sheet  ->  Insert

        A            B              C

 1   rating       (new)         percent
 2   Poor                            0
 3   Average                         5

   the formula still says  2.  it has not changed.
   but column 2 of the block is now the EMPTY one.
X2 0 X3 0 X4 0 X5 0 every row is now 0. nothing errored.
“I did not touch the formula. Why did the answers change?”
Because the third argument is a number you counted by hand, and the thing it was counting moved. Excel does not renumber it for you. Somebody tidying up the lookup table next month will do exactly this and never find out.

I did not touch the formula. Somebody else tidied up a different sheet, and now every bonus in this company is zero.

Ctrl+Z. And remember this one when we get to XLOOKUP at the end, because it is the specific problem that function was invented to solve.

48 – 58

#N/A is a sentence, not a crash

Ten minutes. Make them read the error before hiding it.

Cause it on purpose — type a rating that is not in the lookup table.

Go to any empty cell and look up something that does not exist.

Any spare cell
=VLOOKUP("Outstanding", bonus!$A$2:$B$5, 2, FALSE)
#N/A

#N/A means not available. And it is not Excel failing. It is Excel telling you something true: the value you asked for is not in the table you pointed at.

That is usually a real finding. A rating spelled differently. A department that exists in one file and not the other. A trailing space, which you met on Thursday.

Read every #N/A before you hide it.

The instinct is to make it go away so the sheet looks clean. But each one is a row where your two files disagree, and that disagreement is often the most interesting thing in the data.

Once you have read them and you know why they are there, then you can tidy them up. That is IFERROR.

Wrap the whole thing
=IFERROR( VLOOKUP(G2, bonus!$A$2:$B$5, 2, FALSE) , "not rated" )
Two parts, on the board
  =IFERROR(  the thing to try  ,  what to show if it fails  )

  it does NOT fix anything. it hides the error and
  puts your own words there instead.
Say this plainly, because it is the way IFERROR gets misused. It does not repair the lookup. The value is still not in your table. Wrapping every formula in IFERROR from the start is how people hide data problems from themselves for months. Read the errors first, then hide them.
58 – 70

The one VLOOKUP cannot do

Twelve minutes. One question, and INDEX + MATCH is the answer to it.

One more thing about VLOOKUP, and it is the thing that makes people reach for something else.

Our main sheet has emp_id in column A and name in column C.

Give me an id, I will find you the name — VLOOKUP does that happily, because the name is to the right of the id.

Now give me a name and ask me for the id.

“Can VLOOKUP do that?”
No. The thing you look up has to be in the first column of the block, and it can only bring back something to the right. The id is to the left of the name. Not hard — impossible.

Not difficult. Impossible. So we take the job apart into two pieces.

Piece one: where is that name? Not what is it — where.

MATCH on its own, in a spare cell
=MATCH("Karthik Reddy", C2:C201, 0)
3

Three. Not his id, not his salary. His position — he is the third name in that list.

And note the zero at the end. That is MATCH's version of FALSE. Same trap, same rule: type the zero every time.

Piece two: give me the value at a position.

INDEX on its own
=INDEX(A2:A201, 3)
1003

The third employee id. Now put one inside the other, and the 3 becomes the question instead of a typed number.

Together
=INDEX(A2:A201, MATCH("Karthik Reddy", C2:C201, 0))
1003
Read it inside out, every time.

MATCH finds which row. INDEX brings back the value in that row.

And because you name the two columns separately, it does not matter which one is to the left. That is the entire reason this pair exists.
Twelve minutes, and then stop. Do not drill it, do not do five examples. The goal is that they recognise INDEX(..., MATCH(...)) in somebody else's file and know what it is doing. Writing it fluently is not a day-4 skill.
70 – 84

XLOOKUP, and the legitimate use of TRUE

Fourteen minutes. Check who has it first.

Ask for hands: who has Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021? Whoever does can type along. Everybody else watches and writes it down, because they will meet it on a work laptop.

Everything we just did — the locked block, the counted column number, the compulsory FALSE, the INDEX and MATCH pair — exists because VLOOKUP was designed in the eighties.

Microsoft eventually fixed it. One function.

The same bonus lookup, the modern way
=XLOOKUP(G2, bonus!$A$2:$A$5, bonus!$B$2:$B$5)
0
What changed, point by point
  VLOOKUP                           XLOOKUP

  one block, first column must      TWO SEPARATE columns.
  hold the thing you look up        look left or right, it does not care

  count the columns yourself        no counting. you name the column.
  (breaks when one is inserted)     insert all you like, nothing breaks

  FALSE or it guesses               exact match by DEFAULT

  wrap it in IFERROR                4th argument IS the "if not found"
And the not-found message comes free
=XLOOKUP(G2, bonus!$A$2:$A$5, bonus!$B$2:$B$5, "not rated")

No counting. No compulsory FALSE. No IFERROR wrapped round the outside. And it looks left as happily as it looks right, so INDEX and MATCH are not needed for that either.

“So why did we spend an hour on VLOOKUP?”
Two honest reasons. The interview asks about VLOOKUP, not XLOOKUP. And every file you are handed was built by somebody who only had VLOOKUP — you will spend far more time reading other people's than writing your own. Answer this directly; it is a fair question.
Last ten minutes of the block. Now show the one case where TRUE is the right answer, so the morning's rule has a reason behind it.

One last thing. I told you to always type FALSE. Here is the exception, so you know why the rule exists.

Suppose we grade salaries into bands. Under fifty thousand is band D. Fifty to eighty is C. Eighty to one-twenty is B. Above that is A.

You cannot list every possible salary. But you can list where each band starts.

A third sheet, called bands. Note it is sorted ascending.
        A            B

 1   from         band
 2       0         D
 3   50000         C
 4   80000         B
 5  120000         A
And here TRUE is correct
=VLOOKUP(K2, bands!$A$2:$B$5, 2, TRUE)
K2 47764 -> D under 50000 K4 62990 -> C between 50000 and 80000 K3 86052 -> B between 80000 and 120000 K5 5200000 -> A above 120000

TRUE means if you cannot find it exactly, use the largest value that is still smaller. 47,764 is not in the table, so it falls back to the 0 row — band D.

And that only works because the table is sorted smallest to largest. Sort it any other way and the answers are nonsense, with no error.

TRUE is for bands and ranges, on a sorted table, and nothing else.

Grades, tax slabs, shipping tiers, salary bands. Everywhere else, FALSE. And when you do use TRUE, write it out rather than leaving the argument off — so that anybody reading your sheet can see you meant it.
84 – 90

Close — and the number

Before the summary, one number. Total up the bonus column.

Any empty cell
=SUM(Y2:Y201)
1781426.45

Seventeen lakh eighty-one thousand. That is the company's whole bonus bill.

Now look back at row five. Lakshmi Kumar's bonus on its own was seven lakh eighty thousand.

“What share of the entire bonus bill is one person?”
Forty-four per cent. 780000 divided by 1781426. One employee out of two hundred is nearly half the bonus budget. Let them compute it.
₹7,80,000 of a ₹17,81,426 bill. Forty-four per cent, one person.

Every formula today was correct. The lookup was correct, the percentage was correct, the multiplication was correct. And if you put “total bonus: 17.8 lakh” in a report without mentioning that nearly half of it is one person, you have told the truth and misled everybody.
The five lines. If everything else goes, keep these.
1.  =VLOOKUP( what, where, which column as a NUMBER, FALSE )
    the thing you look up must be in the FIRST column of "where".

2.  LOCK the "where" block. $A$2:$B$5. it is the same for every row.

3.  TYPE FALSE. always. leaving it out means approximate matching
    and approximate matching returns wrong answers with no error.

4.  #N/A means "not in your table". READ IT before you hide it.
    IFERROR hides it. it does not fix it.

5.  can't look LEFT     -> INDEX( column , MATCH( value, column, 0 ) )
    got Excel 2021/365  -> XLOOKUP, and forget all of the above

Thursday is the one that makes all of this feel like hard work for no reason.

Remember the grid we built on Tuesday — sixteen COUNTIFS formulas, departments down the side, ratings across the top? Thursday you build that same grid by dragging two words. No formulas at all.

It is called a pivot table, and it is the most useful thing in Excel.

The session, as a run sheet

Everything in order. Seven steps, every formula, every number. If you lose your place, this page alone is enough.

Ask: “200 rows — how would you do this by hand?” Read the rating, cross to the other sheet, find it, read the number, come back, type it. Two hundred times. That is exactly what VLOOKUP does.

The three breaks — do each, look, undo

670 – 84

XLOOKUP, then the legitimate TRUE

Hands up first: who has Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021? Others watch and write it down — they will meet it on a work laptop.

Then the exception to the morning's rule

new sheet  bands   (SORTED ascending - this is why it works)
   0 D | 50000 C | 80000 B | 120000 A

=VLOOKUP(K2, bands!$A$2:$B$5, 2, TRUE)

   47764 -> D    62990 -> C    86052 -> B    5200000 -> A

784 – 90

Close — the number

=SUM(Y2:Y201)        1781426.45      the whole bonus bill
Lakshmi Kumar, row 5  780000.00      one person
Ask them to compute the share: 44 per cent. One employee of two hundred is nearly half the bonus budget.

Every formula today was correct. Put “total bonus 17.8 lakh” in a report without saying half is one person and you have told the truth and misled everybody.
Set up Thursday: Tuesday's grid — sixteen COUNTIFS formulas — gets rebuilt by dragging two words. No formulas. That is the pivot table.

Ask them these before they leave

Thirteen questions, in order. Numbers 3, 5 and 8 are the three that matter. Take each answer from a different person.

What are the four arguments of VLOOKUP, in order?
What you are looking for, where to look, which column to bring back as a number, and how — FALSE for exact.
Where must the value you are looking up sit, inside the block?
In the first column of the block. That is the rule everything else follows from, and it is why VLOOKUP can only bring back something to the right.
Why is the third argument 2 and not B?
Because it counts from the start of your block, not the start of the sheet. The block starts at column A, so A is 1 and B is 2. If the block started at D, then D would be 1.
I filled my VLOOKUP down. The first three rows are right and the rest say #N/A. What did I forget?
The dollar signs on the lookup block. It slid down one row per row until it ran off the bottom of the table. The first three were right by luck, not because the formula was right.
What happens if you leave the fourth argument out entirely?
It does approximate matching, which on unsorted text returns whatever it lands on. No error, no warning, just a wrong answer. Type FALSE.
Somebody inserted a column into my lookup table and every answer changed, but I never touched my formula. Why?
The third argument is a number you counted by hand. When the columns moved, Excel did not renumber it, so it is now bringing back a different field.
What does #N/A actually mean?
Not available — the value you asked for is not in the table you pointed at. It is not a crash. It is usually a real finding about your data.
Does IFERROR fix the problem?
No. It hides the error and shows your own words instead. The value is still missing from the table. Read the errors before you hide them.
emp_id is column A and name is column C. Can VLOOKUP find the id for a given name?
No — impossible, not just hard. The id is to the left of the name, and VLOOKUP only looks right.
What does MATCH give you back?
A position, not a value. MATCH("Karthik Reddy", C2:C201, 0) returns 3 — he is the third name in the list.
Why does INDEX with MATCH work where VLOOKUP cannot?
Because you name the two columns separately, so neither has to be left or right of the other.
Name two things XLOOKUP fixes.
Any two of: looks left or right; no column counting, so inserting a column does not break it; exact match by default; and the not-found answer is built in.
When is TRUE actually the right answer?
For bands and ranges on a sorted table — grades, tax slabs, salary bands. You list where each band starts, and TRUE takes the largest value still smaller than yours. Nowhere else.

Questions you will get

“Should I just always use XLOOKUP?”

“If everybody who will open your file has it, yes — it is better in every way. But you cannot control who opens your file, and an older Excel shows #NAME? where your formula was. On a shared company file, VLOOKUP is the safe choice. That is not a technical answer, it is a practical one.”

“What is HLOOKUP?”

“The same thing sideways — it searches across the first row instead of down the first column. You will meet it almost never, because data is nearly always stored with one record per row. Know the name, nothing more.”

“Can I use a whole column, like bonus!A:B?”

“It works, and it saves you locking anything. On a four-row table nobody will notice. On a hundred thousand rows it makes the sheet slow, because every formula searches every row. Learn to write the exact range — it is a better habit and it makes you think about where your data actually ends.”

“My VLOOKUP says #N/A but I can see the value is there.”

“Almost always one of three things. A trailing space — which is what TRIM was for on Thursday. Or one side is text and the other is a number, so "1001" never matches 1001. Or the value is outside the block you pointed at.”

“Does it matter if the lookup table is on a different file, not just a different sheet?”

“It works, and I would avoid it. The formula then contains a file path, and the day somebody moves or renames that file every lookup breaks. Keep the lookup table in the same workbook, on its own sheet.”

“What if there are two rows with the same value in the lookup table?”

“VLOOKUP takes the first one it finds and stops. It does not warn you that there was a second. If duplicates are possible in your lookup table, that is a data problem to fix before you look anything up — which is exactly what Remove Duplicates was for.”

“Is INDEX and MATCH faster than VLOOKUP?”

“Slightly, on very large sheets, because it only reads the two columns you named rather than the whole block. At your scale it makes no difference at all. Use it for the left-lookup problem, not for speed.”

“Could pandas do this?”

“Yes — it is merge, and it is one line. It also handles the duplicate problem properly instead of silently taking the first match. The reason you are learning this version is that the files you will be handed have VLOOKUPs in them, and somebody will ask you why a column of them is returning zero.”

“The 44 per cent — should we leave her out of the report?”

“No. She is a real employee and that is real money the company is paying. You report the total and you say that one person accounts for nearly half of it. That sentence is the actual finding — it is far more useful to whoever reads your report than the total on its own.”

Excel day 5 · merged class · 90 minutes · full script · the one they will use every day

The Grid,
Without the Formulas

On Tuesday they built a sixteen-cell grid with sixteen COUNTIFS formulas and a half-locked reference. Today they build the same grid by dragging two words, in about nine seconds.

4boxes, and that is the tool
0formulas written
Countthe default, and usually wrong
32%of the company is Sales

Open on Tuesday's grid, still on the sheet

Do not start with “today we learn pivot tables”. Start by scrolling to the COUNTIFS grid they built on Tuesday, and asking how long it took. Then build the identical thing in front of them with no formula at all, and put the two side by side.

That comparison is the entire argument for the session, and it only works because they did the hard version first. This is the payoff Tuesday was earning.

Before you walk in

  1. They must still have Tuesday's grid on the sheet. The whole opening depends on putting the old grid and the new pivot next to each other. If somebody deleted it, have them rebuild two cells of it — enough to see the formula in the bar.
  2. The default aggregation is Count, and it is usually not what you want. Drag salary into Values and Excel may well count it rather than add it. Let that happen, let them read a column of 64 / 49 / 45 / 42 where they expected money, and fix it together. It is the single most common pivot mistake in the world.
  3. Say “Count of salary is not the salary” out loud at least twice. It is how a wrong pivot gets into a real report — the numbers look plausible and the heading says what it is doing, and nobody reads the heading.
  4. The Tech average comes back today, and it is the same lesson from a new angle. The pivot will cheerfully show 1,89,753 as the Tech average. A pivot table does not protect you from an outlier — it just finds it faster. Say so.
  5. The menu layout differs between Excel versions and between Excel and Sheets. Field names and box names are stable; where the buttons live is not. Do not promise an exact menu path — show it on your screen, then walk the room, because two or three people will have it somewhere else.
  6. Refresh is not automatic, and this is the one thing that will embarrass them in a job. Change a cell in the data and the pivot does not move — the exact opposite of everything they learned on day 1. Demonstrate it deliberately.

Understand this yourself first

Three things: what the four boxes actually do, why Count is the default and why that matters, and the one way a pivot table behaves unlike every other formula in this module.

Part one · the four boxes, and what each one means
Rows
What goes down the side. Excel finds every different value in that column and gives each one a row. Drop department here and you get four rows.
Columns
What goes across the top. Same idea, sideways. Drop rating here and you get four columns.
Values
The number in the middle, and how to work it out — count, sum, average, min, max.
Filters
Sits above the whole table and cuts which rows are included at all. Drop city here and you can see the same table for Chennai only.
Why they already understand this

Rows plus Columns plus a Count is exactly the COUNTIFS grid from Tuesday. Rows plus a Sum is the SUMIF list from Tuesday. A pivot table is not a new idea — it is the same four functions with a drag-and-drop front end.

Say this early, because it changes how the room listens: you already know what a pivot table computes. Today is about not having to write it.
Part two · Count, and the most common pivot mistake there is
What Excel does when you drop a field into Values

If the column is text, Excel counts it — there is nothing else it could do. If the column is numbers, it usually sums it. But when a number column contains blanks or anything it is unsure about, it falls back to Count.

Our salary column has two blanks. So dropping salary into Values can give you Count of salary, and a Tech row reading 48 instead of ₹91,08,170.

Why that gets into real reports
Count of salary Sales 64 Tech 48 HR 44 Marketing 42 Sum of salary Sales 4264991 Tech 9108170 HR 2495026 ...

The count column looks like a perfectly reasonable set of numbers. It is a plausible answer to a different question. And the only thing on screen telling you which one you are looking at is the small heading in the corner that says Count of rather than Sum of.

Teach them to read that heading first, every single time, before they read any number underneath it. It is the one habit that stops a wrong pivot leaving the building. The fix is right-click the number, Summarize Values By, and choose Sum.
One more thing the blanks do

Average of salary for Tech is computed over 48 salaries, not 49 people. The pivot skips the blank, exactly as AVERAGE and AVERAGEIF did. It is consistent — and it means the count beside an average is not always the count of rows.

Part three · the one way a pivot behaves unlike everything else
It does not update itself

Everything in this module so far has recalculated the instant a cell changed. That was the whole argument on day 1 — a spreadsheet is rules that are always running.

A pivot table is not. It takes a snapshot of the data when you build it. Change a salary in the source and the pivot keeps showing the old number, indefinitely, with nothing to indicate it is stale.

change K5 from 5200000 to 520000 the summary block in P and Q updates immediately every COUNTIF and SUMIF updates immediately the pivot table does NOT. it keeps the old number. right-click the pivot -> Refresh (or Data -> Refresh All)
Why this one matters more than it sounds

It is how a stale number ends up in a monthly report. Somebody fixes the data, sends the file on, and the pivot on the next sheet is still reporting last month — and because every other cell in the workbook did update, the file looks perfectly consistent.

Refresh is a habit, not a feature.

Open a file with a pivot in it → refresh before you read anything. Change the data → refresh. Hand the file on → refresh first. It costs one right-click and it is the difference between a current report and a confident wrong one.

26 – 44

Count of salary is not the salary

The most common pivot mistake in the world. Let it happen.

Take rating back out of Columns so the table is simple again. Then drag salary into Values. Do not warn them what is about to happen.

Take rating back out for a moment. Now I want money instead of headcount, so drag salary into Values, and take name out.

Row Labels Count of salary HR 44 Marketing 42 Sales 64 Tech 48 Grand Total 198
“Is that money?”
No. HR does not pay a total of forty-four rupees. It counted the salaries instead of adding them. Wait for somebody to notice the numbers are suspiciously small and suspiciously familiar.

HR is not paying forty-four rupees. Excel counted the salaries instead of adding them.

And look at the heading. It says Count of salary. It told us exactly what it was doing. We just did not read it.

“Two hundred rows, but the Grand Total says 198. Why?”
The two blank salaries, again. Count of salary counts the ones that exist. Fourth session running that those two blanks have shown up, and by now the room should see it coming.

Right-click any number in the pivot. Summarize Values By. Choose Sum.

Row Labels Sum of salary HR 2495026 Marketing 3106086 Sales 4264991 Tech 9108170 Grand Total 18974273

That is money. And those four numbers are exactly the SUMIF answers from Tuesday.

Read the heading before you read the numbers.

Count of salary and Sum of salary are two completely different questions, and the only thing on screen that distinguishes them is one small word in the corner. A pivot showing counts where it should show sums looks entirely reasonable, and that is how it gets into a report.
Now the callback. Same right-click, choose Average. They should see this one coming — and that is the point.

Right-click again. Summarize Values By, then Average.

Row Labels Average of salary HR 56705.14 Marketing 73954.43 Sales 66640.48 Tech 189753.54 Grand Total 95829.66
“Tech again. Does a pivot table protect you from that?”
No. It is the same 1,89,753 from Tuesday, the same one person on row 5. A pivot table does not check your data — it just finds the problem faster.

One lakh eighty-nine thousand. Same number as Tuesday, same person causing it.

A pivot table is faster than writing AVERAGEIF sixteen times. It is not smarter. It will not tell you one person is distorting a department, and nothing ever will.

44 – 58

Per cent of total, and the filter box

The two things that turn a pivot from a table into an answer.

Put it back to a count of name. Sales has 64 people. Is that a lot?

You cannot tell, because 64 only means something next to 200. So let us ask for the share instead.

Drag name into Values a second time, so you have two value columns
  right-click the second one  ->  Show Values As  ->  % of Grand Total
Row Labels Count of name % of total HR 45 22.50% Marketing 42 21.00% Sales 64 32.00% Tech 49 24.50% Grand Total 200 100.00%

Thirty-two per cent of this company is Sales. Almost a third.

That is a sentence you could put in a report. “Sixty-four” is not.

And notice I kept the count next to the percentage. Always show both — a percentage on its own hides how many people it is actually describing.

“% of Grand Total” is one of several options and the others are genuinely useful. % of Row Total and % of Column Total answer different questions on the same grid. Name them, show one, do not drill all of them — they are easy to find once they know the menu exists.
Now the fourth box, which has been empty all session.

One box we have not used. Drag city into Filters.

A dropdown appears above the whole table. Choose Chennai.

city: Chennai Row Labels Count of name HR .. Marketing .. Sales .. Tech .. Grand Total 61

Sixty-one. The whole table has been recomputed for Chennai only, and the breakdown underneath it is now the Chennai breakdown.

Switch it to Bangalore — 54. Hyderabad — 48. Pune — 37. Those four add to two hundred, which is your check again.

“What is the difference between putting city in Filters and putting it in Rows?”
Rows shows you all four cities at once, side by side, so you can compare them. Filters shows you one at a time, with everything else hidden. Use Rows to compare, Filters to focus. Good question to make somebody answer rather than telling them.
Clear the filter before moving on, and say why. A pivot with a filter left on is the second-best way to put a wrong number in a report — the dropdown is small, it sits above the table, and a reader who has not noticed it will take the total at face value. Check the filter box before you trust a pivot anybody else built.
58 – 72

The thing that does not update

The one behaviour that contradicts day 1. Demonstrate it deliberately.

This block is why they will not embarrass themselves in a job. Do the demonstration, do not just describe it.

On day one I told you the whole point of a spreadsheet: a script is instructions you run, a spreadsheet is rules that are always running. Change one cell and everything moves.

Watch this. Go back to the data sheet and change K5 — the fifty-two lakh — to 520000. Then look at your summary block in P and Q.

average salary 72130.82 moved instantly, as always

Moved immediately, as it has all module. Now go to the pivot sheet.

Average of salary Tech 189753.54 unchanged. still the old number.
“Why has the pivot not moved?”
Because a pivot table works from a snapshot taken when you built it, not from the live cells. It is the one thing in Excel that does not recalculate on its own, and there is nothing on screen to tell you it is stale.

The pivot is showing a number that is no longer true, and it looks exactly as confident as it did five minutes ago.

Right-click anywhere in the pivot and choose Refresh.

Average of salary Tech 92253.54 now it agrees with the data
This is how a stale number gets into a monthly report.

Somebody corrects the data. Every formula in the workbook updates. The pivot on the next sheet does not, and the file looks perfectly consistent — because everything else did move.

Refresh when you open a file with a pivot in it. Refresh after you change data. Refresh before you send it. One right-click.

Ctrl+Z to put the salary back, and refresh again so the pivot agrees.

Two more things that bite, worth one sentence each. Adding new rows to the bottom of your data does not add them to the pivot — the pivot remembers the range it was built from, and refreshing will not help; you have to change the source range. And Data → Refresh All updates every pivot in the workbook at once, which is the one to use when a file has several.

Ask them these before they leave

Thirteen questions, in order. Numbers 4, 8 and 10 are the three that matter. Take each answer from a different person.

Name the four boxes and what each one does.
Rows down the side, Columns across the top, Values the number in the middle and how to work it out, Filters cuts which rows are included at all.
Which formulas from Tuesday does a pivot table replace?
COUNTIFS for the grid, SUMIF and AVERAGEIF for the lists. It computes the same things — you just do not write them.
Your pivot says HR is 44 and Sales is 64 for salary. Is that money?
No — it counted instead of adding. The heading says Count of salary. Right-click, Summarize Values By, Sum.
Count of salary gives a Grand Total of 198 but there are 200 rows. Why?
The two blank salaries. Count of salary counts the ones that exist. Fourth session those two have shown up.
What is the first thing you should read on any pivot table?
The heading in the corner — Count of, Sum of, Average of. It is the only thing on screen telling you which question is being answered.
Why show a percentage next to the count rather than instead of it?
Because a percentage alone hides how many people it describes. Thirty-two per cent of two hundred is a different thing from thirty-two per cent of eight.
What is the difference between putting city in Filters and in Rows?
Rows shows all four cities at once so you can compare. Filters shows one at a time with the rest hidden. Compare with Rows, focus with Filters.
I changed a salary in the data. Why did the pivot not move?
Because a pivot works from a snapshot, not from the live cells. It is the one thing in Excel that does not recalculate on its own. Right-click, Refresh.
When should you refresh?
When you open a file with a pivot in it, after you change the data, and before you send it to anybody. One right-click.
I added twenty new rows under my data and refreshed. They are not in the pivot. Why?
The pivot remembers the range it was built from, and new rows are outside it. Refreshing will not help — you have to change the source range.
The pivot says Tech averages 1,89,753. Is the pivot wrong?
No. It is the correct average of the Tech salaries, and one of them is 52 lakh. A pivot does not check your data. It finds the problem faster, it does not notice it for you.
Somebody hands you a pivot table. Name two things to check before you trust a number on it.
Any two of: the Count of / Sum of heading; whether a filter is left on; whether it has been refreshed; and whether the source range covers all the data.
Why did we build the grid by hand on Tuesday if today took nine seconds?
So that you know what the pivot is computing and could check any cell of it yourself. People who only know the button cannot tell when the button is wrong.

Questions you will get

“Can I put more than one field in Rows?”

“Yes, and it nests them — department, then city inside each department, with subtotals. It is genuinely useful and it gets unreadable fast. Two levels is usually the most anybody can read.”

“What is the difference between a pivot table and just sorting and filtering?”

“Sorting and filtering show you rows of your data. A pivot shows you a summary of all of it — a number per group, computed across rows you never see. Filtering hides rows; a pivot aggregates them.”

“Is a pivot table the same as groupby in pandas?”

“Close enough that the answer is yes. Rows is what you group by, Values is what you aggregate and how. df.groupby("department")["salary"].mean() is the Average of salary by department you built today. Same operation, different front end.”

“Why does my pivot table show a blank row?”

“Because some rows in your data have nothing in that field, and the pivot gives them their own group called (blank). That is useful, not untidy — it is telling you how many rows are missing that value.”

“Can I make a chart from a pivot table?”

“Yes — it is called a pivot chart, and it updates with the pivot. That is the next session, and it is the fastest way in Excel to go from raw rows to a picture somebody else can read.”

“Can I edit the numbers inside a pivot table?”

“No, and that is deliberate. A pivot is a view of your data, not a copy you can type over. If a number is wrong, the data is wrong — go and fix it there, then refresh.”

“Does Google Sheets have pivot tables?”

“Yes, and the four boxes are the same four boxes with slightly different names. The menu layout differs and the summarize option is called something else. If you understand the four boxes, you can find your way around any version.”

“My percentages add up to 99.99 per cent.”

“Rounding. Each one got rounded to two decimals and the leftovers do not cancel out. It is not an error and you should not fix it by editing numbers — if it matters for a report, show one fewer decimal place.”

“Should I use pivot tables or formulas?”

“Pivot for exploring — when you do not yet know what you are looking for and you want to try six breakdowns in two minutes. Formulas for anything that has to sit in a report and update itself, because they recalculate and a pivot does not. Most real work uses both on the same file.”

Excel day 6 · merged class · 90 minutes · full script · closes the module

One Sheet
Somebody Else
Can Read

Five sessions of finding things out. This one is about handing it over — charts with a mouse, numbers that look like money, and one page a manager could open without you standing next to them.

3clicks to a chart
2025a year that is not a number
1sheet, built live
6sessions, closed

They have already done the hard half of this

This class spent five sessions on Data Visualisation. They know what a bar chart is for, why a pie chart is usually a bad idea, and that a truncated axis can lie. Do not teach any of that again. Today is only where the buttons are, plus the formatting that decides whether anybody reads the sheet at all.

So the charts half runs fast and the assembly half gets the time. Ending the module on a finished page they built themselves is worth more than another chart type.

Before you walk in

  1. Say in minute one that the chart-choosing rules are not being repeated. They had a whole visualisation module. Treating them as beginners here wastes twenty minutes and is faintly insulting. Point back to it instead: “you already know which chart. Today is where the button is.”
  2. Build charts from the pivot tables, not from the raw data. It is two clicks instead of selecting ranges, it updates with the pivot, and it quietly makes Thursday's session look like it was worth doing.
  3. The number formats matter more than the charts, and they will not believe that. A salary column reading 5200000 instead of ₹52,00,000 is the single thing that makes a sheet look like a student exercise. Spend the time.
  4. The year trap is the one real gotcha of the day. Pull a year out of a date and Excel gives you a number, so a chart of joins per year will happily put a trendline through it and the axis will read 2,015 with a thousands separator. Catch it live.
  5. Budget the last twenty-five minutes for assembly and protect them. If you overrun on charts, cut a chart type — do not cut the dashboard. The finished page is the deliverable.
  6. Decide now whether you are closing the module with a round-up. The last five minutes carry six sessions and hand over to Power BI. It is worth saying properly rather than running out of time and waving.

Understand this yourself first

Three things: what a number format actually changes, the year trap and why it happens, and what makes a sheet readable by somebody who was not in the room.

Part one · a number format changes what you see, never what is stored
They met this on day 1 and it comes back as a tool

Day 1: they pressed Decrease Decimal, the cell showed 38.2, and it still held 38.175. Same idea, now used on purpose.

the cell holds 5200000 you can display it as 5200000 52,00,000 ₹52,00,000 52.0 L 5.2e+06 every formula pointing at it still uses 5200000.
The four that matter today
comma
Thousands separators. Excel's default is the international grouping — 5,200,000. The Indian lakh grouping needs a custom format, and whether it is worth doing depends who is reading.
currency
Adds the symbol. Accounting format also lines the symbols up down the column and puts zeroes as dashes, which reads better in a report.
percentage
Multiplies the displayed value by 100 and adds a sign. This one genuinely catches people — format a cell holding 15 as a percentage and it shows 1500%.
date
A date is stored as a number of days. Format it as General and you get 45678. That is not corruption — it is what was always underneath.
Part two · the year trap
What goes wrong

To chart joins per year you first need a year column, which is =YEAR(L2). That returns 2015 — and 2015 is a number, not a label.

So when you chart it, three things happen that nobody asked for. The axis reads 2,015 with a thousands separator. Excel may offer to put a trendline through the years. And on a scatter or line it will happily interpolate between them.

Why it matters beyond being ugly

It is the dept_id problem again, in its last form. dept_id averaged to 2.32 because a label was stored as digits. A year is the same thing: digits that are a name, not a quantity.

Fifth session, same lesson.

Excel will do arithmetic on anything that looks like a number, and it will never ask whether the arithmetic means anything. Average department: 2.32. Average joining year: 2020.4. Both compute. Neither is a fact.
The fix, and it is a formatting fix

Format the axis labels as text or turn the thousands separator off, and never accept the trendline. If you want to be thorough, build the year column as =TEXT(L2,"yyyy") so it is a label from the start — though a pivot grouped by year handles it for you, which is the easier route.

Part three · what makes a sheet readable to somebody who was not there
The test to teach them

Could you send this to somebody and say nothing? Not “is it correct” — correct is assumed by now. Could a manager open it, read it, and not have to ask you a single question?

a title
On the sheet, not just the tab. What this is, and as at when. A number with no date on it is a number nobody can check.
units
Rupees or lakhs, people or percentages. Say it next to the number, not in your head.
the n
How many rows this is built on. 200. A summary without its denominator is the most common way a sheet misleads honestly.
the caveat
The 52-lakh earner belongs on the page. One line: one employee accounts for 27% of total salary; averages shown alongside medians. That sentence is the difference between a report and a trap.
And the thing they will not think of

Put the summary on its own sheet, and put it first. A reader who opens a workbook and lands on 200 rows of raw data will close it. Right-click the tab, Move, to the front. It costs five seconds and it changes who reads your work.

The session, minute by minute

Everything in a speech box is meant to be said more or less as written. Everything in a grey box is a direction for you, not words to say.

0 – 8

What today is, and what it is not

Set the frame in eight minutes. They are not beginners at charts and should not be treated as any.

Say this plainly at the top. It changes how the room listens for the rest of the session.

You spent five whole sessions on charts in the visualisation module. You know which chart answers which question. You know a pie chart is usually the wrong answer. You know an axis that does not start at zero can tell a true lie.

I am not teaching any of that again.

Today is two things. Where the buttons are in Excel, which takes about half an hour. And then the part nobody teaches — making a sheet that somebody else can actually read.

“In five sessions of statistics and six of Excel, how many times have you handed your work to anybody?”
Not once. Everything has been for them, on their own screen, with them there to explain it. That is the gap this session closes.

Every number you have found in this file, you found for yourself, with yourself there to explain it.

In a job that is not what happens. You find something and somebody else reads it, in a different room, next week, without you. Today is about that.

It reads 2,015 with a thousands separator, because Excel thinks the year is a quantity. Somebody may also be offered a trendline through it. Same problem as dept_id averaging to 2.32 — fifth session, same lesson.

Two thousand and fifteen, written as two comma zero one five. Excel has decided the year is a quantity.

You have met this exactly before. dept_id averaged to 2.32 because a label was stored as digits. A year is the same thing. You can compute the average joining year of this company — it comes to about 2020.4 — and it is not a fact about anything.

Excel will do arithmetic on anything shaped like a number.

It did it to dept_id on day 1. It is doing it to the year now. It has never once asked whether the arithmetic means anything, and it never will.

Numbers that look like money

The part they will not expect to matter. It matters more than the charts.

Put the raw salary column on screen next to a formatted one. The comparison does the arguing.

Look at the salary column. 47764. 86052. 5200000.

Those are correct and they are hard to read. You have to count digits to tell five million from five hundred thousand, and in a column of two hundred you will get it wrong.

Select the salary column — Home tab
  the comma button  (,)     ->  5,200,000
  the currency dropdown     ->  ₹5,200,000
  Accounting format         ->  ₹  5,200,000     symbols aligned, zeroes as -

Same numbers. Every formula still reads the same value. Only the display changed — exactly like Decrease Decimal on day one.

And one honest note. Excel's comma gives you 5,200,000, the international grouping. If your reader expects 52,00,000, that needs a custom format — worth knowing it exists, not worth twenty minutes today.

The percentage trap, and it will happen to somebody. Take the bonus percentage column from Tuesday — it holds 15, meaning fifteen per cent. Format it as Percentage and it shows 1500%. Excel assumes a percentage cell holds 0.15, not 15. Either divide by 100 first, or leave it as a plain number with “%” in the heading.
Now data bars — three clicks, and the one piece of conditional formatting that belongs on a summary.

One more. Select the department counts in your pivot — 64, 49, 45, 42.

Home, Conditional Formatting, Data Bars, pick a colour.

Sales 64 ████████████████████ Tech 49 ███████████████ HR 45 ██████████████ Marketing 42 █████████████

A bar chart inside the cells, and the numbers are still there.

On Thursday you turned the minus four red with conditional formatting. Same menu, different job — that one was finding a problem, this one is helping somebody read.

One caution, because it is the same lie as a truncated axis. By default the longest bar fills the cell, so the bars are relative to each other, not to zero or to a total. Four bars reading 64, 49, 45, 42 look dramatically different when the real spread is modest. They learned this exact point in visualisation — it applies here too.

That is the single most valuable line on the whole sheet, and it is a sentence, not a number.

Six sessions. And every one of them, on the same two hundred rows you have had since the first day of statistics.

That was deliberate. By now you know this file well enough to spot when an answer is wrong, and that is the only reason any of the mistakes in this module were visible.

The five things that were not about Excel at all
1.  a blank is not a zero.
    it showed up in five of the six sessions.

2.  a wrong answer looks exactly like a right one.
    no dollar sign. one-column sort. ">$Q$10" in quotes.
    VLOOKUP with no FALSE. Count of salary. every one silent.

3.  a correct formula is not a correct answer.
    AVERAGEIF on Tech was perfect and useless.

4.  always add the groups back up.
    64+49+45+42 = 200 correct.  12+186 = 198, and that told us something.

5.  no tool asks whether your question makes sense.
    average dept_id = 2.32.  average joining year = 2020.4.
    both compute. neither is a fact.

None of those five are Excel. They are all true of pandas, and they will all be true of Power BI.

Which is where we go next.

Power BI does everything you learned on Thursday — grouping, aggregating, filtering — and it does it on millions of rows instead of two hundred, and it builds the charts for you.

You will recognise more of it than you expect. A pivot table is a Power BI visual. A SUMIF is a measure. The four boxes are the four wells. Different names, same ideas.

And the one thing it will not do for you is the line in A10 — the sentence that says what the number does not. That has been your job since day one and it stays your job.
