Ask them these before they leave

Thirteen questions — the last five are about the whole module, not just today. Numbers 3, 7 and 11 are the ones that matter.

You formatted a salary as currency. What changed in the cell?
Only what you see. The cell still holds the same number and every formula pointing at it still uses the same number. Same as Decrease Decimal on day 1.
When should a chart have a legend and when should it not?
One series, no legend — there is nothing to distinguish. More than one, legend, or nobody knows which colour is which.
Your year axis reads 2,015. What has Excel assumed, and where have you seen this before?
That the year is a quantity rather than a label. Same as dept_id averaging to 2.32 — digits that are a name, not a number.
I formatted a cell holding 15 as a percentage and it says 1500%. Why?
Excel expects a percentage cell to hold 0.15, not 15. Divide by 100 first, or keep it as a plain number with the % in the heading.
What is the problem with data bars, by default?
The longest bar fills the cell, so bars are relative to each other, not to zero. A modest spread can look dramatic. Same lie as a truncated axis.
Why does the summary sheet go first in the workbook?
Because somebody who opens it and lands on 200 rows of raw data will close it. The first thing a reader sees should be the answer.
Why is the median on the summary next to the average?
Because they disagree by twenty-six thousand, and that disagreement is the finding. Either number alone would be a trap.
Four things every summary page needs.
A title with a date. The units. The n — how many rows it is built on. And at least one caveat line saying what the numbers do not say.
You put ₹1,89,754 as the Tech average on a summary. What else must go on the page?
That it is distorted by one 52-lakh salary, and that without it the Tech average is ₹83,153. A number like that on a report with no note is the mistake this whole module has been warning about.
What is the test for whether a sheet is finished?
Could you send it to somebody and say nothing? Not “is it correct” — could a manager open it, read it, and not have to ask you a single question.
Across six sessions, how many times did a blank cell cause a wrong answer?
Five of the six. The gap column, AVERAGE dividing by 199, COUNTIF giving 198, the IF calling Manoj below average, and Count of salary in the pivot. A blank is not a zero.
Name three mistakes from this module that produced no error message.
Any three of: the missing dollar sign; the one-column sort; ">$Q$10" inside quotes returning 0; VLOOKUP with no FALSE; the lookup block not locked; and Count of salary in a pivot. Every one looked like a real answer.
What is the one thing no tool will ever do for you?
Ask whether your question makes sense. Average dept_id is 2.32. Average joining year is 2020.4. Both compute perfectly and neither is a fact about anything.

Questions you will get

“Why can't Excel show 52,00,000 with the comma button?”

“Because the comma button uses the international grouping — every three digits. The Indian lakh-crore grouping needs a custom number format. It is worth knowing it exists; whether you use it depends entirely on who is reading your sheet, and for most company reporting the international one is what is expected.”

“Is this what a dashboard is?”

“It is the simplest version of one. A real dashboard adds slicers, so the reader can filter it themselves, and it refreshes from live data rather than a file. That is Power BI, and it is the next module. But the thinking is identical — one page, a named reader, the headline first, and the caveats visible.”

“Should I use pie charts at all?”

“You answered this yourselves in the visualisation module. Rarely — people compare lengths well and angles badly. The one case it works is a small number of parts of one whole where you only need a rough sense, like our four departments. With more than about five slices it becomes unreadable.”

“Can I paste an Excel chart into PowerPoint?”

“Yes, and you get a choice when you paste. Link it and it updates when the Excel file changes, but breaks if the file moves. Paste it as a picture and it is frozen for ever. For a deck you will present once, paste the picture — a broken link in front of a room is worse.”

“How do I stop somebody editing my summary sheet?”

“Review tab, Protect Sheet. It stops accidental typing, not a determined person. If the numbers genuinely must not change, send a PDF. A protected sheet is a courtesy, not security.”

“Why did we never use macros or VBA?”

“Because you already have a better programming language. VBA exists so that people who only have Excel can automate it; you have Python. No fresher analyst job will ask you for VBA, and the time was better spent on lookups and pivots, which they all ask about.”

“Is Excel or Python better for this?”

“Wrong question, and it is worth answering properly because an interviewer may ask it. Excel for data a human will look at and numbers somebody wants to change while you watch. Python for data a human cannot look at and for anything you have to do every week. The honest answer is that you will use both on the same file, often in the same hour.”

“Do I put Excel on my CV?”

“Yes, and be specific. ‘Excel’ on a CV means nothing. ‘Pivot tables, VLOOKUP and INDEX-MATCH, conditional formatting, summary reporting’ means you have actually used it. And you can now answer follow-up questions on every one of those, which is the part that matters in the interview.”

“What should I practise before Power BI?”

“One thing: pivot tables. Build four or five from this file on questions nobody asked you. Power BI is pivot tables with better charts and more data, so every minute there pays off twice. If you have extra time after that, VLOOKUP — because that is what the interview will ask.”

August B3 Python day 23 · 90 minutes · full script

The Loop You
Have Not Met

Every loop they have written knew how many times it would run before it started. Today, the one that does not — and the two keywords that let you leave a loop early or skip a turn.

7people, not known in advance
4checks saved by break
72.43not 50.7
3keywords, one session

Everything today is a plain list they type themselves

This batch has not met pandas or NumPy — those start at D28. No read_csv, no DataFrame, no file. Every example here is a list of ten numbers typed on screen, which they can read end to end and check by eye. That is also the right call teaching-wise: when the loop is the new thing, the data should be something they can already see.

Before you walk in

  1. Do not open with syntax. Open with a question a for loop cannot answer. If they do not feel the gap, while is just a second way to write something they can already do, and they will never reach for it.
  2. Write the infinite loop on purpose, and let it run. They will meet one by accident in their first week otherwise. Show it, stop it with the keyboard interrupt, and point at the missing line.
  3. Three lines are non-negotiable on the board. Start the counter, check the condition, change the counter. Forgetting the third is the entire bug.
  4. Teach break and continue inside a for, not a while. They know for cold, so all the attention goes to the new keyword rather than to a new loop shape at the same time.
  5. This is a guaranteed interview question. “Difference between break and continue?” comes up constantly. Make them say the one-line answer out loud before they leave.

Understand this yourself first

Three keywords, and the only one with a trap in it is while. Read part one properly.

Part one · what while is actually for
The difference from for, in one sentence

A for loop is handed a list and runs once per item. Before it starts, the number of turns is already decided.

A while loop is handed a condition. It keeps going for as long as that condition is true, and nobody knows how many turns that will be — including the person who wrote it.

Use for when you know how many times. Use while when you only know when to stop. That is the whole decision, and it is the interview answer too.
The three lines, and the one everybody forgets
1. start the counter i = 1 — before the loop, or the condition has nothing to check.
2. the condition while i <= 5: — checked before every turn, including the first.
3. change the counter i = i + 1 — inside the loop. Leave this out and the condition never becomes false.

Step three is the whole bug. Every infinite loop a beginner writes is a missing step three.

Show the infinite loop deliberately

If you only warn them about it, they meet their first one alone, at night, and panic. Run one in class, let it scroll, stop it with Ctrl + C (or the stop button in the editor), and point at the missing line. Thirty seconds, and it removes a whole category of fear.

Part two · break and continue
Two words, two very different jobs
break Leave the loop completely, right now. Nothing after it runs, and the loop does not take another turn.
continue Skip the rest of this turn only. Go straight back to the top and take the next one.

Students merge these constantly. The fix is a physical image: break is walking out of the room; continue is skipping your turn and staying in the game.

The continue example is the one that matters

A list of ten test marks where three students were absent, recorded as 0. Average all ten and you get 50.7. Skip the zeros and the real average is 72.43.

That is a twenty-two mark difference caused by counting absentees as if they scored nothing, and it is the kind of mistake that reaches a report. Worth more than any syntax explanation.

The session, minute by minute

Everything in a speech box is meant to be said more or less as written. Everything in a grey box is a direction for you, not words to say.

0 – 16

A question a for loop cannot answer

Make them feel the gap before you name the solution.

Do not say the word “while” yet. Put the list up, ask the question, and let them try.
Everyone types this list
salaries = [18000, 22000, 25000, 31000, 35000,
            42000, 48000, 55000, 60000, 72000]

print(len(salaries), "people")
print("total payroll:", sum(salaries))
10 people total payroll: 408000

Ten salaries, smallest to biggest. The whole payroll is four lakh eight thousand.

Now here is my question.

Start from the lowest paid person. Add the next. Then the next. Keep adding until the running total passes two lakh.

How many people is that?

“Write me a for loop for that.”
They cannot, and it is worth two minutes of them trying. A for loop has to be told how many turns — range(?). And nobody in the room knows the number. That is the point: the answer is the number of turns.

You cannot. And look at why you cannot.

Every for loop you have written says how many turns it gets up front. for i in range(10) is ten turns. for s in salaries is one turn per item. The number is decided before the loop starts.

But here, the number of turns is the answer. I do not know it. You do not know it. The computer has to find it.

So we need a different kind of loop. One that does not count turns — one that keeps going until something stops being true.

On the board
FOR    you know HOW MANY TIMES before you start
       for i in range(10):      <- ten turns, decided now

WHILE  you only know WHEN TO STOP
       while total < 200000:    <- as many turns as it takes
Use for when you know how many times. Use while when you only know when to stop.

Learn that one line. It is the answer to the interview question, and it is the only decision you ever have to make between them.
16 – 32

The three lines of a while loop

The smallest possible example, then the one that forgets step three.

Before we answer the payroll question, the shape — with the smallest example I can write.

Print the numbers one to five. You could do that with a for loop in your sleep. Watch what it looks like with while.

Type this
i = 1

while i <= 5:
    print(i)
    i = i + 1
1 2 3 4 5
Walk the three lines slowly. Four minutes. The third one is the whole session.

Three things are happening, and I want names for all three.

One. Start the counter. i = 1, and notice it is outside the loop, before it. The loop has to have something to check on its very first turn.

Two. The condition. while i <= 5:. Python checks this before every turn, including the first. True, take a turn. False, stop.

Three. Change the counter. i = i + 1, inside the loop.

And that third line is the one everybody forgets. Let me show you what happens.

Now break it on purpose. Warn them you are about to, so nobody panics, then run it and stop it in front of them.
Watch — I am going to delete one line
i = 1

while i <= 5:
    print(i)
    # i = i + 1      <- the line we removed
1 1 1 1 1 1 ... and it never stops

One, one, one, one, forever.

Why? Because i never changes. It is one at the start, still one at the end of the turn, so i <= 5 is still True. And it will be True for ever.

This is called an infinite loop. You will write one. Everybody writes one. So let me show you how to get out.

Press Control and C together. In most editors there is also a red stop button.

Actually run it and actually stop it in front of them. A student who has only been warned about infinite loops meets their first one alone at eleven at night and thinks they have broken their laptop. A student who has watched you stop one just presses the button.
Every infinite loop a beginner writes is a missing step three. If your loop will not stop, the first thing to check is: does the thing in the condition ever change inside the loop?
32 – 46

Now answer the payroll question

Back to the opening question, now that they have the tool.

Type this
total  = 0
people = 0

while total < 200000:
    total  = total + salaries[people]
    people = people + 1

print("people :", people)
print("total  :", total)
people : 7 total : 221000

Seven people.

And here is the thing I want you to notice. I did not tell the loop to run seven times. I could not have — I did not know it was seven until it finished.

I told it when to stop, and it worked out how many turns that took.

That is the only thing while does that for cannot.

Trace it on the board. It makes the timing of the condition check obvious, and explains the overshoot before anybody asks.
On the board — trace the turns
  start             total = 0        people = 0

  check 0 < 200000    yes -> add 18000   total 18000    people 1
  check 18000         yes -> add 22000   total 40000    people 2
  check 40000         yes -> add 25000   total 65000    people 3
  ...
  check 179000        yes -> add 42000   total 221000   people 7
  check 221000        NO  -> stop

  it checks AFTER adding, so it overshoots past 200000.

Look at the last two lines of that trace. The total came out at two lakh twenty-one thousand, not exactly two lakh.

It overshoots, because the condition is only checked between turns — never in the middle of one. It added the seventh salary, finished the turn, and only then looked.

“What if I write while total < 500000 — more than the whole payroll?”
It runs out of people and crashes with an IndexError, because salaries[people] eventually asks for position 10 in a list of 10. Run it for ten seconds — it shows that a while loop will walk off the end of your list if the condition never becomes false.
46 – 60

break — leave the loop early

Inside a for loop, so the only new thing is the keyword.

Two more keywords, and both go inside a loop. I am going to show them in a for loop, because you know for cold — so the only new thing on screen is the keyword itself.

First: break. I want the first salary above forty thousand.

Without break
checks = 0

for i in range(len(salaries)):
    checks = checks + 1
    if salaries[i] > 40000:
        found = i

print("checks made:", checks)
checks made: 10

The list is sorted, so once I find one above forty thousand, everybody after it is too. I have my answer early.

But the loop checked all ten. It kept going long after it knew.

With break
checks = 0

for i in range(len(salaries)):
    checks = checks + 1
    if salaries[i] > 40000:
        found = i
        break

print("found at position:", found)
print("that salary      :", salaries[found])
print("checks made      :", checks)
found at position: 5 that salary : 42000 checks made : 6

Six checks instead of ten. The moment it found what it wanted, it left.

break means: get out of this loop completely, right now. Nothing else in the loop runs, and it does not take another turn.

Position 5 but 6 checks — that is not a bug, and somebody will ask. Positions start at zero, so position 5 is the sixth item. And checks goes up before the if runs, so it counts the turn it found it on.
The honest use of break is searching. You are looking for the first thing that matches, and once you have it there is no reason to keep looking. On ten items saving four checks is nothing. On ten lakh rows it is the difference between an answer now and an answer after lunch.
60 – 76

continue — skip this one turn

The second keyword, and the example that shows why it matters.

Second keyword. continue. And this example is a real mistake people make at work.

Here are the marks for a test. Ten students. Three of them were absent, and whoever entered the data wrote their marks as zero.

Type this list
marks = [72, 0, 65, 88, 0, 91, 54, 77, 0, 60]

print("average of everything:", round(sum(marks) / len(marks), 2))
average of everything: 50.7
“Fifty point seven. Is that the class average?”
No. Three students did not sit the test. Counting them as having scored zero is counting a non-answer as a wrong answer. Let them spot it — the zeros are visible in the list.
Skip the absentees
total   = 0
counted = 0
absent  = 0

for m in marks:
    if m == 0:
        absent = absent + 1
        continue
    total   = total + m
    counted = counted + 1

print("absent  :", absent)
print("counted :", counted)
print("average :", round(total / counted, 2))
absent : 3 counted : 7 average : 72.43

Seventy-two point four three. Not fifty point seven.

That is a twenty-two mark difference, and it came from treating three absent students as if they had sat the test and scored nothing.

This is not a syntax point. This is the kind of mistake that goes into a report and makes a whole class look worse than it is.

Now the keyword itself. continue means: skip the rest of this turn, and go back to the top.

When m was zero, Python hit continue and jumped straight back up for the next student. The two lines below it never ran for that student.

But the loop kept going. That is the whole difference from break.

Put them side by side. This is the interview answer, so make them say it.
On the board
break      LEAVE THE LOOP COMPLETELY.
           nothing after it runs. no more turns. done.
           -> walking out of the room

continue   SKIP THE REST OF THIS TURN ONLY.
           go straight back to the top. the loop carries on.
           -> skipping your turn, but staying in the game
Ask it straight, and take the answer from three different people: “Difference between break and continue?”
This exact question is asked in interviews constantly. One sentence each. Do not let them leave without being able to say it without thinking.
Expect: “could I have just used an if instead?” Yes, and say so — if m != 0: around the two lines does the same job here. The difference is readability: with two or three things to skip, the if version drifts further and further right, and continue stays flat. Both are correct; one stays readable.
76 – 90

Practice, and close

Ten minutes on their own. Walk the room. Question 2 is the one that needs a while and they should feel that.
Their turn
# 1. print 10 down to 1 using a while loop
#    careful: which way does the counter move?

# 2. same payroll list. how many people before the total
#    passes 3 lakh? is it more or less than double 7? why?

# 3. loop over salaries and print the first one above 50000,
#    then stop

# 4. count how many students scored 70 or more,
#    skipping the absentees with continue
Question 1 catches people. Counting down needs i = i - 1 and the condition flips to while i >= 1. Somebody will write i = i + 1 from habit and get an infinite loop — which is the best possible time for that to happen, with you in the room.
The four lines. If everything else goes, keep these.
1.  FOR    -> you know HOW MANY TIMES before you start
    WHILE  -> you only know WHEN TO STOP

2.  a while loop needs THREE things:
      start the counter   (before the loop)
      the condition       (checked before every turn)
      CHANGE THE COUNTER  (inside the loop)  <- everybody forgets this

3.  break     leave the loop completely. no more turns.
    continue  skip the rest of THIS turn. the loop carries on.

4.  if your loop never stops: does the thing in the condition
    actually change inside the loop?  Ctrl + C to get out.

Tomorrow we do something you have not done once in this course — open a file from your own computer, read what is inside it, and write a new one.

Every list we have used so far, you typed yourself. Tomorrow you go and get the data instead.

The session, as a run sheet

Everything in order. Six steps, every code block, every board item written out. If you lose your place, this page alone is enough.

A question a for loop cannot answer

Land this: do not say “while” yet. Put the list up, ask the question, let them try to write a for loop, and let them fail.

On the board

FOR    you know HOW MANY TIMES before you start
WHILE  you only know WHEN TO STOP

On the board — the interview answer

676 – 90

Practice, and close

# 1. print 10 down to 1 with a while loop
# 2. same list - how many before the total passes 3 lakh?
#    more or less than double 7? why?
# 3. print the first salary above 50000, then stop

Q1 catches people: counting down needs i = i - 1 and while i >= 1. Somebody will write i = i + 1 from habit and get an infinite loop — the best possible time for that, with you in the room.
Tease tomorrow: “every list we have used, you typed yourself. Tomorrow you go and get the data instead” — open a file, read it, write a new one.

Ask them these before they leave

Twelve questions, in order, with the answer under each one. The first six are the ones that matter — if a student can answer those, they have the session. Take each answer from a different person.

What is the difference between a for loop and a while loop?
You use for when you know how many times before you start. You use while when you only know when to stop.
A while loop needs three things. What are they?
Start the counter (before the loop), the condition, and change the counter (inside the loop).
Which of those three does everybody forget?
Changing the counter. That is what an infinite loop is — the condition never becomes false because nothing in it ever moves.
Your loop is stuck and will not stop. What do you press, and what do you check?
Press Ctrl + C (or the red stop button). Then check whether the thing in the condition actually changes anywhere inside the loop.
When does Python check the condition — before each turn or after?
Before every turn, including the very first one. If it is false at the start, the loop body never runs at all.
Difference between break and continue?
break leaves the loop completely — no more turns. continue skips the rest of this turn only, and the loop carries on. Walking out of the room, versus skipping your turn and staying in the game.
We asked for 2 lakh and the total came out at 2,21,000. Why not exactly 2 lakh?
It checks between turns, never in the middle of one. It added the seventh salary, finished the turn, and only then looked. It overshoots by whatever that last salary was.
Seven people got us past 2 lakh. How many to get past 3 lakh — fourteen?
Nine. The list is sorted smallest first, so the first seven were the cheapest people. After that you are adding 55,000 and 60,000, so the next lakh only costs two more. The number of turns depends on what is in the list, not on the size of the target.
We found the salary at position 5, but the program said 6 checks. Is that a bug?
No. Positions start at zero, so position 5 is the sixth item. And checks goes up before the if runs, so it counts the turn it found it on.
Averaging all ten marks gave 50.7. Skipping the zeros gave 72.43. Which is the class average, and why?
72.43. Three students were absent — they did not sit the test. Recording them as zero and averaging it counts a non-answer as a wrong answer, and drags the whole class down by 22 marks.
Could you have used an if instead of continue there?
Yes — if m != 0: around the two lines does the same job. The difference is readability: with two or three things to skip, the if version keeps drifting right, and continue stays flat.
To count down from 10 to 1 instead of up, what two things change?
The counter becomes i = i - 1, and the condition flips to while i >= 1. Change only one of them and you get an infinite loop.

Questions you will get

“When would I actually use while instead of for?”

“Whenever you do not know how many turns you need. Asking the user for input until they type something valid, retrying something until it works, or today's example — adding things up until a total is reached. If you can count the turns in advance, use for: it is shorter and it cannot run forever.”

“My loop is stuck. What do I do?”

“Ctrl + C, or the red stop button. Then look at the thing in your condition and ask whether anything inside the loop actually changes it. Nine times out of ten you forgot the line that moves the counter.”

“Difference between break and continue?”

“break leaves the loop completely — no more turns at all. continue skips the rest of the current turn and goes back to the top, and the loop keeps running. Walking out of the room, versus skipping your turn and staying in the game.”

“Can I use break in a while loop too?”

“Yes, both work in both kinds of loop. We showed them in a for loop today only because you already know for well, so the keyword was the only new thing on screen.”

“Why did the total come to 2,21,000 and not exactly 2 lakh?”

“Because the condition is only checked between turns, never in the middle of one. The loop added the seventh salary, finished the turn, then checked and found the total had already passed. It overshoots by whatever that last salary was.”

“What is while True:? I have seen it online.”

“A loop with a condition that is always true, so it runs forever on purpose — and the only way out is a break inside it. It is a real pattern and you will meet it, but do not write it yet. Get comfortable with a condition that stops on its own first.”

“Does break get me out of both loops if they are nested?”

“No — only the inner one, the loop it is sitting directly inside. Getting out of both takes a bit more work and you do not need it today. Worth knowing the answer, because it is a favourite interview follow-up.”

August B3 Python day 24 · 90 minutes · full script

Going Outside
the Program

Every list they have ever used, they typed themselves. Today the data lives somewhere else — in a file on their own machine — and they go and get it.

5things to learn
1letter that wipes a file
\nthe one that bites
72.43same answer, new source

Write a file before you read one

Most courses start with “download this file and open it”, which means the first thing a student meets is a file they did not make and cannot see inside. Write first. They create the file, they know exactly what is in it, and reading it back is something they can check rather than trust.

Before you walk in

  1. Make them open the file in a text editor. Not once — every time they write one. A file stops being an abstraction the moment they can see it sitting in the folder next to their .py.
  2. The "w" trap is the one that will hurt them. Opening an existing file with "w" empties it immediately, before you write anything. Show it happening to a file with data in it. Nobody forgets after that.
  3. No try / except today. If the file is missing, the program crashes — let it, name the error, and say that tomorrow is about exactly that. Do not teach both in one session.
  4. Teach close() before with. If they meet with first it looks like decoration. Let them close files by hand for twenty minutes, then hand them the thing that does it for them.
  5. Finish by re-running yesterday's answer. Write yesterday's marks list to a file, read it back, and get 72.43 again. Same answer, and the data now lives outside the program.

Understand this yourself first

Five things, and only two of them have anything tricky in them — the mode letter, and the newline.

Part one · open, and the mode letter
Every file operation is three steps
open Tell Python which file, and what you intend to do with it.
read or write The actual work.
close Tell Python you are finished.

That is the whole shape. with, later in the session, does the third one for you — it does not replace the other two.

The mode letter, and the one that destroys data
"r" Read. The file must already exist, or the program crashes.
"w" Write. Empties the file the moment you open it, before you have written a single character. If it does not exist, it is created.
"a" Append. Adds to the end, keeps what was already there.
"w" is the one that will cost somebody their work. It does not wait to see whether you write anything — the file is empty as soon as it opens. Demonstrate it on a file that has data in it, because the warning alone does not land.
What write() will not do for you

write() puts down exactly the characters you give it and nothing else. No newline, no space. Write three numbers without \n and the file reads 726588. You have to add the line breaks yourself.

Part two · two ways to read, and the newline
read() against readlines()
read() The whole file as one long string, newlines and all. Good for looking at it; useless for working through it.
readlines() A list, one item per line. This is the one you will actually use, because a list is a thing they already know how to loop over.
The newline stays, and where it bites

readlines() keeps the \n on the end of every line, so you get ['72\n', '65\n', '88\n'], not ['72', '65', '88'].

Be precise about when this matters, because it does not always:

does NOT break int("72\n") works fine — Python ignores the trailing newline when converting.
DOES break comparing text. "Asha\n" == "Asha" is False, which is the kind of bug you stare at for an hour.
DOES look wrong printing. Every line comes out with a blank line under it.

.strip() removes it, and they already know .strip() from the string methods session. Nothing new — just a new reason to use it.

Part three · why with exists
What forgetting close() actually does

Nothing visible, most of the time — which is exactly why it is a bad habit rather than an obvious error. The file stays open, what you wrote may still be sitting in memory rather than on disk, and on a long-running program you eventually run out of file handles.

The honest teaching line is: it usually works, and that is the problem. You will not find out you were wrong until the one time it matters.

with closes it for you, even if the program crashes

That last part is the real argument. If an error happens halfway through reading, a hand-written close() never runs. with still closes the file on the way out.

The session, minute by minute

Everything in a speech box is meant to be said more or less as written. Everything in a grey box is a direction for you, not words to say.

0 – 14

You cannot type a thousand numbers

Make the problem obvious before naming the solution.

Put yesterday's list back on screen. They typed every character of it.
Yesterday
marks = [72, 0, 65, 88, 0, 91, 54, 77, 0, 60]

Ten marks. You typed all ten of them yesterday, by hand.

Now let me ask you three questions.

What if the class had five hundred students instead of ten?

What if the marks change tomorrow — do you want to edit your program every time?

And what if the person with the marks is not you? They are not going to send you a Python file.

“So where should the data actually live?”
Somewhere outside the program. A file. Somebody will say Excel — accept it, say we will get there, and that underneath it is the same idea.

The data should live outside your program, in a file. Then the program just goes and fetches it.

Change the file, run the same program, get a new answer. You never touch the code again.

That is today. And it is the first time in this course your program is going to touch anything outside itself.

On the board — the shape of everything today
  OPEN      which file, and what you plan to do with it
  READ      or WRITE
  CLOSE     tell python you are finished

  three steps. every single time.
14 – 30

Write one first

They make the file, so they know exactly what is in it.

We are going to write a file before we read one. On purpose.

If I hand you a file to read, you are trusting me about what is inside it. If you make it yourself, you know.

Type this
f = open("marks.txt", "w")

f.write("72")
f.write("65")
f.write("88")

f.close()

print("done")
done
Now make them go and look. Every student opens the folder their .py file is in and opens marks.txt in a text editor. Do not skip this.
“Open the folder your Python file is in. There is a new file there. Open it. What does it say?”
726588 — all on one line, stuck together. Let them find that themselves; it is the whole point of the next two minutes.

Seven two six five eight eight. All one line.

Because write() puts down exactly what you give it, and nothing else. No spaces. No line breaks. If you want a new line, you have to say so.

And the way you say so is \n. Backslash n. It means “new line”.

Again, with line breaks
f = open("marks.txt", "w")

f.write("72\n")
f.write("65\n")
f.write("88\n")

f.close()

Open the file again. Three lines now.

And look at the three steps. open, with the name of the file and the letter w for write. Then the writing. Then close.

Now the trap. Do this live, on the file that already has data in it.

One thing about that w, and I want you to watch carefully.

Your file has three marks in it right now. I am going to open it with w again, write nothing at all, and close it.

Watch
f = open("marks.txt", "w")
f.close()
“Open the file.”
Empty. All three marks gone. The w emptied it the moment it opened — it did not wait to see whether anything got written.
This is the one that will cost somebody real work. Say it plainly: "w" empties the file as it opens, not when you write. If you open a file full of data with "w" by accident, it is already gone. Show it; do not just warn.
The three letters — on the board, leave it up
  "r"    READ      the file must already exist, or it crashes
  "w"    WRITE     EMPTIES the file the moment it opens
  "a"    APPEND    adds to the end, keeps what was there

Put the three marks back with w, and then try a and see the difference for yourself.

30 – 46

Two ways to read it back

read() then readlines(). The second one is the one they will use.

The file exists and you know what is in it, because you put it there. Now read it.

The first way
f = open("marks.txt", "r")
data = f.read()
f.close()

print(data)
print("type   :", type(data))
print("length :", len(data))
72 65 88 type : <class 'str'> length : 9
“It printed three lines. But the length says nine. Nine what?”
Nine characters. Not three lines, not three marks. read() gives you one single string — 7, 2, newline, 6, 5, newline, 8, 8, newline. That is nine characters.

It is one string. The whole file, start to finish, as a single piece of text.

That is fine if you want to look at it. It is useless if you want to work through it, because you cannot loop over marks that are glued together in one string.

So there is a second way, and this is the one you will actually use.

The second way
f = open("marks.txt", "r")
lines = f.readlines()
f.close()

print(lines)
print("type  :", type(lines))
print("items :", len(lines))
['72\n', '65\n', '88\n'] type : <class 'list'> items : 3

A list. One item per line.

And that is the good news, because you have been looping over lists for weeks. Nothing about that changes.

But look carefully at what is inside it.

46 – 58

The backslash n that came along for the ride

Be precise about when it matters. It does not always.

Seventy-two backslash n. Not seventy-two.

The line break you wrote into the file is still attached to every item. readlines() does not take it off.

Now, how much of a problem is that? Let us actually check instead of guessing.

Does it break the maths?
print(int(lines[0]) + 10)
82

No. int() is relaxed about it — it ignores the newline and gives you seventy-two.

So for numbers, you often get away with it. Which is exactly why the next one catches people.

Now with text
f = open("names.txt", "w")
f.write("Asha\n")
f.write("Ravi\n")
f.close()

f = open("names.txt", "r")
names = f.readlines()
f.close()

print(names)
print("is the first one Asha?", names[0] == "Asha")
['Asha\n', 'Ravi\n'] is the first one Asha? False

False. The first name in the file is Asha, and Python says it is not Asha.

Because it is not. It is Asha-backslash-n, and that is a different string.

This is the bug you will stare at for an hour. Everything looks right on screen and the comparison keeps failing.

The fix, and you already know it
print(names[0].strip() == "Asha")
True

strip(). From the string methods session — it takes whitespace off both ends, and a newline is whitespace.

Nothing new today. Just a new reason to reach for it.

The habit: when you read lines from a file, strip() them. It costs nothing when it was not needed, and it saves you the hour when it was.
58 – 70

with — the one that closes it for you

They have closed files by hand for forty minutes. Now hand them the shortcut.

Every single thing we have written today has three lines around it. Open. Do the work. Close.

Now a question. What happens if you forget the close?

“What do you think goes wrong if I never close the file?”
Expect guesses about crashes and errors. The honest answer is worse than that: usually nothing visible happens. Which is exactly why it is a bad habit and not an obvious bug.

Usually, nothing. It looks like it worked.

And that is the problem. The file stays open, what you wrote might still be sitting in memory instead of on the disk, and you do not find out until the one time it matters.

So Python gives you a way to never have to remember.

The same read, written properly
with open("marks.txt", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

print(lines)
print("is the file closed?", f.closed)
['72\n', '65\n', '88\n'] is the file closed? True

No close anywhere, and the file is closed.

with means: open this, let me do my work indented underneath, and close it the moment I step back out.

Look at the indentation, because that is what marks the boundary. Everything indented under the with happens while the file is open. The first line that is not indented, it is already closed.

And here is the real reason to use it. If something goes wrong in the middle of your reading, a close() you wrote by hand never runs — the program has already crashed past it. with closes the file on its way out anyway.

From today, use with. Every time.
One thing that will happen, and today you let it crash. If somebody types the filename wrong, they get FileNotFoundError and the program stops. That is correct behaviour and there is a proper way to handle it — that is tomorrow. Today, name the error and move on.
70 – 82

Yesterday's answer, from a file

Full circle. Same number, data now outside the program.

Let us put the whole thing together, and I want to get back to a number you already know.

Yesterday we had ten marks with three absentees in them, and the real class average was seventy-two point four three.

We are going to write those marks to a file, read them back out, and get the same answer.

Step one — write the list out
marks = [72, 0, 65, 88, 0, 91, 54, 77, 0, 60]

with open("marks.txt", "w") as f:
    for m in marks:
        f.write(str(m) + "\n")

print("written")
written

One new thing in there. str(m).

write() only accepts text. m is a number. So we turn it into text first, then stick the newline on the end.

Go and open the file. Ten lines, one mark each.

Step two — read it back and work it out
with open("marks.txt", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

total   = 0
counted = 0
absent  = 0

for line in lines:
    mark = int(line.strip())
    if mark == 0:
        absent = absent + 1
        continue
    total   = total + mark
    counted = counted + 1

print("students in file:", len(lines))
print("absent          :", absent)
print("average         :", round(total / counted, 2))
students in file: 10 absent : 3 average : 72.43

Seventy-two point four three. The same number as yesterday.

But look at what changed. There is no list in this program any more. Not one mark is typed into the code.

Change the file to five hundred students, run the exact same program, and it gives you the answer for five hundred students.

That is the whole point of today.

Notice how little of that is new. The loop, the if, the continue, strip(), int() — all yours already. The only new part is where the numbers came from.
82 – 90

Practice, and close

Eight minutes. Walk the room. Everyone should open their files in a text editor to check, not just trust the printout.
Their turn
# 1. write the ten salaries from yesterday into salaries.txt,
#    one per line. open the file and check it.

# 2. read salaries.txt back and print the total payroll.
#    (you should get 408000)

# 3. append one more salary, 95000, WITHOUT losing the others.
#    which letter do you need?

# 4. read names.txt and print only the names that start with "A".
#    careful: strip() first.
Question 3 is the one to watch. Somebody will reach for "w" out of habit and wipe their file. That is a good thing to happen with you in the room — it is the second time today they will have seen it, and the last time they will do it.
The four lines. If everything else goes, keep these.
1.  OPEN -> READ or WRITE -> CLOSE.   three steps, every time.

2.  "r" read (must exist)   "w" write (EMPTIES IT)   "a" append
    "w" empties the file the moment it OPENS, not when you write.

3.  read()       -> one big string
    readlines()  -> a LIST, one item per line   <- use this one
    and the \n stays. strip() it.

4.  use WITH. it closes the file for you, even if the code crashes.
        with open("marks.txt", "r") as f:
            lines = f.readlines()

Tomorrow, two things.

Real data does not come as one number per line. It comes as rows with commas in them — a name, a department, a salary, all on one line. We are going to take that apart by hand.

The session, as a run sheet

Everything in order. Seven steps, every code block, every board item written out. If you lose your place, this page alone is enough.

You cannot type a thousand numbers

Somebody will say Excel — accept it, say we get there, same idea underneath.

On the board, leave it up

OPEN   which file, and what you plan to do with it
READ   or WRITE
CLOSE  tell python you are finished
214 – 30

Write one first

Land this: write before read, on purpose — they make the file so they know what is in it. Make every student open it in a text editor.

f = open("marks.txt", "w")

Show it, do not just warn. This is the one that costs somebody real work.
Three letters, on the board: "r" read, must exist · "w" write, EMPTIES IT · "a" append, keeps what was there.
330 – 46

Two ways to read it back

f = open("marks.txt", "r")

72 65 88 length : 9
Ask: “it printed three lines but the length says nine. Nine what?” — nine characters. read() gives one single string. Fine for looking, useless for working through.

Then the one they will actually use

The \n that came along for the ride

Land this: be precise. It does not break the maths, which is exactly why the text case catches people.

print(int(lines[0]) + 10)
82

Now text

f = open("names.txt", "w")

strip() — from the string methods session. Nothing new, just a new reason.
558 – 70

with

Land this: they have closed files by hand for forty minutes. Ask what goes wrong if you forget — the honest answer is “usually nothing”, and that is the problem.

782 – 90

Practice, and close

# 1. write the ten salaries into salaries.txt, one per line
# 2. read it back, print the total  (should be 408000)

Q3 is the one to watch: somebody will reach for "w" out of habit and wipe the file. Good — second time today they have seen it, and the last time they will do it.
Tease tomorrow: real data is not one number per line — it is rows with commas, a name and a department and a salary all on one line. We take that apart by hand. And we deal with the crash I let happen today.

Ask them these before they leave

Twelve questions, in order, with the answer under each one. The first five are the ones that matter. Take each answer from a different person.

What are the three steps of working with a file?
Open, then read or write, then close. Every time.
What do the three letters "r", "w" and "a" mean?
r read, and the file must already exist. w write, and it empties the file. a append, adds to the end and keeps what was there.
I opened a file with "w" and immediately closed it without writing anything. What is in the file now?
Nothing. It is empty. "w" empties the file the moment it opens — it does not wait to see whether you write.
I wrote 72, 65 and 88 and the file says 726588. Why?
write() puts down exactly what you give it and nothing else — no spaces, no line breaks. You have to add \n yourself.
What is the difference between read() and readlines()?
read() gives the whole file as one string. readlines() gives a list, one item per line. Use readlines — you already know how to loop over a list.
The file has three lines but len(data) said 9. Nine what?
Nine characters — 7, 2, newline, 6, 5, newline, 8, 8, newline. That is what tells you read() gave you one string and not three lines.
Does the \n break int()?
No. int("72\n") is 72. Which is exactly why it catches people — numbers keep working, so you do not notice the problem until you compare text.
Then where does the \n actually bite?
Comparing text. "Asha\n" == "Asha" is False. And printing, where every line comes out with a blank line under it. Fix both with .strip().
What goes wrong if you forget to close() a file?
Usually nothing visible — and that is the problem. It looks like it worked. The file stays open, what you wrote may still be in memory rather than on disk, and you find out the one time it matters.
What does with do, and what marks where it ends?
It closes the file for you. The indentation marks the boundary — everything indented under it runs with the file open, and the first unindented line means it is already closed.
Why is with better than writing close() yourself, if you never forget?
Because if something crashes halfway through, your close() never runs — the program jumped past it. with closes the file on its way out anyway.
We got 72.43 yesterday from a list, and 72.43 today from a file. So what actually changed?
There is no list in the program any more. Not one mark is typed into the code. Change the file to 500 students and the same program gives you the answer for 500. That is the whole point of today.

Questions you will get

“Where does the file actually go?”

“Into the same folder as your Python file, unless you tell it otherwise. That is why we keep going and looking at it — it is a real file sitting next to your code, and you can open it, rename it or delete it like any other.”

“I ran it twice and my data disappeared.”

“You opened it with "w" the second time. That empties the file before it writes anything, so the first run's data is gone. If you wanted to add to it, the letter is "a".”

“Why str(m)? It was already a number.”

“That is the problem — write() only accepts text. A file is text all the way through; there is no such thing as a number inside one. So you convert on the way in with str(), and convert back on the way out with int().”

“Can I read the same file twice in one program?”

“Yes, but open it again. Once you have read to the end, a second read() on the same open file gives you an empty string, because it is already at the bottom. Open it fresh, or keep what you read in a variable and reuse that.”

“What if the file does not exist?”

“With "r" the program crashes with FileNotFoundError. With "w" or "a" Python just creates it. Handling that crash properly is tomorrow.”

“Is this how we will read Excel files?”

“Not quite — an Excel file is not plain text, so you cannot open it like this. But a CSV is plain text, and that is what most data actually moves around as. Tomorrow we read one by hand.”

“Do I have to use with, or is close() fine?”

“close() is not wrong, and you will see plenty of code that uses it. But with is shorter, you cannot forget it, and it survives a crash. There is no situation at your level where the longer version is better.”

August B3 Python day 25 · 90 minutes · full script

A CSV,
By Hand

Real data is not one number per line. It is rows with commas in them. Today they take one apart by hand — and then stop their program crashing when the file is missing.

1line, three pieces
257000payroll, from a file
2errors worth catching
0libraries used

This is the session that earns Pandas

Doing a CSV by hand is meant to be tedious. Split every line, convert every number, skip the header, build the structure yourself. When pd.read_csv arrives in a few weeks and does all of it in one line, they will know exactly what it saved them. Do not shorten this and do not import the csv module.

Before you walk in

  1. No import csv. Python has a csv module and it would make this easy, which is exactly why it is banned today. They split on commas themselves.
  2. The header row is the first trap. Everybody forgets it and tries to turn the word salary into a number. Let it happen, read the error out loud, then fix it.
  3. Make them see "72000" + "1000" give "720001000". That one line does more for why int() matters than any explanation.
  4. Catch the specific error, never a bare except. Show that catching ValueError does not catch a missing file. A bare except hides bugs for years.
  5. Finish on the deliberately broken row. One salary written as words. The program should skip it and carry on, not die — that is what error handling is actually for.

Understand this yourself first

Two halves that fit together: taking a row apart, and surviving a row that will not come apart.

Part one · what a CSV actually is
It is a text file. That is the whole secret.

CSV stands for comma separated values, and it is exactly that — a plain text file where each line is a row and the commas mark where one column ends and the next begins.

There is nothing special about it. They can open it in Notepad. Everything they learnt yesterday about reading files applies without change.

The three steps for every line
strip Take the newline off the end, same as yesterday.
split(",") Cut the line at every comma. Gives back a list of pieces.
int() the numbers Every piece comes back as text, including the salary. Nothing from a file is ever a number until you convert it.
The header row

The first line is column names, not data. Loop over lines[1:] and it is gone. They know slicing from D15, so this is one character of new idea, not a new concept.

Part two · try and except
The shape

try: holds the code that might fail. except SomeError: holds what to do if it does. If nothing fails, the except block never runs and nobody notices it is there.

Name the error you are expecting
FileNotFoundError The file is not there. Yesterday this crashed the program and we let it.
ValueError int() was handed something that is not a number — a blank, a word, a stray space.
Why a bare except: is the wrong habit

A bare except: catches everything, including bugs you did not anticipate and typos in your own code. The program then quietly does the wrong thing instead of telling you.

Catch the error you can actually do something about. If you cannot name the error you are expecting, you are not handling it — you are hiding it.

The session, minute by minute

Everything in a speech box is meant to be said more or less as written. Everything in a grey box is a direction for you, not words to say.

0 – 12

Real data has commas in it

Make the file first, so they can see what they are about to take apart.

Yesterday your file had one number per line. Real data is never that tidy.

Real data looks like this: a name, a department and a salary, all on one line, with commas between them.

That has a name. It is called a CSV — comma separated values — and it is the single most common way data moves around in the world.

Make the file
rows = ["name,department,salary",
        "Asha,Tech,72000",
        "Ravi,HR,48000",
        "Meera,Tech,60000",
        "Kiran,Sales,35000",
        "Divya,HR,42000"]

with open("staff.csv", "w") as f:
    for r in rows:
        f.write(r + "\n")

print("written")
written
Send them to the folder again. This one is worth opening because the extension is different and they will expect something exotic.
“Open staff.csv in a text editor. What is in it?”
Plain text, exactly what they wrote. A CSV is just a text file. There is nothing special inside it — the only thing that makes it a CSV is the commas and the name. Say that out loud; several of them will be expecting something more.

Nothing magic. A text file, with commas in it.

Which means everything you learnt yesterday still works. Let us read it.

12 – 28

Take one line apart

One line, slowly, before touching the loop.

Read it the way you already know
with open("staff.csv", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

print(len(lines), "lines")
print(lines[0])
print(lines[1])
6 lines name,department,salary Asha,Tech,72000

Six lines. And line zero is not a person — it is the column names. We will deal with that in a minute.

Take line one. It is one string: Asha comma Tech comma seventy-two thousand. I need those as three separate things.

And you already have the tool. From the string methods session.

Split it
parts = lines[1].strip().split(",")

print(parts)
print("pieces:", len(parts))
print("name  :", parts[0])
print("dept  :", parts[1])
print("salary:", parts[2])
['Asha', 'Tech', '72000'] pieces: 3 name : Asha dept : Tech salary: 72000

Two things in that one line of code, and both are yours already.

.strip() takes the newline off the end — yesterday's habit.

.split(",") cuts the string at every comma and hands back a list. Three pieces.

Now the trap. Do this before anybody needs it, because it is the one that will waste their time otherwise.
Add a thousand to that salary
print(parts[2] + "1000")
720001000
“Seventy-two thousand plus a thousand. Is that seven hundred and twenty thousand and one thousand?”
It is not addition at all — it is two bits of text stuck together. Everything that comes out of a file is text, including things that look like numbers.
The fix
print(int(parts[2]) + 1000)
73000
Nothing that comes out of a file is a number. Not ever. It looks like one, it prints like one, and it is text until you call int() on it.
28 – 46

All the rows, and the header trap

Let the header crash it first. The error message teaches better than you do.

One line works. Now all of them. Just put a loop around it.

The obvious version — type it and run it
for line in lines:
    parts = line.strip().split(",")
    print(parts[0], int(parts[2]))
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'salary'
“Read the error. What is it complaining about?”
It tried to turn the word salary into a number. That is the header row. It is column names, not data, and it went through the loop like everything else.

The first line of the file is not a person. It is the column names, and we fed it to int() along with everybody else.

So skip it. And you already know how — slicing, from the strings session.

Skip line zero
for line in lines[1:]:
    parts = line.strip().split(",")
    print(parts[0], int(parts[2]))
Asha 72000 Ravi 48000 Meera 60000 Kiran 35000 Divya 42000

lines[1:]. From line one to the end. One character of new idea, and the header is gone.

Now build the structure properly. This is where it starts to feel like work, and that is intentional.
Build a list of dictionaries
staff = []

for line in lines[1:]:
    parts = line.strip().split(",")
    person = {"name": parts[0],
              "dept": parts[1],
              "salary": int(parts[2])}
    staff.append(person)

for p in staff:
    print(p)
{'name': 'Asha', 'dept': 'Tech', 'salary': 72000} {'name': 'Ravi', 'dept': 'HR', 'salary': 48000} {'name': 'Meera', 'dept': 'Tech', 'salary': 60000} {'name': 'Kiran', 'dept': 'Sales', 'salary': 35000} {'name': 'Divya', 'dept': 'HR', 'salary': 42000}

A list of dictionaries. Five people, each one a dictionary with three labelled pieces.

Why bother? Because parts[2] tells you nothing and person["salary"] tells you everything. In two weeks you will not remember what was in position two.

And now it is just Python again
total = 0
for p in staff:
    total = total + p["salary"]

print("people :", len(staff))
print("payroll:", total)
print("average:", round(total / len(staff), 2))

print()
print("Tech only:")
for p in staff:
    if p["dept"] != "Tech":
        continue
    print("  ", p["name"], p["salary"])
people : 5 payroll: 257000 average: 51400.0 Tech only: Asha 72000 Meera 60000
Say this out loud, and mean it. Count the lines it took to get here. Read the file, strip, split, skip the header, convert the number, build the dictionary, append. Seven steps before any actual analysis. In a few weeks one line called pd.read_csv will do all of it. Today is so that you know what that line is doing.
46 – 62

The crash from yesterday

Second half. Start by reproducing the crash deliberately.

Yesterday somebody typed a filename wrong and the program died. I said we would come back to it.

Let us make it happen on purpose.

Ask for a file that is not there
with open("missing.csv", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

print("this line never runs")
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'missing.csv'

The program stopped. Dead. Nothing after that line ran at all.

And notice Python told you exactly what went wrong. FileNotFoundError. It even named the file.

Sometimes stopping is correct. But often you want the program to notice, say something sensible, and carry on. That is what try and except are for.

Type this
try:
    with open("missing.csv", "r") as f:
        lines = f.readlines()
    print("read", len(lines), "lines")

except FileNotFoundError:
    print("That file is not there. Check the name.")

print("and the program carries on")
That file is not there. Check the name. and the program carries on

No crash. A sensible message, and the program kept going.

Read the shape of it. try holds the code that might fail. except holds what to do if it does.

And if nothing fails, the except block simply never runs. You would not even know it was there.

Prove that — point it at the real file
try:
    with open("staff.csv", "r") as f:
        lines = f.readlines()
    print("read", len(lines), "lines")

except FileNotFoundError:
    print("That file is not there. Check the name.")
read 6 lines
62 – 78

One bad row should not kill the file

The second error, and the reason you name the error you catch.

A missing file is one kind of problem. Here is the one you will actually meet more often — the file is there, and one row inside it is rubbish.

Somebody typed a salary in words.

Make a broken file
bad = ["name,department,salary",
       "Asha,Tech,72000",
       "Ravi,HR,forty eight thousand",
       "Meera,Tech,60000"]

with open("bad.csv", "w") as f:
    for r in bad:
        f.write(r + "\n")

with open("bad.csv", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

for line in lines[1:]:
    parts = line.strip().split(",")
    print(parts[0], int(parts[2]))
Asha 72000 ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'forty eight thousand'

It did Asha, then died on Ravi. And Meera, who is perfectly fine, never got read at all.

One bad row out of three stopped the whole thing. If that file had ten thousand rows and row four was broken, you would lose nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-six good rows.

Skip the bad one, keep the rest
good    = 0
skipped = 0

for line in lines[1:]:
    parts = line.strip().split(",")

    try:
        salary = int(parts[2])
    except ValueError:
        print("  skipping", parts[0], "- salary is not a number")
        skipped = skipped + 1
        continue

    good = good + 1
    print("  ", parts[0], salary)

print()
print("usable:", good, " skipped:", skipped)
Asha 72000 skipping Ravi - salary is not a number Meera 60000 usable: 2 skipped: 1

Two good rows kept, one bad row reported and skipped, and the program finished.

Look at continue doing its job again. Same keyword as two days ago, now inside an except.

Last point of the session, and it is a habit point. Show them catching the wrong error.
What if you catch the wrong thing?
try:
    open("missing.csv", "r")
except ValueError:
    print("this will not run")
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'missing.csv'

Still crashed. Because I asked it to catch a ValueError, and what happened was a FileNotFoundError. Different problem, so it was not caught.

Now, you can write except: on its own, with no error name, and it catches everything. And I want you to not do that.

Because it will also catch your own typos, and your own logic mistakes, and quietly swallow them. Your program will do the wrong thing and never tell you.

Name the error you are expecting. If you cannot name it, you are not handling the problem — you are hiding it.
78 – 90

Practice, and close

Their turn
# 1. from staff.csv, print only the people earning more than 45000

# 2. count how many people are in each department.
#    hint: a dictionary, dept -> count

# 3. write a NEW file, tech_only.csv, containing just the Tech rows
#    (header included)

# 4. wrap question 1 in try / except so that if staff.csv is
#    missing it prints a message instead of crashing
The four lines. If everything else goes, keep these.
1.  a CSV is a TEXT FILE with commas in it. nothing more.
    line.strip().split(",")  ->  a list of the pieces

2.  NOTHING out of a file is a number. int() it.
    "72000" + "1000" is "720001000", not 73000.

3.  the first line is the HEADER. skip it with  lines[1:]

4.  try:  the code that might fail
    except FileNotFoundError:   the file is not there
    except ValueError:          int() got something that isn't a number
    NAME the error. a bare except: hides your own bugs.

Count what we did today. Open, read, strip, split, skip the header, convert, build a dictionary, append it to a list. Eight steps before we had anything we could actually work with.

Remember that, because in a few weeks you will type pd.read_csv("staff.csv") and get all of it in one line.

Tomorrow, something different. Every piece of data we have had so far has been loose — a list here, a dictionary there. Tomorrow we start building our own types of thing.

The session, as a run sheet

Everything in order. Six steps, every code block, every board item written out. If you lose your place, this page alone is enough.

10 – 12

Real data has commas in it

rows = ["name,department,salary",
        "Asha,Tech,72000",
        "Ravi,HR,48000",

        "Kiran,Sales,35000",

with open("staff.csv", "w") as f:

Send them to open it. Several expect something exotic because of the .csv. It is a text file with commas in it. Everything from yesterday still works.
212 – 28

One line, slowly

parts = lines[1].strip().split(",")
print(parts)
['Asha', 'Tech', '72000']
.strip() takes the newline off · .split(",") cuts at every comma and returns a list. Both are theirs already.

Then the trap — before anybody needs it

print(parts[2] + "1000")
print(int(parts[2]) + 1000)
720001000 73000
NOTHING that comes out of a file is a number. It looks like one, prints like one, and is text until int().
328 – 46

All the rows, and the header trap

Land this: run the obvious loop without skipping the header and let it crash. The error message teaches it better than you can.

for line in lines:
    parts = line.strip().split(",")
    print(parts[0], int(parts[2]))
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'salary'
Ask them to read it: it tried to turn the word salary into a number. That is the header row. Fix: lines[1:] — slicing, from D15.

Then build the structure

staff = []
for line in lines[1:]:
    parts = line.strip().split(",")
    person = {"name": parts[0],
              "dept": parts[1],
              "salary": int(parts[2])}
    staff.append(person)

total = 0
for p in staff:
    total = total + p["salary"]
print("payroll:", total)
payroll: 257000
Why dictionaries: parts[2] tells you nothing; person["salary"] tells you everything.

Then say it and mean it: eight steps before any analysis. pd.read_csv does all of it in one line. Today is so they know what that line is doing.

try = the code that might fail · except = what to do if it does. If nothing fails, the except never runs.

One bad row should not kill the file

Land this: the missing file is rare. A broken row is normal.

bad = ["name,department,salary",

Asha 72000 ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'forty eight thousand'
