You can write a bare except: that catches everything. Do not. It will swallow your own typos and logic mistakes, and the program will quietly do the wrong thing.

Name the error. If you cannot name it, you are hiding it, not handling it.
678 – 90

Practice, and close

# 1. print only people earning more than 45000
# 2. count how many people per department (a dict, dept -> count)
# 3. write tech_only.csv with just the Tech rows + header
# 4. wrap Q1 in try/except for a missing staff.csv
Close on the count: open, read, strip, split, skip header, convert, build dict, append — eight steps before any analysis. In a few weeks, pd.read_csv("staff.csv").

Tease tomorrow: all our data has been loose so far — a list here, a dictionary there. Tomorrow we start building our own kinds of thing.

Ask them these before they leave

Ten questions with the answer under each. Take each answer from a different person.

What is a CSV file, really?
A plain text file where each line is a row and the commas mark where one column ends and the next begins. Nothing special inside it — you can open it in Notepad.
What do .strip() and .split(",") each do to a line?
strip() takes the newline off the end. split(",") cuts the line at every comma and gives back a list of the pieces.
parts[2] holds 72000. Why did parts[2] + "1000" give 720001000?
Because it is text, not a number, so the + stuck two strings together. Nothing that comes out of a file is a number until you call int().
Our first loop crashed with invalid literal for int(): 'salary'. What had happened?
The header row went through the loop with everybody else, and we tried to turn the word salary into a number. Skip it with lines[1:].
Why build a list of dictionaries instead of just using parts[0], parts[1], parts[2]?
Because parts[2] tells you nothing and person["salary"] tells you everything. In two weeks you will not remember what was in position two.
What goes in the try block, and what goes in the except?
try holds the code that might fail. except holds what to do if it does. If nothing fails, the except block never runs.
Which error means the file is missing, and which means int() was handed rubbish?
FileNotFoundError for the missing file. ValueError for int() getting something that is not a number.
One row out of ten thousand has a broken salary. Without try, how many rows do you get?
However many came before the broken one. The program dies there, and everything after it is never read. One bad row can cost you the whole file.
I wrote except ValueError and the program still crashed with FileNotFoundError. Why?
You named the wrong error. except only catches the error you name, and a missing file is not a ValueError.
Why should you not just write except: with no error name?
Because it catches everything — including your own typos and logic mistakes. The program then quietly does the wrong thing instead of telling you. If you cannot name the error, you are hiding it, not handling it.

Questions you will get

“Can I open a CSV in Excel?”

“Yes, and Excel will show it as a nice grid, which is confusing — it makes the file look like a spreadsheet. It is not. Open the same file in Notepad and you will see the commas. Excel is just being helpful.”

“What if a name has a comma in it?”

“Then split(",") cuts it in the wrong place and your row falls apart. Real CSV files handle that with quotes, and handling it properly is exactly the sort of fiddly thing pd.read_csv does for you. Today, keep the commas out of your data.”

“Why not just import csv? I looked it up.”

“Good — and yes, it exists and it works. I am keeping it off the table today on purpose, because doing it by hand once is what makes you understand what the shortcut is doing. After today, use whichever you like.”

“Can I have more than one except?”

“Yes. Stack them — one for FileNotFoundError, another for ValueError — and Python runs whichever one matches. That is the right way to do it, and it is still naming your errors.”

“How do I know what error to expect?”

“Let it crash once and read the name. Python prints it for you, as the first word of the last line. That is the name you put after except. Crashing on purpose is a perfectly good way to find out.”

“Should I skip bad rows or stop?”

“Depends what the data is for, and it is a real decision rather than a technical one. For a rough average, skip and say how many you skipped. For a payroll run, stop — you do not want to pay people based on a file you know is broken. Either way, report the count.”

August B3 Python day 26 · 90 minutes · full script

Making Your
Own Kind of Thing

A dictionary can hold what a person is. It cannot hold what a person can do. Today they build something that holds both — one class, and nothing more.

3lists that fall out of step
selfthe only confusing word
1class, two methods
79200after a 10% raise

Two sessions on this, not six

An analyst writes groupby, not classes. But every interview asks what a class is, and every library they are about to meet is built out of them. So: one class, one __init__, two methods today, and inheritance tomorrow. No encapsulation, no polymorphism, no abstract base classes. That is a backend course.

Before you walk in

  1. Start from three parallel lists, not from a definition. Show the lists getting out of step when somebody is deleted. The class then arrives as a fix for a problem they have just watched happen.
  2. Go via the dictionary they already know. A dictionary solves the first half — it keeps one person's data together. Then ask what it cannot do, and that is the gap the class fills.
  3. self is the only genuinely confusing thing here. Budget real time for it. The one-line version: self means “the particular one we are talking about right now”.
  4. Make two objects, not one. With one object you cannot see that each has its own data. Give Asha a raise and show Ravi is untouched — that is the moment it clicks.
  5. Resist every extension. Somebody will ask about private variables or getters. Say it exists, say it is not for analysts, move on. The scope is the lesson.

Understand this yourself first

Three words to get right: class, object, and self. The third one is where the session is won or lost.

Part one · the problem, in two steps
Parallel lists fall out of step

Three lists — names, departments, salaries — and the only thing holding a person together is that their pieces happen to be at the same position. Delete from one list and forget the others, and from then on every row is wrong, silently.

A dictionary fixes half of it

They already know the fix for that: put one person in one dictionary. Now the pieces travel together and cannot drift apart.

So ask the better question: what can a dictionary still not do? It can hold what a person is. It cannot hold what a person can do. There is no way to say asha.give_raise(10).

A class is a dictionary that can also do things. That is close enough to true to teach, and it lands immediately because they already have the dictionary.
Part two · class, object, and the two pieces inside
Class against object
class The design. Written once. Employee describes what any employee has and can do.
object One actual thing built from that design. Asha is an object. Ravi is a different object. Both from the same class.

The form-and-filled-in-form comparison works well and costs nothing: the class is the blank form, each object is one filled-in copy.

__init__

It runs automatically the moment you make an object, and its job is to set up that object's data. Nobody calls it by hand. The double underscores look alarming and mean only “Python calls this one for you”.

self — budget time for this

Every method's first parameter is self, and students find it baffling because they never pass anything for it.

The honest explanation: one class, many objects. When you write asha.give_raise(10), Python has to tell the method which employee. It passes the object in automatically, and inside the method that object is called self.

self means “the particular one we are talking about right now”. And self.salary means “this employee's salary, not anybody else's”.

The session, minute by minute

Everything in a speech box is meant to be said more or less as written. Everything in a grey box is a direction for you, not words to say.

0 – 16

Three lists that drift apart

Let the bug happen on screen before naming any solution.

Suppose I am keeping track of three employees, and all I have is what you knew in week two.

Type this
names    = ["Asha", "Ravi", "Meera"]
depts    = ["Tech", "HR", "Tech"]
salaries = [72000, 48000, 60000]

print(names[0], depts[0], salaries[0])
print(names[1], depts[1], salaries[1])
Asha Tech 72000 Ravi HR 48000

That works. The only thing holding Asha together is that her three pieces all sit at position zero.

Now Ravi leaves the company, and I remove him. But I am in a hurry and I only remember two of the three lists.

Watch
names.remove("Ravi")
depts.remove("HR")

print(names[1], depts[1], salaries[1])
Meera Tech 48000
“Meera is in Tech and earns forty-eight thousand. Is that right?”
No. Meera earns 60,000 — 48,000 was Ravi's. The salaries list still has Ravi in it, so everything after him is shifted by one. And nothing crashed.

Meera is now being paid Ravi's salary, and every person after him in the list is wrong too.

And here is the dangerous part. Nothing went wrong. No error, no warning. The program will happily keep running and keep being wrong.

The problem is that Asha was never really one thing. She was three separate pieces that happened to be in the same place, and nothing was holding them together.

16 – 28

A dictionary gets you halfway

Use what they have, then find its limit honestly.

“You already know something that would keep Asha's three pieces together. What?”
A dictionary. They have had them since week two and used them again yesterday on the CSV.
The version you already know
asha = {"name": "Asha", "dept": "Tech", "salary": 72000}
ravi = {"name": "Ravi", "dept": "HR",   "salary": 48000}

print(asha["name"], "earns", asha["salary"])
Asha earns 72000

Much better. Asha is one thing now. Delete her and all three pieces go together, because they are together.

So, is that the end of the session? Almost. There is one thing a dictionary still cannot do, and it is worth seeing.

Ask it as a request, not a statement. They should feel the thing missing.

Give Asha a ten percent raise.

You can do it — asha["salary"] = asha["salary"] * 1.1. Fine.

Now do it for five hundred employees. Where does that line live? You write it out again every time, or you write a separate function and hope everybody remembers to use it.

The dictionary holds what Asha is. It has nowhere to keep what an employee can do.

That is the gap. A class is a dictionary that can also do things — the data and the actions that belong with it, kept in one place.
28 – 48

One class, built line by line

Type it in three stages. Do not show the finished thing first.

Build this in three passes: the shell, then __init__, then run it. Explaining a finished class is much harder than growing one.
Stage one — the shell
class Employee:
    pass

class, then the name. And the name starts with a capital letter — that is a convention everybody follows so you can tell a class from a variable at a glance.

pass just means “nothing here yet”. We are about to fill it in.

Right now this is a design for an employee. It is not an employee. Nobody has been hired.

Stage two — what every employee has
class Employee:

    def __init__(self, name, dept, salary):
        self.name   = name
        self.dept   = dept
        self.salary = salary
Stop here. Do not run it yet. Spend four minutes on these four lines, because everything confusing in the session is in them.

Four lines, and three things to explain.

__init__. Two underscores, the word init, two underscores. It is short for initialise, and it runs automatically the moment you create an employee. You never call it yourself.

Its job is to set up that employee's data.

self. This is the one everybody finds strange, so let me be clear about it.

You write one class, but you will make many employees from it. So when some code runs, Python has to know which employee we are talking about.

That is self. It means “the particular one we are dealing with right now”.

So self.name = name means: take the name that was handed in, and store it on this employee.

On the board — leave this up all session
  class        the DESIGN.  written once.  Employee
  object       one ACTUAL THING made from it.  Asha.  Ravi.

  __init__     runs automatically when you make one.
               its job: set up THIS one's data.

  self         "the particular one we are talking about right now"
               self.salary  =  THIS employee's salary
Stage three — now make two
e1 = Employee("Asha", "Tech", 72000)
e2 = Employee("Ravi", "HR", 48000)

print(e1.name, e1.dept, e1.salary)
print(e2.name, e2.dept, e2.salary)
print(type(e1))
Asha Tech 72000 Ravi HR 48000 <class '__main__.Employee'>

Two employees. One design.

Notice how you make one — Employee(...), like calling a function, and you hand it the three things __init__ asked for.

And notice what you did not hand it. You did not pass anything for self. Python filled that in for you, because it knows which one you are making.

Then e1.name with a dot. Not square brackets like a dictionary — a dot.

“What does type(e1) say?”
Employee. Not dict, not list. They have just created a brand new kind of thing that did not exist in Python until they wrote it. Say that out loud — it is the most satisfying moment in the session.
48 – 66

Now the part a dictionary could not do

Methods. And the demo that proves each object has its own data.

So far this is a dictionary with a different kind of bracket. Now the bit that is actually new.

We are going to give an employee something it can do.

Add two methods
class Employee:

    def __init__(self, name, dept, salary):
        self.name   = name
        self.dept   = dept
        self.salary = salary

    def details(self):
        print(self.name, "works in", self.dept)

    def raise_pay(self, percent):
        self.salary = self.salary + (self.salary * percent / 100)

Those are methods. A method is just a function that lives inside a class.

And look — both of them start with self, for the same reason as before. When details() runs, it needs to know whose details.

raise_pay takes two things: self, which Python fills in, and percent, which you hand over.

Use them
e1 = Employee("Asha", "Tech", 72000)
e2 = Employee("Ravi", "HR", 48000)

e1.details()
e2.details()

print()
print("before:", e1.salary)
e1.raise_pay(10)
print("after :", e1.salary)
print("Ravi  :", e2.salary)
Asha works in Tech Ravi works in HR before: 72000 after : 79200.0 Ravi : 48000
This is the moment. Point at the last two lines and wait.
“I gave a ten percent raise. Why did Ravi not get one?”
Because raise_pay was called on e1, so inside the method self was Asha. self.salary meant Asha's salary and nobody else's. Ravi was never involved. That is what self is for.

One class. Two employees. Each with their own data.

When I wrote e1.raise_pay(10), Python went into the method and set self to e1. So self.salary was Asha's seventy-two thousand.

If I had written e2.raise_pay(10), self would have been Ravi.

Same code. Different object. That is the whole idea.

Expect this question and answer it plainly: “why is it 79200.0 and not 79200?” Because dividing by 100 produces a decimal, and Python keeps it. It is correct, just untidy. round() fixes the display — do not get drawn into float representation today.
66 – 82

A list of objects, which is where this goes

Connect it back to yesterday's CSV so it is not an island.

Yesterday you read a CSV and built a list of dictionaries. Let us do the same thing with a list of employees instead.

Type this
staff = [
    Employee("Asha",  "Tech",  72000),
    Employee("Ravi",  "HR",    48000),
    Employee("Meera", "Tech",  60000),
    Employee("Kiran", "Sales", 35000)
]

for e in staff:
    e.details()

total = 0
for e in staff:
    total = total + e.salary

print()
print("payroll:", total)
Asha works in Tech Ravi works in HR Meera works in Tech Kiran works in Sales payroll: 215000

A normal list. A normal for loop. Nothing new except what is inside the list.

And now the useful bit — give everyone in Tech a raise.

One loop, and the method does the work
for e in staff:
    if e.dept != "Tech":
        continue
    e.raise_pay(10)

for e in staff:
    print(e.name, round(e.salary))
Asha 79200 Ravi 48000 Meera 66000 Kiran 35000

Both Tech people went up. The other two did not move.

And look at the loop. There is no arithmetic in it at all. The rule for how a raise works lives inside Employee, where it belongs. If the company changes how raises are calculated, you change one method and every piece of code that uses it is already correct.

That is the actual argument for classes, and it is the only one you need today.

82 – 90

Practice, and close

Their turn
# 1. add a method years_to_retire(self) that prints how many
#    years until 60. you will need an age in __init__.

# 2. make a Student class: name, marks. add a method
#    passed(self) that prints pass if marks >= 35, else fail.

# 3. make three Students in a list and loop over them,
#    calling passed() on each.

# 4. what happens if you forget self in a method's brackets?
#    try it. read the error.
Question 4 is deliberate. Leaving self out gives TypeError: details() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given — which is Python saying “you did not make room for the object I pass in”. That error message is the best explanation of self there is.
The four lines. If everything else goes, keep these.
1.  class  = the DESIGN, written once.     Employee
    object = one ACTUAL thing made from it.  Asha, Ravi

2.  __init__ runs AUTOMATICALLY when you make an object.
    its job is to set up that object's data. never call it yourself.

3.  self = "the particular one we are talking about right now"
    self.salary = THIS employee's salary, nobody else's.
    python fills self in for you. you never pass it.

4.  a METHOD is a function that lives inside a class.
    a dictionary holds what a thing IS.
    a class holds what it is AND what it can DO.

Tomorrow, two things.

First, what happens when one kind of thing is a special version of another — a manager is an employee, but with extra.

And then something I think you will enjoy. You have been typing a dot in front of things since week two. .upper(). .append(). .strip(). Tomorrow you will find out exactly what that dot has been doing.

The session, as a run sheet

Everything in order. Six steps, every code block, every board item written out. If you lose your place, this page alone is enough.

10 – 16

Three lists that drift apart

Land this: let the bug happen on screen. Do not define anything yet.

names    = ["Asha", "Ravi", "Meera"]
depts    = ["Tech", "HR", "Tech"]
salaries = [72000, 48000, 60000]

names.remove("Ravi")
depts.remove("HR")

print(names[1], depts[1], salaries[1])
Meera Tech 48000
Ask: “Meera earns 48,000. Is that right?” — no, that was Ravi's. And nothing crashed. No error, no warning, just wrong from now on.

Asha was never one thing — three pieces that happened to share a position.
216 – 28

A dictionary gets you halfway

Land this: let them name the dictionary. Then find its limit.

asha = {"name": "Asha", "dept": "Tech", "salary": 72000}
Then ask for a 10% raise. They can do it — but where does that line live? For 500 employees you rewrite it every time.

The gap: a dictionary holds what Asha is. It has nowhere for what an employee can do.

A class is a dictionary that can also do things.
328 – 48

One class, in three passes

Land this: grow it, do not reveal it. Shell → __init__ → run it. Stop after __init__ and spend four minutes on self.

class Employee:

    def __init__(self, name, dept, salary):
        self.name   = name
        self.dept   = dept
        self.salary = salary
Capital letter on the class name — universal convention · __init__ runs automatically, you never call it · self = “the particular one we are talking about right now”.

On the board, leave it up

class    the DESIGN. written once.
object   one ACTUAL THING made from it. Asha. Ravi.
__init__ runs automatically. sets up THIS one's data.
self     "the particular one we are talking about right now"

Then make TWO

e1 = Employee("Asha", "Tech", 72000)
e2 = Employee("Ravi", "HR", 48000)
print(e1.name, e1.dept, e1.salary)
print(type(e1))
Asha Tech 72000 <class '__main__.Employee'>
You did not pass anything for self — Python filled it in.

type(e1) says Employee. Not dict, not list. They just made a new kind of thing that did not exist in Python until they wrote it. Say it out loud.
448 – 66

Methods — the part a dictionary could not do

    def details(self):
        print(self.name, "works in", self.dept)

    def raise_pay(self, percent):
        self.salary = self.salary + (self.salary * percent / 100)

Then the demo that proves it

print("before:", e1.salary)
e1.raise_pay(10)
print("after :", e1.salary)
print("Ravi  :", e2.salary)
before: 72000 after : 79200.0 Ravi : 48000
THE MOMENT. Point at the last two lines and wait.

“I gave a 10% raise. Why did Ravi not get one?” — because it was called on e1, so inside the method self was Asha. Ravi was never involved.

That is what self is for.
Expect: “why 79200.0?” — dividing by 100 makes a decimal. Correct, just untidy. round() for display. Do not get drawn into floats.
566 – 82

A list of objects

Land this: connect it to yesterday — same shape as the list of dictionaries from the CSV.

staff = [
    Employee("Asha",  "Tech",  72000),
    Employee("Ravi",  "HR",    48000),
    Employee("Meera", "Tech",  60000),
    Employee("Kiran", "Sales", 35000)
]

    e.raise_pay(10)

for e in staff:
    print(e.name, round(e.salary))
Asha 79200 Ravi 48000 Meera 66000 Kiran 35000
The argument for classes, and the only one needed today: there is no arithmetic in that loop. The rule for a raise lives inside Employee. Change it once and every piece of code that uses it is already correct.
682 – 90

Practice, and close

# 1. add years_to_retire(self) - needs an age in __init__
# 2. a Student class: name, marks, passed() -> 35 or more
# 3. three Students in a list, loop and call passed()
# 4. forget self in a method's brackets. read the error.
Q4 is deliberate: TypeError: details() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given — Python saying “you did not make room for the object I pass in”. That error is the best explanation of self there is.
Tease tomorrow: a manager is an employee with extra. And — “you have been typing a dot since week two. .upper(), .append(), .strip(). Tomorrow you find out what that dot has been doing.”

Ask them these before they leave

Ten questions with the answer under each. Questions 4 to 6 are the ones that matter — if they can answer those, they have self.

Three parallel lists, and I removed Ravi from two of them. What went wrong, and why was there no error?
Everything after Ravi shifted out of step, so Meera got paid his salary. No error, because nothing is actually wrong as far as Python is concerned — the lists are just lists. It stays silently wrong.
A dictionary already fixes that. So what can it still not do?
It holds what a person is, but it has nowhere to keep what a person can do. There is no way to say asha.give_raise(10).
What is the difference between a class and an object?
The class is the design, written once. An object is one actual thing made from it. One Employee class; Asha and Ravi are two objects.
When does __init__ run, and who calls it?
It runs automatically, the moment you create an object. Nobody calls it by hand. Its job is to set up that object's data.
What does self mean?
“The particular one we are talking about right now.” One class, many objects — so the code needs to know which one. self.salary is this employee's salary.
I made an employee with Employee("Asha", "Tech", 72000) — three things. But __init__ has four in its brackets. Where did the fourth come from?
Python filled in self for you. You never pass it; it passes the object in automatically.
I called e1.raise_pay(10). Why did Ravi's salary not change?
Because it was called on e1, so inside the method self was Asha. self.salary meant her salary and nobody else's. Ravi was never involved.
What is a method?
A function that lives inside a class. That is the only difference — and it takes self as its first parameter.
What does type(e1) print, and why does that matter?
Employee. Not dict, not list. You have created a new kind of thing that did not exist in Python until you wrote it.
In the Tech-raise loop there was no arithmetic at all. Where did the maths go, and why is that good?
Inside the raise_pay method, where it belongs. If the company changes how raises work, you change one method and every piece of code that uses it is already correct.

Questions you will get

“Why not just use dictionaries? They are shorter.”

“For pure data, use dictionaries — and as an analyst you often will. The moment you want behaviour attached to the data, and the same behaviour used in twenty places, a class keeps it in one place. The honest answer is that you will use both.”

“Do I have to call it self?”

“Technically no — it is just the name of the first parameter and you could call it anything. In practice always call it self. Every Python programmer alive expects that word, and changing it only confuses whoever reads your code next.”

“Why the double underscores on __init__?”

“They mark it as a name Python itself uses — a method that gets called for you rather than by you. There are several of them. You only need this one.”

“Can a class have no __init__?”

“Yes — our first version had pass and nothing else. You just get an object with no data set up. It is rare to want that; almost every class you write will have one.”

“What about private variables? I read about those.”

“They exist, and the word is encapsulation. It matters when a team of people is sharing a large codebase and you want to stop them reaching inside your object. It does not matter for anything you will do as an analyst, so we are not covering it.”

“Will we actually use classes as data analysts?”

“You will write very few. But you will use them constantly, because every library you are about to meet is made of them. Knowing what a class is turns those libraries from magic into something you can reason about — and tomorrow makes that connection.”

“Why 79200.0 and not 79200?”

“Dividing by 100 produces a decimal, and Python keeps it rather than quietly rounding. The value is correct. If you want it tidy on screen, wrap it in round().”

August B3 Python day 27 · 90 minutes · full script · closes the core Python block

What the Dot
Has Been Doing

One class built out of another, and then the payoff: every .upper() and .append() they have typed since week two was a method, on an object, all along.

1parent, one child
0lines copied
.explained at last
27sessions, and it closes here

The second half is the reason for the first

Inheritance on its own is a backend topic they will rarely write. But it is the last piece needed to explain the dot — and the dot is something they have used a thousand times without being told what it was. Teach inheritance quickly, then spend the real time on "hello".upper().

Before you walk in

  1. Make them copy-paste first. Write Manager by duplicating the whole of Employee. It is obviously wrong and they will say so — inheritance then arrives as the fix for a mess they made.
  2. Stop at one parent and one child. No multiple inheritance, no super() chains three deep, no abstract classes. One override is enough to make the point.
  3. The second half is the real session. Budget 25 minutes for the dot. It reframes six weeks of typing and it is the thing they will remember from this module.
  4. Use type() relentlessly in that half. type("hello") is str; str is a class; .upper() is one of its methods. Each step is one line and they can run every one.
  5. Close the Python block properly. This is session 27 of core Python. Name what they have, and say plainly that from tomorrow everything is libraries.

Understand this yourself first

Two halves. The first is small. The second is the one worth preparing.

Part one · inheritance, kept small
The problem it solves

A manager is an employee — same name, same department, same salary, same raise rule — plus a team size. Writing a separate Manager class means copying all of Employee and adding one line, and then maintaining both forever.

The one line that does it

class Manager(Employee):. The brackets mean “start from this one”. Every attribute and method of Employee is now available on a Manager without being written again.

parent The class being inherited from. Employee.
child The class doing the inheriting. Manager.
override Writing a method the parent already has, to replace it for the child.
Calling the parent's __init__

The child's __init__ needs to set up the parent's fields too, and the plain way to say that is Employee.__init__(self, name, salary).

Do not teach super() today. It is the more common style and you should mention the word exists, but explaining why it is better needs the method resolution order, which is a rabbit hole. The explicit Employee.__init__(...) form reads exactly like what it does.
Part two · the dot, and why this is the real session
They have been using objects since week two

Every one of these is a method call on an object, and not one of them has ever been described that way:

"hello".upper() a str object, a str method
nums.append(5) a list object, a list method
line.strip() a str object again
f.readlines() a file object, a file method
e1.raise_pay(10) their own object, their own method

The last line is the point. The thing they built yesterday has exactly the same shape as everything Python has been handing them for six weeks.

The chain to walk, one line at a time

type("hello") says str. str is a class, written by somebody else. "hello" is an object made from it. .upper() is one of its methods. Nothing new — just a name for what was already happening.

The dot means “belonging to this object”. Six weeks of typing, explained in one sentence, and it is worth the twenty-five minutes.

The session, minute by minute

Everything in a speech box is meant to be said more or less as written. Everything in a grey box is a direction for you, not words to say.

0 – 16

Copy and paste it first

Let them build the mess, so the fix is a relief rather than a rule.

Yesterday you built an Employee. Today the company wants managers as well.

A manager is an employee. Same name, same department, same salary, same raise rule. The only extra thing is how many people they manage.

So go ahead and write me a Manager class.

Let them actually do it. They will copy the Employee class and add a line. That is exactly what you want.
What everybody writes
class Manager:

    def __init__(self, name, salary, team_size):
        self.name      = name
        self.salary    = salary
        self.team_size = team_size

    def details(self):
        print(self.name, "earns", self.salary)

    def raise_pay(self, percent):
        self.salary = self.salary + (self.salary * percent / 100)
“How much of that did you type fresh, and how much did you copy?”
Almost all copied. details and raise_pay are identical to Employee, word for word. Only team_size is new.

Nearly all of that is a copy. And copies are a problem.

Next month the company changes how a raise is calculated. You go and fix it in Employee. Do you remember to fix it in Manager too?

And when there are five kinds of employee, do you fix it in all five?

You do not. One of them gets missed, and from then on managers are paid by a different rule than everybody else — and nothing crashes to tell you.

16 – 34

Start from the other one instead

One line of new syntax. Then prove the child really got everything.

The whole of Manager, properly
class Employee:

    def __init__(self, name, salary):
        self.name   = name
        self.salary = salary

    def details(self):
        print(self.name, "earns", self.salary)


class Manager(Employee):

    def __init__(self, name, salary, team_size):
        Employee.__init__(self, name, salary)
        self.team_size = team_size

Look at the brackets. class Manager(Employee).

That means: start from Employee, and add to it. Everything Employee has, Manager now has too, without being written again.

Employee is the parent. Manager is the child.

And inside the child's __init__, that first line calls the parent's __init__ to do the name and salary, then we add the one new thing.

Prove it got everything
e = Employee("Ravi", 48000)
m = Manager("Asha", 95000, 6)

e.details()
m.details()

print()
print("m.name     :", m.name)
print("m.team_size:", m.team_size)
Ravi earns 48000 Asha earns 95000 m.name : Asha m.team_size: 6
“I never wrote a details method inside Manager. So why does m.details() work?”
Because Manager inherited it. Python looked on Manager, did not find it, looked at the parent, and found it there. Zero lines copied.

There is no details in Manager. Python went looking, did not find it, went up to Employee, and used that one.

So if we change details in Employee tomorrow, Manager changes too. Automatically. That is the entire point.

34 – 46

When the child needs to be different

Override. One method, and then stop.

Inheriting is useful when the child wants the same behaviour. What if it wants something different?

A manager's details should mention the team. So we write details again, inside Manager.

Write it again in the child
class Manager(Employee):

    def __init__(self, name, salary, team_size):
        Employee.__init__(self, name, salary)
        self.team_size = team_size

    def details(self):
        print(self.name, "earns", self.salary,
              "and manages", self.team_size, "people")
Run both again
e = Employee("Ravi", 48000)
m = Manager("Asha", 95000, 6)

e.details()
m.details()
Ravi earns 48000 Asha earns 95000 and manages 6 people

Same call — details() on both — and two different results.

Python looks on Manager first. It finds a details there now, so it uses that one and never goes up to the parent.

That is called overriding. The child's version wins.

On the board
  class Manager(Employee):     <- start from Employee

  PARENT     Employee      the one being inherited from
  CHILD      Manager       the one doing the inheriting
  OVERRIDE   writing a method the parent already has,
             so the child's version wins

  python looks on the CHILD first. then the parent.
Somebody will have read about super(). Say it exists, say it is the more common way to write that first line, and say we are using the explicit Employee.__init__(self, ...) form today because it reads like exactly what it does. Then move on — explaining why super() is better needs the method resolution order, and that is a rabbit hole.
46 – 72

Now the thing you have been doing since week two

The real session. Twenty-five minutes, one line at a time.

Slow down here. This is the part that reframes the whole module and it should not feel rushed.

Put the classes aside. I want to show you something about code you wrote weeks ago.

Type this.

Something from week two
text = "hello"
print(text.upper())
HELLO

You have typed that, or something like it, a hundred times.

Now I want you to look at the shape of it. A thing, then a dot, then a word with brackets.

Where else have you seen that shape?

Put these four on the board and ask what they have in common.
text.upper() · nums.append(5) · line.strip() · e1.raise_pay(10)

All four are a thing, a dot, and something it can do. And the last one they wrote themselves yesterday.

The last one is yours. You built that yesterday.

And it has exactly the same shape as the other three, which Python gave you.

So let us find out what the other three actually are.

One line at a time. Run each one.
text = "hello"
print(type(text))
<class 'str'>
Stop on that output. The word they need is sitting in it.
“Read that out. What is the first word inside the brackets?”
class. It has been saying that every time they have ever used type(), for six weeks, and nobody could read it until today.

Class.

Python has been telling you this since the first week. Every time you ran type(), it said class, and it meant nothing to you.

So: str is a class. Somebody wrote it, the same way you wrote Employee yesterday.

"hello" is an object made from that class — the same way Asha was an object made from Employee.

And .upper() is one of its methods.

Check the others
nums = [3, 1, 2]
print(type(nums))

e1 = Employee("Asha", 72000)
print(type(e1))
<class 'list'> <class '__main__.Employee'>

list is a class. Employee is a class.

One of them was written by the people who made Python. The other one you wrote yesterday afternoon.

Python does not treat them differently.

On the board — the whole thing, side by side
  text.upper()         text is a str OBJECT
                       upper is a METHOD of the str class
                       somebody else wrote that class

  nums.append(5)       nums is a list OBJECT
                       append is a METHOD of the list class

  f.readlines()        f is a file OBJECT
                       readlines is a METHOD of the file class

  e1.raise_pay(10)     e1 is an Employee OBJECT
                       raise_pay is a METHOD of YOUR class


  THE DOT MEANS "BELONGING TO THIS OBJECT".
  that is all it has ever meant.
You have been using objects since the second week of this course. Nobody told you, because there was no point until you had built one yourself.

Every library you are about to meet is made of classes like the one you wrote yesterday. That is why we spent two days on this.

And one last thing, which is practical.

The reason text.upper() works and nums.upper() does not is that upper belongs to the str class, and a list is a different class with a different set of methods.

So when you get AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'upper' — and you will — that is Python saying: that method does not belong to this kind of thing.

See the error on purpose
nums = [3, 1, 2]
print(nums.upper())
AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'upper'

Read it in your new vocabulary. A list object has no method called upper. Because upper lives on str, not on list.

That error used to be noise. It is now a sentence you can read.

That is core Python finished. Twenty-seven sessions.

Let me tell you what you actually have, because you have been looking at it one piece at a time.

You can store data — lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries, and now your own classes.

You can control what runs — if, for, while, break, continue.

You can package work up — functions, arguments, lambda, map, filter, reduce, recursion.

You can handle text — slicing, string methods, formatting, and regular expressions.

Ask them these before they leave

Ten questions with the answer under each. Questions 6 to 10 are the ones that matter today.

What does class Manager(Employee): mean?
Start from Employee and add to it. Manager gets everything Employee has without it being written again.
Which is the parent and which is the child?
Employee is the parent — the one being inherited from. Manager is the child — the one doing the inheriting.
I never wrote details inside Manager. Why does m.details() work?
Python looked on Manager, did not find it, went up to the parent and found it there.
What is overriding?
Writing a method the parent already has, inside the child, so the child's version wins. Python checks the child first and never goes up.
Why is copying the parent's code into the child a bad idea?
Because when the rule changes you have to remember every copy. One gets missed, and nothing crashes to tell you — it just behaves differently from then on.
print(type("hello")) gives <class 'str'>. What is the important word in that?
class. str is a class that somebody else wrote, exactly like the Employee class you wrote yesterday.
So what is "hello", and what is .upper()?
"hello" is an object made from the str class. .upper() is one of its methods. Same as Asha being an Employee object with a raise_pay method.
What does the dot actually mean?
“Belonging to this object.” That is all it has ever meant.
Why does nums.upper() fail when text.upper() works?
Because upper belongs to the str class, and a list is a different class with a different set of methods.
Read this out properly: AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'upper'
A list object has no method called upper. That error used to be noise. Now it is a sentence you can read.

Questions you will get

“What is super()? I have seen it.”

“It is the more common way to write that first line — super().__init__(name, salary) instead of naming the parent. Both work. We used the explicit form because it reads like exactly what it does. Use super() once you are comfortable.”

“Can a class inherit from two parents?”

“Yes, and it gets complicated fast — Python needs rules for which parent wins when both have the same method. It is real, it has a name, and you will not need it. One parent covers essentially everything you will write.”

“How deep can inheritance go?”

“As deep as you like, and that is usually a warning sign. If you find yourself four levels down trying to work out where a method came from, the design has gone wrong. One level is almost always enough.”

“So is everything in Python an object?”

“Yes — strings, lists, dictionaries, numbers, even functions. That is why the dot appears everywhere. It is one idea used consistently, which is a large part of why Python is pleasant to learn.”

“Can I see all the methods a thing has?”

“dir(str) lists them, and most editors show you the same list when you type the dot. That autocomplete popup you have been using for six weeks — that is the class telling you what its methods are.”

“Will we write classes as analysts?”

“Rarely. But you will use them every single day, because every library is made of them. Knowing what a class is turns a library from magic into something you can reason about, and that is worth two sessions.”

August B3 Python day 28 · 90 minutes · full script · opens the library block

The First
Library

One line tells the whole story: [100, 200, 300] * 2 gives you six numbers, and np.array([100, 200, 300]) * 2 gives you three doubled ones. Everything else follows from that.

* 2two different answers
~50xfaster, on a million
0loops written
1type per array

Open on * 2 and nothing else

Do not open with “NumPy is a library for numerical computing”. Open by multiplying a list by two and an array by two, side by side, and letting them read the two outputs. That one contrast is the entire reason NumPy exists, and it needs no vocabulary at all.

Before you walk in

  1. Install NumPy before the session. pip install numpy on sixty laptops on college wifi will eat twenty minutes. Tell them the day before, and have a plan for the three who did not.
  2. The first thing on screen is * 2, twice. No definition, no history, no “NumPy stands for”. Show the two outputs and ask what happened.
  3. Make them write the loop before you remove it. They should see their own five-line loop collapse to arr * 2. Showing the short version first wastes the moment.
  4. Time the million-number comparison live. Not a slide with a number on it — run it in front of them and let the first one visibly take a moment. The exact multiple varies by machine; say “about fifty times”.
  5. Say plainly that this is the foundation, not the destination. They are learning NumPy because Pandas is built on it. Nobody becomes an analyst by writing raw NumPy all day.

Understand this yourself first

Two ideas: what an array does differently, and why it is faster. The second one has a real answer — do not hand-wave it.

Part one · the one behaviour that changes everything
Operations apply to every element

On a list, * means repeat. On an array it means multiply each element. Same symbol, completely different meaning, and the array version is what people actually want nine times out of ten.

This has a name — element-wise — and it extends to everything: arr + 50, a + b, a * b, a > 150.

Every one of those replaces a for loop they would otherwise have written. That is the offer: you stop writing loops for arithmetic.
Boolean arrays, and why they matter later

a > 150 returns an array of True and False, one per element. Feed that back in as a[a > 150] and you get only the matching values.

Worth showing today even though it looks strange, because it is exactly how Pandas filtering works. df[df.salary > 50000] is this idea, unchanged.

Part two · why it is faster, honestly
Two real reasons, both teachable
one type, packed together A list can hold anything, so each item is a separate object scattered in memory with a label saying what it is. An array is one type only, stored in a single continuous block.
the loop is not in Python arr * 2 still loops — but the loop runs in C, underneath, not line by line in Python.

That is enough. Do not go further into vectorisation or SIMD; it does not change anything they will do.

The honest size of the win

On a million numbers, roughly fifty times on a typical laptop. It varies, so run it live rather than quoting a figure. On ten numbers it is slower than a list, because building the array costs more than the work saved — worth admitting if asked.

The cost: one type only

np.array([1, 2, 3.0]) turns everything into floats. A list would have kept them as they were. That is the trade: arrays give up flexibility to get speed, and for columns of numbers that is exactly the right trade.

The session, minute by minute

Everything in a speech box is meant to be said more or less as written. Everything in a grey box is a direction for you, not words to say.

0 – 16

Double every number in this list

Their loop first. Then the one line that replaces it.

Yesterday I said everything from here is libraries. Here is the first one, and I am going to show you what it does before I tell you what it is.

Three prices. I want all of them doubled. Write it.

Everyone writes this
prices = [100, 200, 300]

doubled = []
for p in prices:
    doubled.append(p * 2)

print(doubled)
[200, 400, 600]

Correct. Five lines, and you could write it in your sleep by now.

Now somebody will have wondered this at some point — why not just multiply the list?

Try the obvious thing
print(prices * 2)
[100, 200, 300, 100, 200, 300]
“What did that do?”
It repeated the list twice. Six items, none of them doubled. For a list, * 2 means “give me two of these”.

It gave you the list twice over. For a list, star two means repeat, not multiply.

Which is reasonable. But it is almost never what you want when the list is full of numbers.

So, the library.

Type this
import numpy as np

arr = np.array([100, 200, 300])

print(arr)
print(arr * 2)
[100 200 300] [200 400 600]
Put the two results on the board together and stop. This is the whole session in two lines.
On the board
  list   * 2   ->  [100, 200, 300, 100, 200, 300]     repeated
  array  * 2   ->  [200 400 600]                      DOUBLED

Same symbol. Two completely different meanings.

On an array, an operation happens to every element. And that replaced your five-line loop with one line.

That is the whole reason this library exists. Everything else today follows from it.

Two small things about the code. import numpy as np — the nickname again, same as plt and pd. Everybody writes np.

And np.array(...) takes a list and gives you back an array. Notice when you print it there are no commas. That is how you can tell at a glance which one you are looking at.

16 – 34

Everything works that way

Five one-liners, each replacing a loop they can picture.

It is not just multiply. Every operation behaves like that.

Type all of these
a = np.array([100, 200, 300])
b = np.array([10, 20, 30])

print("a + 50 :", a + 50)
print("a + b  :", a + b)
print("a * b  :", a * b)
print("a / 10 :", a / 10)
a + 50 : [150 250 350] a + b : [110 220 330] a * b : [1000 4000 9000] a / 10 : [10. 20. 30.]

a + 50 added fifty to every one. a + b matched them up in pairs — first with first, second with second.

Every one of those is a for loop you did not have to write.

And there is a word for this, which you will see in documentation. It is called element-wise. It means exactly what you just watched: the operation happens to each element separately.

Expect: “why does a / 10 have dots in it?” Because dividing produces decimals, so NumPy switched the whole array to floats. An array is one type all the way through — it cannot have some integers and some decimals. That is the next block.
Now the comparison one. It looks strange and it is the most important thing today after the first slide, because Pandas filtering is this exact idea.
Compare a whole array at once
print(a > 150)
[False True True]
“I asked one question and got three answers. Why three?”
Element-wise again. It asked the question of every element — is 100 more than 150? No. Is 200? Yes. Is 300? Yes. One True or False per item.

Three answers, one per element. False, True, True.

Now the part that looks like a trick. Take that array of True and False, and put it back inside the square brackets.

Watch
print(a[a > 150])
[200 300]

Only the ones where the answer was True.

Read it out loud in the order it happens. a > 150 gives False, True, True. Then a[...] keeps the positions that said True.

I want you to remember this one, because in a few weeks you will write df[df.salary > 50000] to filter a table of employees — and that is this, exactly, with a bigger thing in front of it.

Condition in the brackets. It looks odd today and it is the single most used pattern in the whole of data analysis. Everything you filter from here on is this shape.
34 – 52

Now do it a million times

Run the timing live. Let the slow one be visibly slow.

Three numbers is a bad test. One line or five lines, neither takes any time.

So let us do a million.

Type this — we will run it in two halves
import numpy as np
import time

n = 1000000

# --- the way you already know ---
py_list = list(range(n))

start = time.time()
result = []
for x in py_list:
    result.append(x * 2)
list_time = time.time() - start

print("python loop:", round(list_time, 3), "seconds")
python loop: 0.069 seconds

time.time() gives you the clock. Take it before, take it after, subtract. That is all the timing is.

Now the same million numbers, the other way.

The array version
np_arr = np.arange(n)

start = time.time()
result2 = np_arr * 2
numpy_time = time.time() - start

print("numpy      :", round(numpy_time, 4), "seconds")
print("numpy is about", round(list_time / numpy_time), "times faster")
numpy : 0.0014 seconds numpy is about 51 times faster
The exact number will differ on your machine and theirs. Anywhere from about twenty to a hundred. Say “about fifty times” and do not promise a figure — the point is the order of magnitude, not the digit.

np.arange is the array version of range — same idea, gives you an array instead of a list.

And one line, roughly fifty times faster.

Now I want to tell you why, because there are two real reasons and neither is magic.

On the board — why it is faster
  1. ONE TYPE, PACKED TOGETHER

     a list can hold anything, so every item is a separate
     object sitting somewhere in memory with a label on it.
     an array is all one type, in one solid block.
     the computer can go straight down it.

  2. THE LOOP IS NOT IN PYTHON

     arr * 2 still loops. but that loop runs underneath,
     in C, not line by line in python.

  you did not stop looping. you stopped looping SLOWLY.

That last line matters. The loop did not disappear. It moved somewhere faster.

“So should I always use NumPy?”
No, and be honest about it. On ten numbers a list is faster, because building the array costs more than the work it saves. NumPy wins when there is a lot of data, and for columns of numbers. For a shopping list of strings, use a list.
52 – 68

What it costs you

One type only. Show the trade honestly.

Nothing is free. Here is what you give up.

A list will hold anything
mixed = [1, "two", 3.0, True]
print(mixed)
[1, 'two', 3.0, True]
An array will not
print(np.array([1, 2, 3]))
print(np.array([1, 2, 3.0]))
[1 2 3] [1. 2. 3.]
“I gave it two whole numbers and one decimal. What came back?”
Three decimals. It converted the lot. An array is one type all the way through, so it picked the type that could hold everything.

One decimal in, and all three came out as decimals. The array cannot hold a mix, so it picked the type that fits everybody.

There is a word for “what type is in here”, and you will see it constantly.

dtype
print(np.array([1, 2, 3]).dtype)
print(np.array([1, 2, 3.0]).dtype)
int64 float64

dtype. Data type. int64 for whole numbers, float64 for decimals.

You will see that word a lot from here on, and now you know what it is telling you.

The trade, in one line: an array gives up being able to hold anything, in exchange for being fast. For a column of numbers — which is what analysis is made of — that is exactly the right trade.
68 – 82

Summarising a whole array

The handful of functions they will actually use, on numbers they know.

Last piece. Once you have an array, there are ready-made ways to summarise it.

And I am going to use a list of salaries you have seen before.

Yesterday's salaries, as an array
salaries = np.array([18000, 22000, 25000, 31000, 35000,
                     42000, 48000, 55000, 60000, 72000])

print("how many :", len(salaries))
print("total    :", salaries.sum())
print("average  :", salaries.mean())
print("lowest   :", salaries.min())
print("highest  :", salaries.max())
how many : 10 total : 408000 average : 40800.0 lowest : 18000 highest : 72000

Four lakh eight thousand. The same total you got on Tuesday with a loop and a running variable.

And look at the shape of those calls. salaries.sum(). A thing, a dot, something it can do.

You know exactly what that is now. salaries is an object, and sum is a method of the array class. Same as yesterday.

Put it together with the filtering
high = salaries[salaries > 40000]

print("earning over 40000:", high)
print("how many          :", len(high))
print("their average     :", high.mean())
earning over 40000: [42000 48000 55000 60000 72000] how many : 5 their average : 55400.0

Filter, then summarise. Two lines, no loops anywhere.

On Tuesday that would have been a loop with an if inside it and three variables to keep track of.

82 – 90

Practice, and where this is going

Their turn
# 1. make an array of the ten marks from last week
#    [72, 0, 65, 88, 0, 91, 54, 77, 0, 60]
#    print its sum, mean, min and max

# 2. use a condition in the brackets to get only the marks
#    above 0, then take the mean of those.
#    you should get 72.43 - the same answer as last week,
#    with no loop and no continue.

# 3. add 5 bonus marks to everybody in one line

# 4. what is the dtype of np.array([1, 2, "three"]) ?
#    guess first, then run it.
Question 2 is the one to land on. It is last week's absentee problem solved with no loop, no if and no continue — and it gives the identical answer, 72.43. Let them get there and then point it out.

Question 4 surprises people: everything becomes a string, dtype <U21. The array picked the only type that could hold all three.
The four lines. If everything else goes, keep these.
1.  list  * 2  ->  REPEATS the list
    array * 2  ->  DOUBLES every element
    that one difference is why numpy exists.

2.  ELEMENT-WISE: the operation happens to every item.
    a + 50,  a + b,  a * b,  a > 150   - no loops.

3.  a[a > 150]   condition inside the brackets.
    remember this one. all filtering from here looks like it.

4.  an array is ONE TYPE all the way through  (.dtype)
    it gives up flexibility to get speed.
    ~50x faster on a million numbers. slower on ten.

Last thing, and it is about where this goes.

You are not learning NumPy because you will spend your career writing NumPy. You will not.

You are learning it because the thing you will use every day is built on top of it. It is called Pandas, and it takes everything you saw today and gives it column names.

Every condition in brackets, every dtype, every .mean() — all of it comes back, with labels on.

The session, as a run sheet

Everything in order. Six steps, every code block, every board item written out. If you lose your place, this page alone is enough.

list * 2 → repeated · array * 2 → DOUBLED

That one contrast is the whole session. Also: np is the universal nickname, and printed arrays have no commas — that is how you tell them apart.

Practice, and where this goes

# 1. array of [72,0,65,88,0,91,54,77,0,60] - sum/mean/min/max
