Summary — every line from today

15 functions

Put this on screen in the last two minutes, or paste it into a cell and let them keep it. Every command from the session, in order, with what it does.

import numpy as np
b = np.array([15, 8, 42, 4, 23])
a = np.array([[10,20,30],[40,50,60]])

# ---- FILTERING: the most transferable idea in NumPy ----
b > 20                       # [F F T F T]        a MASK, one answer per element
b[b > 20]                    # [42 23]            keep only the Trues
b[(b > 10) & (b < 40)]       # [15 23]            & = and,  BRACKETS on each
b[(b < 10) | (b > 40)]       # [8 42 4]           | = or
b[~(b > 20)]                 # [15 8 4]           ~ = not
# b[(b>10) and (b<40)]       # ValueError         'and' expects ONE true/false
(b > 20).sum()               # 2                  True counts as 1
(b > 20).mean()              # 0.4                the PROPORTION, i.e. 40%
(b > 40).any()               # True               is any True?
(b > 40).all()               # False              are all True?

# ---- np.where: replace instead of remove ----
np.where(b > 20, "hi", "lo")  # ['lo','lo','hi','lo','hi']   vectorised if-else
np.where(b > 20, b, 0)        # [0 0 42 0 23]     keep value or zero it

# ---- SORTING ----
np.sort(b)                   # [4 8 15 23 42]     a sorted COPY
np.argsort(b)                # [3 1 0 4 2]        the POSITIONS that would sort
b[np.argsort(b)]             # sorted             use to reorder a second array

# ---- RESHAPING: element count must be preserved ----
m = np.arange(1, 13)         # 12 elements
m.reshape(3, 4)              # 3 rows, 4 cols
m.reshape(4, -1)             # -1 = "work it out" -> 3 columns
m.reshape(3, 4).flatten()    # back to 1-D, always a COPY
a.T                          # transpose, (2,3) -> (3,2), no brackets

# ---- JOINING ----
np.vstack([x, y])            # stack rows        v = vertical
np.hstack([x, y])            # end to end        h = horizontal
np.concatenate([a, a], axis=0)   # general form, you pick the direction
np.unique(np.array([3,1,3,2,1])) # [1 2 3]       distinct values, sorted

Pandas day 1 · merged class · 90 minutes · 23 functions

Why Pandas exists,
and getting at your data

They already met read_csv, head, info and describe in statistics day 1. So this session starts with why the library was built at all, revises what they know in twelve fast minutes, then goes properly into selecting and filtering.

90minutes
23functions
12min revision
201rows

The one idea today has to land

Pandas exists because real data is messy in ways NumPy cannot handle. Mixed types in one table, missing values, and names instead of positions. Everything else today is a consequence of those three.

Before you walk in

  1. Check your file path. Every example here uses pd.read_csv('../employees.csv') because it was run from a subfolder. Change it to match where your notebook actually sits, or the first line fails in front of the room.
  2. Run the NumPy failure demo yourself first. It is the opening of the session and it has to work exactly as shown.
  3. Keep the revision block to twelve minutes. Ask, do not explain. The moment you start re-teaching describe() you have lost the session.
  4. Call back to N3 when you reach filtering. They already did boolean masks in NumPy. Saying so out loud saves you ten minutes and makes them feel ahead rather than behind.
0 – 15

Why Pandas came into existence

Do not define pandas. Show them the problem it solves. Fifteen minutes.

You have been using pandas for a week now. Today I want to answer a question nobody asked: why does this library exist at all?

You already know NumPy. NumPy is fast, it does maths on whole arrays, it is excellent. So why did somebody sit down and write a second library on top of it?

Let me show you, rather than tell you.

The problem NumPy cannot solve
Definition
NumPy arrays hold ONE type only. Real data does not.
How it works

Try to put a name and a salary into the same NumPy array and watch what happens.

Type this
import numpy as np a = np.array(['Rahul', 72000, 28]) print(a) print('dtype:', a.dtype) try: print(a[1] + 1000) except TypeError as err: print('ERROR:', err)
You get
['Rahul' '72000' '28'] dtype: <U21 ERROR: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
Watch out for
Everything silently became a string. The number is no longer a number.
What a DataFrame does instead
Definition
Each column keeps its own type.
How it works

The same data in pandas. Look at the dtypes.

Type this
d = pd.DataFrame({'name': ['Rahul'], 'salary': [72000], 'age': [28]}) print(d) print(d.dtypes) print(d['salary'][0] + 1000) # still a number
You get
name salary age 0 Rahul 72000 28 name object salary int64 age int64 dtype: object 73000
Missing values
Definition
NumPy has no real idea of a missing value. Pandas does.
How it works

Pandas uses NaN, and every function knows to skip it.

Type this
s = pd.Series([10, np.nan, 30]) print(s) print('mean skips the gap:', s.mean()) print('count skips it too:', s.count())
You get
0 10.0 1 NaN 2 30.0 dtype: float64 mean skips the gap: 20.0 count skips it too: 2
Watch out for
np.nan is a float, so a column with any missing value cannot be int.
Labels instead of positions
Definition
NumPy has positions only. Pandas has names.
How it works

This is why you can write df['salary'] instead of remembering it is column 10.

Type this
print(df['salary'].head(3).tolist()) print('column 10 is:', df.columns[10])
You get
[47764.0, 86052.0, 62990.0] column 10 is: salary

So that is the answer. NumPy was built for numbers — one type, no labels, no gaps. Real business data is none of those things. It has names and salaries and dates in the same table, it has blanks where somebody did not fill the form, and you need to say df['salary'] rather than remember it is column number ten.

A man called Wes McKinney was working at an investment firm in 2008, hit exactly these problems every day, and built pandas to fix them. The name comes from panel data, which is an economics term for tables measured over time.

Everything you learn today and tomorrow comes out of those three problems.

Put the three on the board and leave them there: mixed types · missing values · labels not positions.
15 – 27

Fast revision — ask, do not teach

They know these six. Twelve minutes, quiz format, no explaining.

Ask the question first, let somebody answer, then run the code. If you find yourself explaining, stop and move on. This block is to confirm, not to teach.
read_csv()
Definition
Loads a CSV file into a DataFrame.
How it works

They know this one. Run it and move on.

Type this
df = pd.read_csv('../employees.csv') print(df.shape)
You get
(201, 12)
head() / tail()
Definition
The first or last few rows.
How it works

Ask them what the default number is before you run it.

Type this
print(df.head(3))
You get
emp_id dept_id name department city education rating \ 0 1001 3 Rahul Sharma HR Hyderabad Masters Poor 1 1002 4 Karthik Kumar Marketing Bangalore Diploma Poor 2 1003 2 Karthik Reddy Tech Bangalore Masters Good experience age height_cm salary join_date 0 4 53.0 169.5 47764.0 2018-01-03 1 13 57.0 169.5 86052.0 2024-07-02 2 1 56.0 166.5 62990.0 2025-03-04
shape
Definition
Rows and columns as a pair.
How it works

Ask: how do you get just the row count?

Type this
print(df.shape) print(df.shape[0], 'rows')
You get
(201, 12) 201 rows
Watch out for
No brackets. df.shape() is an error.
info()
Definition
Column names, filled counts, and data types.
How it works

Ask them to spot which columns have missing values from this output alone.

Type this
df.info()
You get
<class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'> RangeIndex: 201 entries, 0 to 200 Data columns (total 12 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 emp_id 201 non-null int64 1 dept_id 201 non-null int64 2 name 201 non-null object 3 department 201 non-null object 4 city 201 non-null object 5 education 201 non-null object 6 rating 201 non-null object 7 experience 201 non-null int64 8 age 200 non-null float64 9 height_cm 201 non-null float64 10 salary 199 non-null float64 11 join_date 201 non-null object dtypes: float64(3), int64(3), object(6) memory usage: 19.0+ KB
Watch out for
The Non-Null Count is the part that matters.
describe()
Definition
Summary statistics for the number columns.
How it works

Ask why emp_id and dept_id appear here, and whether those numbers mean anything.

Type this
print(df[['age','experience','salary']].describe().round(1))
You get
age experience salary count 200.0 201.0 199.0 mean 38.2 7.8 95648.4 std 16.6 4.5 364031.9 min -4.0 0.0 33085.0 25% 28.0 4.0 59003.5 50% 37.0 8.0 68647.0 75% 47.0 12.0 80599.5 max 210.0 15.0 5200000.0
Watch out for
It averages ID columns. That is the day 1 statistics hook, not a feature.
columns / dtypes
Definition
The column names and their types.
How it works

object means text.

Type this
print(list(df.columns)) print(df.dtypes.head(4))
You get
['emp_id', 'dept_id', 'name', 'department', 'city', 'education', 'rating', 'experience', 'age', 'height_cm', 'salary', 'join_date'] emp_id int64 dept_id int64 name object department object dtype: object
Close the block with this
“Everything so far tells you what is in the file. Nothing so far lets you get a specific piece of it out. That is the rest of today.”
27 – 55

Series, DataFrames, and selecting

The distinction most students never actually learn. Twenty-eight minutes.

1. pd.Series()
Definition
A Series is ONE column. A DataFrame is many Series side by side.
How it works

Most students use DataFrames without knowing this. Show it directly.

Type this
s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30]) print(s) print(type(df['salary'])) print(type(df[['salary']]))
You get
0 10 1 20 2 30 dtype: int64 <class 'pandas.core.series.Series'> <class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'>
Watch out for
df['x'] gives a Series. df[['x']] gives a DataFrame. That is the only difference.
2. Selecting one column
Definition
Gets a single column as a Series.
How it works

One pair of brackets, name in quotes.

Type this
print(df['name'].head(3))
You get
0 Rahul Sharma 1 Karthik Kumar 2 Karthik Reddy Name: name, dtype: object
3. Selecting several columns
Definition
Gets a smaller table.
How it works

Two pairs of brackets. The inner one is a list.

Type this
print(df[['name','department','salary']].head(3))
You get
name department salary 0 Rahul Sharma HR 47764.0 1 Karthik Kumar Marketing 86052.0 2 Karthik Reddy Tech 62990.0
Watch out for
Forgetting the inner brackets is the most common error in this whole session.
4. loc[]
Definition
Selects by NAME - row labels and column names.
How it works

Write df.loc[rows, columns].

Type this
print(df.loc[0, 'name']) print(df.loc[0:2, ['name','salary']])
You get
Rahul Sharma name salary 0 Rahul Sharma 47764.0 1 Karthik Kumar 86052.0 2 Karthik Reddy 62990.0
Watch out for
loc INCLUDES the last row. 0:2 gives three rows.
5. iloc[]
Definition
Selects by POSITION - numbers only.
How it works

Write df.iloc[rows, columns].

Type this
print(df.iloc[0, 2]) print(df.iloc[0:2, 0:3])
You get
Rahul Sharma emp_id dept_id name 0 1001 3 Rahul Sharma 1 1002 4 Karthik Kumar
Watch out for
iloc EXCLUDES the last position. 0:2 gives two rows.
6. at[] and iat[]
Definition
Gets one single cell. Faster than loc for one value.
How it works

at uses names, iat uses numbers.

Type this
print(df.at[0, 'name']) print(df.iat[0, 2])
You get
Rahul Sharma Rahul Sharma
55 – 85

Filtering rows

The heart of the session. Thirty minutes.

Now, before we start — you have already done this. In NumPy, session three, we wrote a[a > 20], and I told you the idea would come back.

It is back. Same idea, same syntax, on a whole table instead of one array.

7. Boolean filtering
Definition
Keeps only the rows where a condition is true.
How it works

Exactly the same idea as the NumPy masks they did in N3.

Type this
print(df['salary'] > 150000) high = df[df['salary'] > 150000] print(high[['name','salary']].head(3)) print('rows kept:', len(high))
You get
0 False 1 False 2 False 3 True 4 False ... 196 False 197 False 198 False 199 False 200 False Name: salary, Length: 201, dtype: bool name salary 3 Lakshmi Kumar 5200000.0 rows kept: 1
Watch out for
Use == to compare. A single = is assignment.
8. Two or more conditions
Definition
& means and. | means or.
How it works

Every condition needs its own brackets.

Type this
r = df[(df['department']=='Tech') & (df['salary']>100000)] print(r[['name','department','salary']].head(3)) print('rows:', len(r))
You get
name department salary 3 Lakshmi Kumar Tech 5200000.0 31 Kavya Rao Tech 105413.0 32 Ramesh Sharma Tech 103136.0 rows: 8
Watch out for
The words 'and' and 'or' do not work here. You must use & and |.
9. isin()
Definition
Keeps rows where the value is in a list.
How it works

Shorter than writing many | conditions.

Type this
r = df[df['city'].isin(['Bangalore','Chennai'])] print(r['city'].value_counts())
You get
city Chennai 61 Bangalore 54 Name: count, dtype: int64
10. between()
Definition
Keeps rows where a number is inside a range.
How it works

Both ends are included.

Type this
r = df[df['salary'].between(50000, 60000)] print('rows:', len(r)) print(r[['name','salary']].head(3))
You get
rows: 28 name salary 20 Anita Patel 59760.0 22 Rahul Rao 58186.0 35 Deepa Singh 55611.0
11. str.contains()
Definition
Keeps rows where text contains something.
How it works

You must write .str first because it works on text.

Type this
r = df[df['name'].str.contains('Kumar')] print('rows:', len(r)) print(r[['name','department']].head(3))
You get
rows: 25 name department 1 Karthik Kumar Marketing 3 Lakshmi Kumar Tech 7 Manoj Kumar HR
Watch out for
Case sensitive by default. Add case=False to ignore capitals.
12. query()
Definition
Filters using a readable sentence.
How it works

The condition goes inside quotes.

Type this
r = df.query('salary > 100000 and department == "Tech"') print(r[['name','salary']].head(3))
You get
name salary 3 Lakshmi Kumar 5200000.0 31 Kavya Rao 105413.0 32 Ramesh Sharma 103136.0
Watch out for
Inside query you CAN use the words and / or.
13. ~ for NOT
Definition
Flips a condition.
How it works

Put ~ in front of the whole thing.

Type this
r = df[~(df['department']=='Tech')] print(r['department'].value_counts())
You get
department Sales 65 HR 45 Marketing 42 Name: count, dtype: int64
85 – 90

Close

Five minutes. Set up tomorrow.

Today you learned to find things. Tomorrow you learn to fix and summarise them.

Because here is the thing about this file. Some rows have no salary. Somebody's age is minus four. There is a duplicate row in there. And I have not told you how to deal with any of it.

That is tomorrow, and it is the part that is actually your job.

End of session — put this on screen
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("employees.csv")     # the function you will use most

# ---- WHAT THE TWO OBJECTS ACTUALLY ARE ----
pd.Series([10, 20, 30])                        # ONE column, index 0,1,2 added for you
pd.Series([87, 92], index=["Rahul", "Priya"])  # your own row labels
pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Rahul"], "age": [28]}) # a TABLE - dict keys become columns
type(df["salary"])                             # Series      <- ONE pair of brackets
type(df[["salary"]])                           # DataFrame   <- TWO pairs

# ---- LOOK BEFORE YOU TOUCH ----
df.head(3)                    # first 3 rows        always run this first
df.tail(2)                    # last 2 rows
df.shape                      # (201, 12)           NO brackets after shape
df.info()                     # types + non-null    the counts are the point
df.describe()                 # count mean std min max quartiles
df.columns                    # the column names
df.dtypes                     # object = text, int64/float64 = numbers

# ---- PICK COLUMNS AND ROWS ----
df["name"]                    # one column  -> Series
df[["name", "salary"]]        # two columns -> DataFrame, inner list required
df.loc[0, "name"]             # by LABEL      0:2 gives THREE rows, end included
df.iloc[0, 2]                 # by POSITION   0:2 gives TWO rows, end excluded
df.at[0, "name"]              # one single cell, faster than loc

# ---- FILTER ROWS ----
df[df["salary"] > 150000]                            # one condition
df[(df["department"] == "Tech") & (df["salary"] > 100000)]   # & not "and"
df[df["city"].isin(["Bangalore", "Chennai"])]        # value is in a list
df[df["salary"].between(50000, 60000)]               # range, both ends included
df[df["name"].str.contains("Kumar")]                 # text search, needs .str
df.query("salary > 100000")                          # readable string form
df[~(df["department"] == "Tech")]                    # ~ means NOT

Why this session stops where it does

The merged class is paused until Monday. Tomorrow is B2 alone, so the goal is parity, not progress. Every function below was verified present in the B3 recordings:

D34 sorting and isnull · D35 missing values, dropna, fillna, mean/median/mode for filling · D36 duplicates, astype, new columns · D37 merge, concat, aggregate, group by.

Thirty further functions — value_counts, apply, map, pivot, dates, and the rest — are new to both batches. They are held for the merged class so everybody meets them together. That list is on the next card.

Before you walk in

  1. Do not teach beyond this list. Anything extra puts B2 ahead of B3 and you lose the merge on Monday. If you finish early, go deeper on groupby rather than adding functions.
  2. Fix your file path. Every example reads pd.read_csv('../employees.csv') because it was run from a subfolder.
  3. Know the planted flaws: two missing salaries, one missing age, one duplicate row, an age of minus four.
  4. The missing-values block is the heart of it. B3 spent a whole session on this (D35). Give it the time it deserves rather than rushing to reach merge.

The functions, in teaching order

Eight blocks. Every output is the real result of running that code against employees.csv.

Sorting 3

1. sort_values()
Definition
Arranges the rows in order of a column.
How it works

Smallest first by default.

Type this
print(df.sort_values('salary')[['name','salary']].head(3))
You get
name salary 150 Aditya Gupta 33085.0 169 Pooja Iyer 35118.0 192 Karthik Patel 36711.0
Watch out for
It returns a NEW table. The original df is unchanged unless you assign the result back.
2. sort_values() descending
Definition
Largest first.
How it works

Add ascending=False.

Type this
print(df.sort_values('salary', ascending=False)[['name','salary']].head(3))
You get
name salary 3 Lakshmi Kumar 5200000.0 130 Kavya Gupta 116894.0 159 Suresh Patel 106170.0
3. Sorting by two columns
Definition
Sort by the first, then break ties with the second.
How it works

Pass a list to both arguments to control each direction separately.

Type this
r = df.sort_values(['department','salary'], ascending=[True, False]) print(r[['department','name','salary']].head(5))
You get
department name salary 15 HR Ramesh Nair 80039.0 162 HR Sneha Gupta 75210.0 74 HR Sanjay Reddy 74401.0 119 HR Deepa Iyer 71760.0 18 HR Sanjay Nair 71154.0

Missing values 6

4. isnull() and notnull()
Definition
Marks each cell True or False depending on whether it is missing.
How it works

They are exact opposites. Use whichever reads more naturally.

Type this
print(df['age'].isnull().head(5)) print('any missing?', df['age'].isnull().any())
You get
0 False 1 False 2 False 3 False 4 False Name: age, dtype: bool any missing? True
Watch out for
You covered info() last class, which shows non-null counts. This is the same information as a value you can act on.
5. isnull().sum()
Definition
Counts the missing values in every column at once.
How it works

The single most useful line when you open a new file.

Type this
print(df.isnull().sum())
You get
emp_id 0 dept_id 0 name 0 department 0 city 0 .. experience 0 age 1 height_cm 0 salary 2 join_date 0 Length: 12, dtype: int64
Watch out for
Run it before anything else. Every decision after this depends on it.
6. dropna()
Definition
Removes rows that contain missing values.
How it works

Check the shape before and after, every time.

Type this
print('before :', df.shape) print('dropna() :', df.dropna().shape) print('salary only :', df.dropna(subset=['salary']).shape)
You get
before : (201, 12) dropna() : (198, 12) salary only : (199, 12)
Watch out for
Plain dropna() removes a row if ANY column is missing, which can delete far more than you intended.
7. dropna() on columns
Definition
Removes whole columns that contain gaps, rather than rows.
How it works

axis=1 switches it from rows to columns.

Type this
print('columns before:', df.shape[1]) print('columns after :', df.dropna(axis=1).shape[1])
You get
columns before: 12 columns after : 10
Watch out for
Rarely what you want, but worth showing so axis=1 makes sense.
8. fillna()
Definition
Fills the gaps with a value you choose.
How it works

A number, a label, or a calculation like the median.

Type this
print('missing before:', df['age'].isnull().sum()) filled = df['age'].fillna(df['age'].median()) print('missing after :', filled.isnull().sum()) print('median used :', df['age'].median())
You get
missing before: 1 missing after : 0 median used : 37.0
Watch out for
Use the median rather than the mean when the column has extreme values, because the mean gets dragged towards them.
9. fillna() on text
Definition
Fills a missing category with a label rather than a number.
How it works

Never leave a text gap as NaN if you are going to group by that column.

Type this
s = pd.Series(['Tech', None, 'Sales']) print(s.fillna('Unknown').tolist())
You get
['Tech', 'Unknown', 'Sales']

Duplicates 3

10. duplicated()
Definition
Marks rows that are exact copies of an earlier row.
How it works

Add .sum() to count them.

Type this
print('duplicate rows:', df.duplicated().sum())
You get
duplicate rows: 1
11. drop_duplicates()
Definition
Removes the repeated rows.
How it works

Always measure before and after so you know what you removed.

Type this
before = len(df) clean = df.drop_duplicates() print('removed:', before - len(clean))
You get
removed: 1
Watch out for
A cleaning step that silently deletes rows is dangerous. Report the number every time.
12. drop_duplicates() on chosen columns
Definition
Treats rows as duplicates based only on the columns you name.
How it works

subset= decides what counts as the same row.

Type this
print(df.drop_duplicates(subset=['department'])[['department','name']])
You get
department name 0 HR Rahul Sharma 1 Marketing Karthik Kumar 2 Tech Karthik Reddy 5 Sales Sneha Reddy
Watch out for
keep='first' is the default. keep='last' keeps the final one instead.

Data types 2

13. dtypes
Definition
The data type held in each column.
How it works

object means text. int64 and float64 are numbers.

Type this
print(df.dtypes)
You get
emp_id int64 dept_id int64 name object department object city object ... experience int64 age float64 height_cm float64 salary float64 join_date object Length: 12, dtype: object
Watch out for
A column of numbers showing as object means something non-numeric is hiding inside it.
14. astype()
Definition
Changes a column's data type.
How it works

Most often used to turn a number stored as text into a real number.

Type this
clean = df.dropna(subset=['age']).copy() clean['age'] = clean['age'].astype(int) print(clean['age'].head(3).tolist(), '|', clean['age'].dtype)
You get
[53, 57, 56] | int64
Watch out for
astype(int) fails while missing values are present, because NaN is a float. Clean the gaps first.

Changing the table 2

15. rename()
Definition
Changes column names.
How it works

Pass a dictionary of old name to new name.

Type this
r = df.rename(columns={'experience':'years_exp','department':'dept'}) print(list(r.columns))
You get
['emp_id', 'dept_id', 'name', 'dept', 'city', 'education', 'rating', 'years_exp', 'age', 'height_cm', 'salary', 'join_date']
Watch out for
Returns a new table. Assign it back or nothing changes.
16. Adding a new column
Definition
Creates a column from a calculation.
How it works

Assign to a new name in square brackets. The maths runs on the whole column at once.

Type this
d = df.copy() d['bonus'] = d['salary'] * 0.10 print(d[['name','salary','bonus']].head(3))
You get
name salary bonus 0 Rahul Sharma 47764.0 4776.4 1 Karthik Kumar 86052.0 8605.2 2 Karthik Reddy 62990.0 6299.0

Summary statistics 2

17. median() and mode()
Definition
The middle value, and the most common value.
How it works

Part revision. They already met the median as the 50% row of describe() — you called it “the middle value”. Now call it directly as a function. mode() is genuinely new, and is the only one of the three averages that works on text.

Type this
print('median salary :', df['salary'].median()) print('most common dept:', df['department'].mode()[0])
You get
median salary : 68647.0 most common dept: Sales
Watch out for
Neither was covered last class. mode() returns a Series because there can be more than one most-common value, hence the [0].
18. std() and var()
Definition
How spread out the values are.
How it works

Part revision. std already appeared in the describe() output in both classes. Calling it on its own is the new part. Variance is its square and is new.

Type this
print('std:', round(df['salary'].std())) print('var:', round(df['salary'].var()))
You get
std: 364032 var: 132519227501
Watch out for
The number here is huge because one person earns 52 lakh. That is the statistics day 3 conversation.

Grouping 5

19. groupby() with one summary
Definition
Splits the table into groups, then summarises each group.
How it works

Revision. You demonstrated this at the end of statistics day 1 — “finally you have something called group by, I will just show it to you”. It was rushed and nothing was built on it. Re-teach it slowly here: split, apply, combine. Everything after this block extends it.

Type this
print(df.groupby('department')['salary'].mean().round(0))
You get
department HR 56705.0 Marketing 73954.0 Sales 66535.0 Tech 189754.0 Name: salary, dtype: float64
20. groupby() with size() and count()
Definition
How many rows are in each group.
How it works

size() counts every row. count() skips missing values.

Type this
print(df.groupby('department').size()) print(df.groupby('department')['salary'].count())
You get
department HR 45 Marketing 42 Sales 65 Tech 49 dtype: int64 department HR 44 Marketing 42 Sales 65 Tech 48 Name: salary, dtype: int64
Watch out for
Where the two differ, that column has gaps in that group.
21. groupby() with agg()
Definition
Several summaries at once.
How it works

Pass a list of the summaries you want.

Type this
print(df.groupby('department')['salary'].agg(['count','mean','max']).round(0))
You get
count mean max department HR 44 56705.0 80039.0 Marketing 42 73954.0 106170.0 Sales 65 66535.0 93417.0 Tech 48 189754.0 5200000.0
22. agg() on different columns
Definition
A different summary for each column.
How it works

Pass a dictionary of column to function.

Type this
print(df.groupby('department').agg({'salary':'mean','experience':'max'}).round(0))
You get
salary experience department HR 56705.0 15 Marketing 73954.0 15 Sales 66535.0 15 Tech 189754.0 15
23. Grouping by two columns
Definition
Groups inside groups.
How it works

Pass a list of column names.

Type this
print(df.groupby(['department','city'])['salary'].mean().round(0).head(6))
You get
department city HR Bangalore 58425.0 Chennai 52352.0 Hyderabad 61062.0 Pune 55183.0 Marketing Bangalore 71691.0 Chennai 73025.0 Name: salary, dtype: float64

Joining tables 4

24. pd.concat()
Definition
Stacks tables on top of each other.
How it works

Use it when two files have the same columns.

Type this
a = df.head(2)[['name','department']] b = df.tail(2)[['name','department']] print(pd.concat([a, b]))
You get
name department 0 Rahul Sharma HR 1 Karthik Kumar Marketing 199 Kavya Singh Tech 200 Anita Patel Sales
25. pd.concat() side by side
Definition
Joins columns rather than rows.
How it works

axis=1 places tables next to each other, aligning on the index.

Type this
a = df[['name']].head(3) b = df[['salary']].head(3) print(pd.concat([a, b], axis=1))
You get
name salary 0 Rahul Sharma 47764.0 1 Karthik Kumar 86052.0 2 Karthik Reddy 62990.0
Watch out for
Alignment happens by index label, so mismatched indexes produce unexpected NaN rows.
26. pd.merge()
Definition
Joins two tables on a shared column. The same idea as a SQL join.
How it works

on= names the column they share.

Type this
emp = pd.DataFrame({'name':['Rahul','Priya'], 'dept_id':[1,2]}) dept = pd.DataFrame({'dept_id':[1,2], 'dept_name':['Tech','Sales']}) print(pd.merge(emp, dept, on='dept_id'))
You get
name dept_id dept_name 0 Rahul 1 Tech 1 Priya 2 Sales
27. merge() types
Definition
how= decides which rows survive the join.
How it works

inner keeps matches only. left keeps everything from the left table.

Type this
a = pd.DataFrame({'id':[1,2,3], 'x':['a','b','c']}) b = pd.DataFrame({'id':[2,3,4], 'y':['B','C','D']}) print(pd.merge(a,b,on='id',how='inner')) print(pd.merge(a,b,on='id',how='left'))
You get
id x y 0 2 b B 1 3 c C id x y 0 1 a NaN 1 2 b B 2 3 c C
Watch out for
inner is the default and it silently drops non-matching rows. Compare len() before and after, every time.
End of session — put this on screen
# ---- SORT ----
df.sort_values("salary")                        # smallest first, returns a NEW table
df.sort_values("salary", ascending=False)       # largest first
df.sort_values(["department", "salary"])        # tie-break with a second column

# ---- MISSING VALUES ----
df.isnull().sum()                       # gaps per column      RUN THIS FIRST
df["age"].isnull().any()                # is anything missing at all
df.dropna()                             # drop rows with ANY gap - check .shape
df.dropna(subset=["salary"])            # only look at one column
df.dropna(axis=1)                       # drop whole COLUMNS instead of rows
df["age"].fillna(df["age"].median())    # median, not mean, when skewed
df["department"].fillna("Unknown")      # label the gap in a text column

# ---- DUPLICATES ----
df.duplicated().sum()                   # how many repeated rows
df.drop_duplicates()                    # remove them - report the count
df.drop_duplicates(subset=["department"])      # duplicates on chosen columns only

# ---- TYPES AND COLUMNS ----
df.dtypes                               # object = text, int64/float64 = numbers
df["age"].astype(int)                   # fails while NaN is present - clean first
df.rename(columns={"experience": "years_exp"}) # new column names
df["bonus"] = df["salary"] * 0.10       # add a calculated column

# ---- SUMMARISE ----
df["salary"].median()                   # the honest middle
df["department"].mode()[0]              # the only average that works on text
df["salary"].std()                      # spread around the mean
df["salary"].var()                      # the square of the std

# ---- GROUP: split, apply, combine ----
df.groupby("department")["salary"].mean()              # one number per group
df.groupby("department").size()                        # rows per group
df.groupby("department")["salary"].agg(["count", "mean", "max"])
df.groupby("department").agg({"salary": "mean", "experience": "max"})
df.groupby(["department", "city"])["salary"].mean()    # groups inside groups

# ---- JOIN ----
pd.concat([a, b])                       # stack rows
pd.concat([a, b], axis=1)               # side by side, aligns on the index
pd.merge(emp, dept, on="dept_id")       # join on a shared column
pd.merge(a, b, on="id", how="left")     # keep every row from the left table

Verified absent from both batches

Checked against the seven B3 Pandas recordings (D31–D37) and both July B2 sessions. None of the functions below appears in any of them.

value_counts is the one to open with. B2 watched it fail at the 80-minute mark of their intro class — “still we are not able to get the count” — and B3 has never seen it at all. It is also the correct summary for every text column, so it earns its place first.

Before you walk in

  1. Nothing here is revision for anybody. Both batches meet all of it for the first time, so pace it as new material throughout.
  2. Open on value_counts. B2 saw it fail. Getting it working in the first two minutes closes that loop.
  3. Call back to .str when you reach .dt. B2 learned .str in their intro class. Same idea, different data type.
  4. Do not resolve the 2.32 at the end if statistics day 2 has not run yet.

The functions, in teaching order

Ten blocks. Every output is real.

Finish what was left hanging 5

1. value_counts()
Definition
Counts how many times each value appears in a column.
How it works

You reached this at the very end of the last class and it did not land. Start here and do it properly, because it is the correct summary for any text column.

Type this
print(df['department'].value_counts())
You get
department Sales 65 Tech 49 HR 45 Marketing 42 Name: count, dtype: int64
Watch out for
It sorts by count, not by any logical order. For the rating column that means Poor comes first because it is most common, not because it is lowest.
2. value_counts() as a share
Definition
The same counts expressed as proportions.
How it works

Add normalize=True. Multiply by 100 for percentages.

Type this
print(df['department'].value_counts(normalize=True).round(3))
You get
department Sales 0.323 Tech 0.244 HR 0.224 Marketing 0.209 Name: proportion, dtype: float64
3. sample()
Definition
Shows random rows instead of the first few.
How it works

Better than head() when the file is sorted, because the top rows may not be typical.

Type this
print(df[['name','department','salary']].sample(3, random_state=1))
You get
name department salary 97 Divya Gupta Sales 77675.0 117 Meena Singh Sales 62973.0 59 Divya Menon Tech 69104.0
Watch out for
random_state keeps the same rows each time you run it, which matters when demonstrating live.
4. query()
Definition
Filters using a readable sentence instead of brackets.
How it works

You taught bracket filtering last class. This is the same thing in a form that reads like English.

Type this
print(df.query('salary > 150000 and department == "Tech"')[['name','salary']].head(3))
You get
name salary 3 Lakshmi Kumar 5200000.0
Watch out for
Inside query you CAN use the words and / or, unlike bracket filtering where you must use & and |.
5. unique() and nunique()
Definition
unique() lists the distinct values. nunique() counts them.
How it works

Run these before grouping, to see what you are about to group into.

Type this
print(df['city'].unique()) print('distinct cities:', df['city'].nunique())
You get
['Hyderabad' 'Bangalore' 'Chennai' 'Pune'] distinct cities: 4
Watch out for
If a column has more distinct values than you expect, it is usually inconsistent text: trailing spaces or different capitalisation.

Sorting 2

6. nlargest() and nsmallest()
Definition
The top or bottom few rows directly.
How it works

Shorter than sorting the whole table and taking the head.

Type this
print(df.nlargest(3,'salary')[['name','salary']]) print(df.nsmallest(2,'salary')[['name','salary']])
You get
name salary 3 Lakshmi Kumar 5200000.0 130 Kavya Gupta 116894.0 159 Suresh Patel 106170.0 name salary 150 Aditya Gupta 33085.0 169 Pooja Iyer 35118.0
7. sort_index()
Definition
Sorts by the row labels instead of a column.
How it works

Useful to restore the original order after sorting by a value.

Type this
print(df.sort_values('salary').sort_index()[['name','salary']].head(3))
You get
name salary 0 Rahul Sharma 47764.0 1 Karthik Kumar 86052.0 2 Karthik Reddy 62990.0

Data types 1

8. pd.to_numeric()
Definition
Converts to numbers and can turn bad values into NaN instead of failing.
How it works

errors='coerce' is the difference from astype.

Type this
s = pd.Series(['100', '200', 'abc']) print(pd.to_numeric(s, errors='coerce').tolist())
You get
[100.0, 200.0, nan]
Watch out for
Useful, but check how many NaNs you created afterwards. You have just discarded data silently.

Changing the table 2

9. drop()
Definition
Removes columns or rows.
How it works

Say columns= or index= explicitly.

Type this
print(list(df.drop(columns=['height_cm','join_date']).columns)) print('rows after dropping 2:', df.drop(index=[0,1]).shape[0])
You get
['emp_id', 'dept_id', 'name', 'department', 'city', 'education', 'rating', 'experience', 'age', 'salary'] rows after dropping 2: 199
Watch out for
df.drop('x') on its own assumes you meant a row label, which is rarely what you want.
10. copy()
Definition
Makes a genuinely independent table.
How it works

Without it, two names point at the same data and changing one changes both.

Type this
a = df[['name','salary']] b = a.copy() b['salary'] = 0 print('original untouched:', a['salary'].head(2).tolist())
You get
original untouched: [47764.0, 86052.0]
Watch out for
This is the same reference behaviour as Python lists. Skipping copy() is how people quietly corrupt their source data.

Transforming values 6

11. apply()
Definition
Runs your own function on every value in a column.
How it works

Use it when there is no built-in function for the logic you need.

Type this
def band(s): if s > 100000: return 'High' if s > 60000: return 'Medium' return 'Low' d = df.dropna(subset=['salary']).copy() d['band'] = d['salary'].apply(band) print(d['band'].value_counts())
You get
band Medium 135 Low 54 High 10 Name: count, dtype: int64
Watch out for
Slower than built-in pandas operations. Reach for it only when nothing built in will do.
12. apply() with lambda
Definition
The same thing, written inline for short logic.
How it works

A lambda is a one-line function with no name.

Type this
d = df.dropna(subset=['salary']) print(d['salary'].apply(lambda x: round(x/1000)).head(5).tolist())
You get
[48, 86, 63, 5200, 63]
Watch out for
Drop the missing values first. round() on a NaN raises an error, and apply will not skip it for you.
13. map()
Definition
Replaces values using a dictionary.
How it works

The standard way to turn ordered words into numbers.

Type this
order = {'Poor':1, 'Average':2, 'Good':3, 'Excellent':4} print(df['rating'].map(order).head(6).tolist())
You get
[1, 1, 3, 4, 4, 1]
Watch out for
Anything missing from your dictionary silently becomes NaN. Check with isnull().sum() afterwards.
14. replace()
Definition
Swaps specific values for other values.
How it works

Simpler than map when you only want to change a few values and leave the rest alone.

Type this
print(df['department'].replace({'Tech':'Engineering'}).value_counts())
You get
department Sales 65 Engineering 49 HR 45 Marketing 42 Name: count, dtype: int64
Watch out for
Unlike map, anything you do not mention is left as it is rather than becoming NaN.
15. np.where()
Definition
Picks one of two values based on a condition.
How it works

Shorter than apply when there are only two outcomes.

Type this
d = df.copy() d['level'] = np.where(d['salary'] > 80000, 'Senior', 'Junior') print(d['level'].value_counts())
You get
level Junior 147 Senior 54 Name: count, dtype: int64
16. pd.cut()
Definition
Puts numbers into named bands.
How it works

You supply the cut points and the labels.

Type this
bands = pd.cut(df['salary'], bins=[0,60000,100000,10**9], labels=['Low','Medium','High']) print(bands.value_counts().sort_index())
You get
salary Low 54 Medium 135 High 10 Name: count, dtype: int64
Watch out for
This is how a ratio column becomes an ordinal one. You can always go down a scale, never up.

Summary statistics 3

17. quantile()
Definition
The value below which a given share of the data falls.
How it works

Revision, then extend. You explained quantiles from the 25/50/75 rows of describe() in both classes. What is new is asking for any cut point you like, not just the three describe() gives you.

Type this
print(df['salary'].quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75]).round(0).tolist())
You get
[59004.0, 68647.0, 80600.0]
18. corr()
Definition
How strongly two numeric columns move together.
How it works

Always between -1 and 1.

Type this
print(round(df['experience'].corr(df['salary']), 3))
You get
0.079
Watch out for
A near-zero answer does not always mean no relationship. One outlier can destroy it, which is statistics day 5.
19. Mean against median
Definition
Comparing the two tells you whether the data is skewed.
How it works

Put them side by side and let the gap speak.

Type this
print('mean :', round(df['salary'].mean())) print('median:', round(df['salary'].median())) print('gap :', round(df['salary'].mean() - df['salary'].median()))
You get
mean : 95648 median: 68647 gap : 27001
Watch out for
A large gap means extreme values. This one line sets up the whole of statistics day 3.

Grouping 2

20. reset_index()
Definition
Turns the group labels back into a normal column.
How it works

Use it so the result is a proper table you can select from again.

Type this
g = df.groupby('department')['salary'].mean().round(0).reset_index() print(g)
You get
department salary 0 HR 56705.0 1 Marketing 73954.0 2 Sales 66535.0 3 Tech 189754.0
Watch out for
Without this the department names are the index, not a column, and df['department'] will fail.
21. Sorting a grouped result
Definition
Ranking the groups rather than the rows.
How it works

Chain sort_values onto the grouped output.

Type this
print(df.groupby('department')['salary'].mean().round(0).sort_values(ascending=False))
You get
department Tech 189754.0 Marketing 73954.0 Sales 66535.0 HR 56705.0 Name: salary, dtype: float64

Reshaping 4

22. pivot_table()
Definition
Summarises data into a grid. The same idea as a pivot table in Excel.
How it works

index goes down the side, columns across the top.

Type this
print(pd.pivot_table(df, values='salary', index='department', columns='city', aggfunc='mean').round(0))
You get
city Bangalore Chennai Hyderabad Pune department HR 58425.0 52352.0 61062.0 55183.0 Marketing 71691.0 73025.0 76685.0 75701.0 Sales 59223.0 72631.0 66964.0 68694.0 Tech 88365.0 383893.0 84007.0 70859.0
23. crosstab()
Definition
Counts how often each combination appears.
How it works

A frequency table of two categorical columns.

Type this
print(pd.crosstab(df['department'], df['city']))
You get
city Bangalore Chennai Hyderabad Pune department HR 13 12 10 10 Marketing 10 15 7 10 Sales 18 16 19 12 Tech 13 18 12 6
24. melt()
Definition
Turns wide data into long data.
How it works

One row per observation instead of one column per measurement.

Type this
w = pd.DataFrame({'name':['Rahul','Priya'],'maths':[87,92],'science':[78,85]}) print(pd.melt(w, id_vars='name', var_name='subject', value_name='marks'))
You get
name subject marks 0 Rahul maths 87 1 Priya maths 92 2 Rahul science 78 3 Priya science 85
25. set_index() and reset_index()
Definition
Makes a column the row label, or puts it back.
How it works

Useful when you want to look rows up by name.

Type this
d = df.set_index('name') print(d.loc['Rahul Sharma', ['department','salary']].head(1)) print(d.reset_index().columns[0])
You get
department HR Name: Rahul Sharma, dtype: object name

Dates 3

26. pd.to_datetime()
Definition
Turns a text column into real dates.
How it works

Until you do this, a date column is just text and cannot be sorted or subtracted properly.

Type this
d = df.copy() d['join_date'] = pd.to_datetime(d['join_date']) print(d['join_date'].dtype) print(d['join_date'].min().date(), 'to', d['join_date'].max().date())
You get
datetime64[ns] 2015-01-19 to 2025-12-21
27. .dt accessor
Definition
Pulls the year, month or day out of a date column.
How it works

.dt is to dates what .str is to text. You used .str last class, so call back to it.

Type this
d = df.copy() d['join_date'] = pd.to_datetime(d['join_date']) print(d['join_date'].dt.year.head(3).tolist()) print(d['join_date'].dt.month.head(3).tolist()) print(d['join_date'].dt.day_name().head(2).tolist())
You get
[2018, 2024, 2025] [1, 7, 3] ['Wednesday', 'Tuesday']
Watch out for
This only works after to_datetime. On a text column it fails.
28. Grouping by year
Definition
Counting how many joined each year.
How it works

Combine .dt.year with groupby.

Type this
d = df.copy() d['join_date'] = pd.to_datetime(d['join_date']) print(d.groupby(d['join_date'].dt.year).size().tail(5))
You get
join_date 2021 24 2022 25 2023 17 2024 17 2025 19 dtype: int64

Saving your work 2

29. to_csv()
Definition
Saves the cleaned table back to a file.
How it works

index=False stops pandas adding an extra unnamed column.

Type this
clean = df.dropna(subset=['salary']).drop_duplicates() clean.head(2).to_csv('cleaned.csv', index=False) print(open('cleaned.csv').read())
You get
emp_id,dept_id,name,department,city,education,rating,experience,age,height_cm,salary,join_date 1001,3,Rahul Sharma,HR,Hyderabad,Masters,Poor,4,53.0,169.5,47764.0,2018-01-03 1002,4,Karthik Kumar,Marketing,Bangalore,Diploma,Poor,13,57.0,169.5,86052.0,2024-07-02
Watch out for
Forgetting index=False is the most common mistake here. Open the file and check.
30. The closing hook
Definition
Everything they now know, pointed at statistics.
How it works

Run this last and let it sit without explaining it.

Type this
print('average department id:', round(df['dept_id'].mean(), 2)) print('departments :', df['department'].unique())
You get
average department id: 2.32 departments : ['HR' 'Marketing' 'Tech' 'Sales']
Watch out for
Do not resolve it. That is the whole of statistics day 2.
End of session — put this on screen
# ---- THE TEXT-COLUMN SUMMARY ----
df["department"].value_counts()          # counts per category
df["department"].value_counts(normalize=True)   # as shares
df["city"].unique()                      # the distinct values
df["city"].nunique()                     # how many distinct
df.sample(3, random_state=1)             # random rows, not the top ones
df.query("salary > 150000")              # filtering as a readable sentence

# ---- MORE SORTING ----
df.nlargest(3, "salary")                 # top 3 without sorting everything
df.sort_index()                          # back to the original row order

# ---- CLEANING EXTRAS ----
pd.to_numeric(s, errors="coerce")        # bad values become NaN, not an error
df.drop(columns=["height_cm"])           # remove a column
df.copy()                                # a genuinely independent table

# ---- TRANSFORM VALUES ----
df["salary"].apply(band)                 # run your own function
df["salary"].apply(lambda x: x / 1000)   # same thing, written inline
df["rating"].map({"Poor": 1, "Good": 3}) # replace using a dictionary
df["department"].replace({"Tech": "IT"}) # swap some, leave the rest
np.where(df["salary"] > 80000, "Senior", "Junior")     # two outcomes
pd.cut(df["salary"], bins=[0, 60000, 10**9], labels=["Low", "High"])

# ---- MORE STATISTICS ----
df["salary"].quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75]) # the quartiles
df["experience"].corr(df["salary"])      # between -1 and 1
df["salary"].mean() - df["salary"].median()    # the gap = how skewed it is

# ---- GROUPING EXTRAS ----
df.groupby("department")["salary"].mean().reset_index()   # index back to a column
df.groupby("department")["salary"].mean().sort_values()   # rank the groups

# ---- RESHAPE ----
pd.pivot_table(df, values="salary", index="department", columns="city", aggfunc="mean")
pd.crosstab(df["department"], df["city"])      # frequency of each combination
pd.melt(w, id_vars="name")               # wide -> long
df.set_index("name")                     # look rows up by name

# ---- DATES ----
pd.to_datetime(df["join_date"])          # text -> real dates
df["join_date"].dt.year                  # .dt is to dates what .str is to text
df["join_date"].dt.day_name()            # the weekday

# ---- SAVE ----
df.to_csv("cleaned.csv", index=False)    # index=False or you get a junk column

df["dept_id"].mean()                     # 2.32  <- there is no department 2.32
